name: Genesis
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint (with Codex Alexandrinus where it differs), the Syriac, and the Vulgate. For Genesis 1 to 3 it was also checked against the Qumran fragments (4QGen-b, 4QGen-d, 4QGen-g, 4QGen-h, 4QGen-k), which agree closely with the Masoretic consonants. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve little of Genesis 4 to 11 and none of the ages in chapters 5 and 11, so those chapters rest on the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint, whose differences are given in the footnotes. For Genesis 12 to 50, every Septuagint reading cited in the footnotes was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation of the Septuagint. Readings of the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Dead Sea Scrolls, and other ancient versions are stated in general terms until they can be checked against the critical editions.

verses.text: In the beginning{a} God{b} created the heavens and the earth.{c}
Now the earth was formless and empty,{d} and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit{e} of God was hovering{f} over the surface of the waters.
Then God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
God saw the light, that it was good, and God separated between the light and the darkness.
God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning: day one.{g}
Then God said, “Let there be an expanse{h} in the middle of the waters, and let it separate between waters and waters.”
So God made the expanse, and he separated between the waters that were under the expanse and the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.{i}
God called the expanse Heavens. And there was evening and there was morning: a second day.
Then God said, “Let the waters under the heavens be gathered into one place,{j} and let the dry land appear.” And it was so.
God named the dry ground Earth, and the collected waters he named Seas. God saw that this was good.
Then God said, “Let the earth sprout green growth: plants that yield seed, and fruit trees that bear fruit according to their kind, with their seed in it, on the earth.” And it was so.
The earth brought forth green growth: plants that yield seed according to their kind, and trees that bear fruit with their seed in it, according to their kind. And God saw that it was good.
And there was evening and there was morning: a third day.
Then God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate between the day and the night, and let them serve as signs and for appointed times,{k} and for days and years.
Let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth.” And it was so.
God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night,{l} and also the stars.
God placed them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,
to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate between the light and the darkness. And God saw that it was good.
And there was evening and there was morning: a fourth day.
Then God said, “Let the waters swarm with teeming living creatures,{m} and let flying birds soar above the land, beneath the dome of the sky.”
So God created the huge sea monsters{n} and all the living creatures that glide and swarm in the waters, each by its own species, and every winged bird by its species. God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth.”
And there was evening and there was morning: a fifth day.
Then God said, “Let the land produce living creatures by their species: tame animals, crawling creatures, and wild beasts, each by its species.” And so it happened.
God made the wild beasts of the earth by their species, the tame animals by their species, and everything that crawls on the soil by its species. God saw that it was good.

Then God said, “Let us make humankind{o} in our image, to be like us. They will govern the fish in the sea, the birds in the sky, the tame animals, all the earth,{p} and every creature that crawls along the ground.”
So God created humankind in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.{q}

God blessed them, and God said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and bring it under control. Rule over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that creeps on the earth.”
Then God said, “See, I give you every plant that yields seed, across the whole face of the earth, and every tree whose fruit holds its seed. These will be your food.
To all the wild animals, to all the birds in the sky, and to every creature crawling on the earth that has the breath of life, I give every green plant for food.” And so it happened.
God saw everything that he had made, and look, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning: the sixth day.{r}

notes.text: Hebrew bereshit. It can also be read as the start of a longer sentence: “When God began to create the heavens and the earth, the earth was formless…” The Septuagint (en archē, “in the beginning”) supports the traditional reading kept here.

Hebrew Elohim. The word is plural in form, but here it takes a singular verb (bara, “he created”), so it names the one God. Elohim is a title, not a personal name; this translation renders it “God” when it refers to the true God, and keeps the personal name Yahweh where the Hebrew has it (see the note on 2:4 and Conventions).
“The heavens and the earth” pairs two opposites to mean everything that exists.
Hebrew tohu wabohu, a rhyming pair: “a waste and a void,” land not yet shaped or filled. Days 1 to 3 give it shape; days 4 to 6 fill it.
Hebrew ruach means spirit, wind, or breath. Some render “a wind from God” or “a mighty wind.”
The same verb describes an eagle hovering over its young in Deuteronomy 32:11.
Literally “one day.” Hebrew uses the number one here, not “first.” Days 2 to 5 have no article (“a second day”); day 6 has one (see 1:31).
Hebrew raqia, from a verb meaning to hammer out or spread thin, as with metal. Septuagint stereōma, Latin firmamentum (“firmament”). Also called a vault or dome.
The Septuagint places “And it was so” at the end of 1:6, and in 1:8 it adds “And God saw that it was good,” which the Hebrew lacks for the second day.

Masoretic Text maqom, “place.” A Qumran fragment (4QGen-h) and the Septuagint reflect miqweh, “one gathering,” which matches “gathering” in 1:10. The Septuagint also adds: “And the water under the heaven was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared.” A Qumran fragment (4QGen-k) appears to support this added clause in Hebrew.
Hebrew moadim, the word later used for Israel’s appointed festivals. Also translated “seasons.”
The sun and moon are not named. Israel’s neighbors worshiped them as gods; here they are lamps that God made and placed.
Hebrew nefesh chayyah, “living being” or “living soul.” The same phrase is used of the first human in 2:7. The Septuagint adds “And it was so” at the end of this verse.
Hebrew tanninim, used elsewhere of sea monsters and serpents (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1). Even these are only creatures God made.

Hebrew adam, here meaning the human race (note “let them rule”). “Us” and “our” have been read as a royal plural, a plural of self-deliberation, God speaking to his heavenly court, or, in Christian reading, a first hint of the Trinity.
The Syriac Peshitta reads “over all the wild animals of the earth,” which matches the list in 1:25 and may preserve the original wording.

“Humankind” is again Hebrew adam, the word that later becomes the name Adam. The Hebrew moves from “him” (singular) to “them” (plural): one human race, created male and female. The verse is written as a short three-line poem.
This is the first day with the definite article in Hebrew (“the sixth day”), marking the high point of the account.

verses.text: So the heavens and the earth were completed, and everything in them.{a}
On the seventh day{b} God brought to an end the work he had been doing, and on the seventh day he ceased{c} from all the work he had been doing.
God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all his work that God had created and made.{d}
This is the account{e} of the heavens and the earth when they were created, on the day that Yahweh{f} God made earth and heavens.
No bush of the field had yet appeared on the earth, and no grain of the field had yet sprouted, because Yahweh God had not caused rain to fall on the land, and there was no human{g} to farm the soil.
But a mist{h} used to rise from the ground and moisten the entire surface of the soil.
Then Yahweh God formed{i} Adam{j} from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and Adam became a living being.{k}
Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden,{l} and there he set Adam, whom he had formed.
From the soil Yahweh God made grow every tree that was lovely in appearance and good to eat, and in the center of the garden stood the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.{m}
A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four headwaters.
The first is named Pishon. It circles through all the territory of Havilah, a land with gold.
The gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone{n} are there.
The name of the second river is Gihon. It is the one that winds through the whole land of Cush.{o}
The third river is named Tigris;{p} it runs along the east side of Assyria. The fourth is the Euphrates.
Yahweh God took Adam and placed him in the garden of Eden to work it and to keep it.{q}
And Yahweh God commanded Adam, saying, “From every tree of the garden you may freely eat,{r}
but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you must not eat, for on the day that you eat from it you will surely die.”{s}
Then Yahweh God said, “It is not good for Adam to be alone. I will make a helper for him who corresponds to him.”{t}

Now out of the ground Yahweh God had formed every animal of the field and every bird of the heavens, and he brought them to Adam to see what he would call each one. Whatever Adam called each living creature, that became its name.
Adam gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the heavens, and to every animal of the field. But for Adam{u} no helper was found who corresponded to him.
So Yahweh God made Adam fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, God removed one of his sides{v} and filled in the flesh where it had been.
Yahweh God built{w} the side that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and he brought her to Adam.
Then Adam said, “This one, at last, is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. This one shall be called Woman, for from Man this one was taken.”{x}
That is why a man leaves his father and his mother and holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.{y}
The two of them were naked,{z} Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.

notes.text: Literally “and all their host,” that is, their whole array or army: everything that fills the sky and the land.

The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read “on the sixth day,” probably to avoid any hint that God worked on the seventh day. The Masoretic “seventh” is the harder reading and is kept here; the Hebrew verb can mean “had completed.”
Hebrew shavat, “ceased” or “stopped,” the root of the word Sabbath (shabbat). It means stopping work, not recovering from tiredness.
Literally “which God created to make.”
Hebrew toledot, “generations” or “family history.” This is the first of the toledot headings that divide Genesis into its main parts.

Here the personal name of God, YHWH, appears for the first time. In Exodus 3:14–15 the name is linked with the verb “to be”: “I am who I am” (or “I will be what I will be”); many scholars also understand it as “he causes to be.” Ancient Jews stopped saying the name aloud, so its original vowels were not written. “Yahweh” is the pronunciation reconstructed by scholars from early Greek transcriptions and from shortened forms in Hebrew names. The Masoretic Text points the name with the vowels of Adonai (“Lord”), and older English Bibles therefore print “the LORD.” Some Dead Sea Scrolls write the name in the older paleo-Hebrew letters as a mark of reverence. The Septuagint usually renders it kyrios, “Lord.” See Conventions.

Hebrew adam, “human,” sounds like adamah, “ground.” The wordplay runs through chapters 2 and 3: the human (adam) comes from the ground (adamah), works the ground, and returns to it (3:19). English might echo it as “earthling” from “earth.”
Hebrew ed, a rare word. It may mean a spring or an underground stream (compare Akkadian edû, “flood”). The Septuagint reads pēgē, “spring.”
Hebrew yatsar, the word for a potter shaping clay (Jeremiah 18:4–6). This image of God as potter and people as clay vessels gives this translation its name.

Hebrew ha-adam, literally “the human” or “the man.” Adam sounds like adamah, “ground”: the human is formed from the ground, works it, and returns to it (2:5; 3:19). Through most of chapters 2–3 the Hebrew has the article (“the human”), and the word is clearly used as a personal name only later (4:25; 5:1–5). This translation writes “Adam” from here on wherever the one man is meant; where adam means the human race (1:26–27; 5:1–2) it is rendered “humankind.”
Hebrew nefesh chayyah, the same phrase used of the animals in 1:20, 24. Older translations: “a living soul.”
Eden probably means “delight” or “abundance.” The Septuagint calls the garden paradeisos, a park, from which comes the English word paradise.
“Good and evil” may be a pair of opposites meaning knowledge of everything, or the claim to decide for oneself what is good and what is evil.
Bdellium (Hebrew bedolach) is a fragrant tree resin. The stone (Hebrew shoham) is uncertain: onyx, carnelian, and lapis lazuli have all been proposed.
Cush usually means the land south of Egypt (ancient Nubia). Some scholars connect it here with the Kassites of Mesopotamia.
Hebrew Hiddeqel is the Tigris; Hebrew Perat is the Euphrates.
Hebrew avad and shamar. Elsewhere the same pair describes the priests who serve and guard the sanctuary (Numbers 3:7–8), so the garden is pictured as a place of worship as well as work.
Literally “eating you may eat.” Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis: the permission is generous.
Literally “dying you will die.” The serpent echoes and denies these exact words in 3:4.

Hebrew ezer kenegdo. Ezer, “helper,” is most often used of God helping his people (Exodus 18:4; Psalm 33:20; 121:1–2), so it does not imply lower rank. Kenegdo means “as in front of him”: a partner who matches him. The Septuagint and Latin Vulgate read “Let us make.”
Here the Hebrew vowel pointing lacks the article, so even the Masoretic Text may read adam as the personal name Adam (compare 3:17, 21; 4:25). See the note on 2:7.
Hebrew tsela, which usually means “side” (for example, the side of the tabernacle in Exodus 26:20). Traditionally “rib.”
Literally “built,” the verb used for building a house or an altar.
Hebrew ishshah, “woman,” sounds like ish, “man.” English “woman” and “man” keep the play. “At last” is literally “this time.” The verse is a short poem, the first recorded human words.

The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Vulgate read “and the two of them will become one flesh.” Jesus and Paul quote this longer form (Matthew 19:5; Mark 10:8; Ephesians 5:31).
Hebrew arummim, “naked,” sounds like arum, “crafty,” in the very next verse (3:1).

verses.text: The serpent was more cunning{a} than any wild creature Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “So God has said,{b} ‘You are not to eat from any tree in the garden’?”
The woman answered the serpent, “We are allowed to eat the fruit from the trees in the garden,
Only of the fruit of the tree in the center of the garden God said, ‘Do not eat of it or even touch it, or you will die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You will not surely die.
God knows that when you eat of it, your eyes will open, and you will be like God,{c} knowing good and evil.”

The woman saw that the tree was good to eat, that it delighted the eyes, and that it was to be desired for gaining wisdom.{d} So she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband, who was beside her, and he ate it.
Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked. So they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.
They heard the sound{e} of Yahweh God walking in the garden in the cool of the day,{f} and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence{g} of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
But Yahweh God called out to Adam, “Where are you?”
He answered, “I heard your sound in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid myself.”
He said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”
Then Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman answered, “The serpent misled me,{h} and I ate.”
Yahweh God said to the serpent, “Since you have done this, you are cursed beyond all cattle and beyond every wild creature. You will go on your belly and eat dust as long as you live.
I will set enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed{i} and her seed. He will crush{j} your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said, “I will multiply your suffering in pregnancy;{k} you will bear children in pain. Your longing{l} will be toward your husband, and he will have authority over you.”

And to Adam{m} he said, “You heeded your wife’s voice and ate from the tree I forbade you, when I said, ‘Do not eat of it.’ So the ground is cursed on your account. With painful toil{n} you will draw your food from it as long as you live.
Thorns and thistles it will grow for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.
With sweat on your face{o} you will eat bread until you go back to the ground, since from it you were taken. Dust is what you are, and to dust you will go back.”
Adam named his wife Eve,{p} because she became the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made garments of skin for Adam and for his wife, and he clothed them.
Then Yahweh God said, “Look, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, so that he does not reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever…”{q}
So Yahweh God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.
He drove out Adam,{r} and on the east side of the garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim{s} and the flame of a sword that turned every way,{t} to guard the way to the tree of life.

notes.text: Hebrew arum, “crafty” or “shrewd.” In Proverbs the word is a virtue (“prudent”). It plays on arummim, “naked,” in 2:25.
Hebrew af ki, literally “Indeed, that God said…?” The serpent’s question twists God’s generous “every tree” (2:16) into “not any tree.”
Hebrew elohim can mean “God,” “gods,” or “divine beings.” The word for “knowing” is plural, so “like gods” is possible; the Septuagint reads “like gods.”
Hebrew lehaskil, “to make wise” or “to gain insight.” It may also mean “to look at”; the Septuagint has “beautiful to contemplate.”
Hebrew qol, “sound” or “voice”; also in 3:10, 17.
Thought for thought. Literally “at the wind (ruach) of the day,” most likely the breezy time of late afternoon or evening.
Literally “from the face of.”
Hebrew hishshiani, “led me astray” or “tricked me.” Paul alludes to this in 2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Timothy 2:14.

Literally “seed.” The word is singular and can mean many descendants or one descendant. Hebrew then says “he” (hu). The Septuagint also uses “he” (autos), even though “seed” is a neuter word in Greek, which suggests early readers saw one person here. From the second century (Irenaeus) Christians have read this verse as the first announcement of the gospel.
Hebrew shuf, a rare verb used in both halves of the line; it may mean “crush,” “bruise,” or “strike.” The Septuagint has “watch for”; the Vulgate has “crush.”
Thought for thought. Literally “your pain and your conception,” two nouns joined to express one idea (pain connected with pregnancy).
Hebrew teshuqah, used again in 4:7 (sin’s desire for Cain) and in Song of Songs 7:10. The Septuagint reads “your turning” (apostrophē), as if from Hebrew teshuvah.
Here the Hebrew vowel pointing lacks the article, so the Masoretic Text itself reads the personal name Adam (see the notes on 2:7 and 2:20).
Hebrew itstsavon, from the same root as the woman’s “pain” in 3:16. Man and woman share the same word of grief.
Literally “of your nostrils” or “of your face.”
Hebrew Chavvah, which sounds like chai, “living.”
The Hebrew sentence breaks off without finishing. Verse 23 supplies the action.
The Septuagint reads: “He drove out Adam and settled him opposite the garden of delight, and stationed the cherubim…”
Cherubim is the Hebrew plural of cherub: winged guardian beings, later pictured over the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22).
Literally “the flame of the sword that turns itself about,” that is, a flashing, whirling blade.

verses.text: Adam knew{a} Eve his wife. She conceived and bore Cain,{b} and she said, “With Yahweh’s help I have gained a man.”{c}
She later bore his brother Abel.{d} Abel tended flocks, while Cain farmed the soil.
In the course of time{e} Cain brought an offering to Yahweh from the fruit of the ground.
And Abel, for his part, brought some of the firstborn of his flock and some of their fat portions. Yahweh looked with favor on Abel and on his offering,
but on Cain and on his offering he did not look with favor. So Cain became very angry, and his face fell.
Yahweh asked Cain, “Why are you so angry? Why is your face cast down?
Do right, and will you not be lifted up?{f} But if you do not do right, sin lies crouching at your door.{g} It longs to have you, but you are to master it.”
Cain spoke to Abel his brother.{h} And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him.
Yahweh asked Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” “I have no idea,” he replied. “Is it my job to guard my brother?”{i}
Yahweh said, “What have you done? Hear it: the blood{j} of your brother is crying to me out of the soil.
So now you are under a curse, driven from the soil that opened wide to take in your brother’s blood from your hand.
When you till the soil, it will not yield its strength to you again. You will be a drifter and a wanderer{k} on the earth.”
Cain said to Yahweh, “My punishment{l} is greater than I can bear.
Today you are driving me off the face of the land, and I must hide from your face. I will drift and wander on the earth, and anyone who comes upon me will kill me.”
But Yahweh said to him, “Therefore{m} anyone who kills Cain will suffer sevenfold vengeance.” Then Yahweh set a sign{n} upon Cain, so that none who met him would strike him dead.
Cain left Yahweh’s presence and made his home in the land of Nod,{o} east of Eden.
Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch.{p} Cain then built a city and called it Enoch, after his son.
Enoch had a son, Irad. Irad became the father of Mehujael, Mehujael of Methushael, and Methushael of Lamech.
Lamech took two wives for himself. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other was Zillah.
Adah bore Jabal, the ancestor of those who dwell in tents and raise herds.
His brother’s name was Jubal. He was the father of all who play the lyre and the pipe.{q}
Zillah also gave birth to Tubal-cain, who forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron.{r} The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives:{s} “Adah and Zillah, hear me; wives of Lamech, give heed to my words. I killed a man for bruising me, a youth for a blow he gave me.
If sevenfold vengeance is for Cain, for Lamech it is seventy-sevenfold.”{t}
Once more Adam knew his wife. She bore a son and called him Seth,{u} “because,” she said, “God has granted me another child in Abel’s place, since Cain killed him.”
Seth too had a son, whom he called Enosh.{v} It was then that people first called on the name of Yahweh.{w}

notes.text: Hebrew yada, “knew,” a common idiom for sexual union.
Cain (Hebrew Qayin) sounds like qaniti, “I have gained.” The name itself may also mean “metalworker” (compare Tubal-cain, 4:22).
Literally “with Yahweh” (et-YHWH). The Septuagint reads “through God.” Other proposals: “I have created a man, as Yahweh did” or “I have gained a man, Yahweh.”
Abel (Hebrew Hevel) means “breath” or “vapor,” the word translated “meaningless” or “vanity” in Ecclesiastes. It hints at his brief life.
Literally “at the end of days.”
Hebrew seet, literally “a lifting.” It may mean acceptance, forgiveness (sin “lifted”), or a lifted face, the opposite of the fallen face in 4:5–6. This is one of the hardest verses in Genesis.

“Crouching” (rovets) pictures an animal lying in wait; it may echo the Akkadian rabisu, a demon thought to lurk at doorways. The next words, “its desire is for you, but you must rule over it,” repeat the wording of 3:16.

Literally “Cain said to Abel his brother,” but the Masoretic Text gives no words, and some Hebrew manuscripts leave a gap here. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint (“into the plain”), the Syriac, and the Vulgate add: “Let us go out to the field.” We keep the shorter Hebrew and render “said to” as “spoke to.”
Hebrew shomer, from the same verb as “keep” in 2:15.
“Blood” is plural in Hebrew (“bloods”). Jewish tradition (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5) took it to include the descendants Abel never had.
Thought for thought. Hebrew na wanad, a rhyming pair meaning “wandering and drifting,” like tohu wabohu in 1:2. Nad anticipates the land of Nod (4:16). The Septuagint reads “groaning and trembling.”

Hebrew avon means both guilt and its punishment. The verse can also be read, “My guilt is too great to be forgiven” (literally “to be lifted,” the same verb as in 4:7). The Septuagint reads “My crime is too great for me to be forgiven.”
Hebrew lakhen, “therefore.” The Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Vulgate read “Not so!” (lo khen).
Hebrew ot, the same word used for the “signs” in the sky (1:14) and the rainbow (9:12). Its nature is not described; it is a mark of protection, not of shame.
Nod means “wandering,” from the same root as “wanderer” in 4:12, 14.
Enoch (Hebrew Chanokh) may mean “dedicated.” This is Cain’s son, not the Enoch of 5:18–24. The Hebrew can also be read to mean that Enoch built the city and named it after his own son.
Hebrew kinnor, a stringed instrument, and ugav, probably a flute or pipe.
Thought for thought. Literally “a sharpener of every cutting tool of bronze and iron.” Hebrew nechoshet means copper or bronze.
Lamech’s words (4:23–24) are the first poem after Eden, a boast of revenge. The verbs can also be read as a threat: “I will kill a man for wounding me.”
Or “seventy times seven.” Jesus seems to reverse this boast when he tells Peter to forgive “seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22).
Seth (Hebrew Shet) sounds like shat, “he has appointed” or “granted.”
Enosh means “human” or “mortal,” a synonym of adam (Psalm 8:4).
Literally “then it was begun to call on the name of Yahweh.” The Septuagint reads “he hoped to call on the name of the Lord God,” reading the Hebrew verb differently.

verses.text: This is the book of the generations{a} of Adam. On the day that God created humankind,{b} he made him in the likeness of God.
He made them male and female. He blessed them, and on the day of their creation he gave them the name Humankind.{c}
At 130 years of age{d} Adam fathered a son like himself, in his own image, and called him Seth.{e}
After Seth’s birth Adam lived 800 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Adam’s life came to 930 years in all, and then he died.
At 105 years of age Seth fathered Enosh.
After Enosh’s birth Seth lived 807 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Seth’s life came to 912 years in all, and then he died.
At 90 years of age Enosh fathered Kenan.{f}
After Kenan’s birth Enosh lived 815 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Enosh’s life came to 905 years in all, and then he died.
At 70 years of age Kenan fathered Mahalalel.{g}
After Mahalalel’s birth Kenan lived 840 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Kenan’s life came to 910 years in all, and then he died.
At 65 years of age Mahalalel fathered Jared.{h}
After Jared’s birth Mahalalel lived 830 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Mahalalel’s life came to 895 years in all, and then he died.
At 162 years of age Jared fathered Enoch.
After Enoch’s birth Jared lived 800 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Jared’s life came to 962 years in all, and then he died.
At 65 years of age Enoch fathered Methuselah.{i}
Enoch walked with God{j} after he fathered Methuselah 300 years, and he fathered sons and daughters.
So all the days of Enoch were 365 years.{k}
Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, for God took him.{l}
At 187 years of age Methuselah fathered Lamech.
After Lamech’s birth Methuselah lived 782 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Methuselah’s life came to 969 years in all, and then he died.{m}
At 182 years of age Lamech fathered a son.
He named him Noah, saying, “This one will comfort us{n} in our work and in the painful toil of our hands, from the ground that Yahweh has cursed.”
After Noah’s birth Lamech lived 595 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
Lamech’s life came to 777 years in all, and then he died.
After Noah had reached 500 years of age, he fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.{o}

notes.text: Hebrew sefer toledot, “the written record of the family line.” It is the second toledot heading (see 2:4). Matthew 1:1 opens with the same phrase in Greek.
Hebrew adam. In 5:1–2 the word looks back to 1:26–28 and means humankind; from 5:3 on it is the personal name Adam.
Hebrew adam, the same word as the name Adam in 5:1, 3. Here it names the human race, male and female (compare 1:26–27).
Hebrew writes numbers in words, often smaller units first (literally “thirty and a hundred years”). We use figures for clarity throughout the genealogies.

The ages in Genesis 5 differ among the witnesses; no Dead Sea Scroll preserves them. The Septuagint adds 100 years to the age at fatherhood of Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, and Enoch (230, 205, 190, 170, 165, 165) and subtracts 100 from the years that follow, so the life spans stay the same. It gives Methuselah 167 years at fatherhood and 802 after (Codex Alexandrinus: 187 and 782), and Lamech 188, 565, and 753 in all. The Samaritan Pentateuch agrees with the Masoretic Text except for Jared (62, 785, 847 in all), Methuselah (67, 653, 720), and Lamech (53, 600, 653). From creation to the flood these give 1,656 years (Masoretic), 1,307 (Samaritan), and 2,242 (Septuagint).
Kenan (Hebrew Qenan) is related to the name Cain. Several names in this line resemble names in Cain’s line (4:17–18): Enoch, Lamech, Irad/Jared, Methushael/Methuselah.
Mahalalel means “praise of God.”
Jared probably means “descent.”
Methuselah probably means “man of the spear” or “man of Shelah.”
Literally “walked about with God,” a picture of close, daily fellowship, said also of Noah (6:9). The Septuagint reads “was well-pleasing to God,” the wording quoted in Hebrews 11:5.
365, the number of days in a solar year. The book of 1 Enoch, quoted in Jude 14–15, develops traditions about Enoch, including a solar calendar.
Literally “and he was not.” “Took” (laqach) is the verb used when Elijah is taken up (2 Kings 2:3, 10). The Septuagint reads “he was not found, because God transferred him” (Hebrews 11:5).

By the Masoretic numbers Methuselah dies in the year of the flood. By the main Septuagint numbers he would outlive the flood by 14 years, an early difficulty that the reading of Codex Alexandrinus (187 years) avoids.
Noah (Hebrew Noach) sounds like nuach, “rest,” and is linked here with nacham, “comfort.” The Septuagint reads “will give us rest.” “Painful toil” (itstsavon) and the cursed ground look back to 3:17.
Shem means “name.” Ham may mean “hot” or “warm.” Japheth is played on in 9:27 (“enlarge”). The order may not be by age (see 9:24; 10:21).

verses.text: When humankind began to multiply on the face of the ground, and daughters were born to them,
the sons of God{a} saw that the daughters of humankind were beautiful, and they took as wives any of them they chose.
Then Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not remain{b} in humankind forever, because they are flesh.{c} Their days will be 120 years.”{d}

The Nephilim{e} were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of humankind and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men{f} of old, the men of renown.{g}
Yahweh saw how great human wickedness had grown on the earth, and that every plan{h} formed by their hearts’ thoughts was nothing but evil, all day long.
Yahweh was sorry{i} he had made human beings on the earth, and grief pierced{j} his heart.
Yahweh said, “I will blot humankind, whom I created, off the surface of the ground, together with the animals, the crawling creatures, and the birds of the sky, for I am sorry that I made them.”
But Noah found favor{k} in the eyes of Yahweh.
This is the account of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless{l} among the people of his time.{m} Noah walked with God.
Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
In God’s sight the earth had gone to ruin,{n} and it was full of violence.{o}
God looked at the earth, and it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.
God said to Noah, “The end of all living creatures has come before me,{p} for through them the earth is full of violence. I am about to bring them to ruin, and the earth with them.
Make yourself an ark{q} of gopher wood.{r} Make rooms in the ark, and coat it inside and outside with pitch.{s}
This is how you are to build it: make it about 450 feet in length, 75 feet in breadth, and 45 feet in height.{t}
Make a roof{u} for the ark and finish it off about eighteen inches from the top. Set a door in its side, and build it with three decks, lower, middle, and upper.
For my part, I am going to bring the flood{v} of waters on the earth, to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life, from under the heavens. Everything that is on the earth will perish.
But I will establish my covenant{w} with you, and you will go into the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you.
From every living creature, from all flesh, you must bring a pair into the ark so that they may survive with you, one male and one female.
From the birds by their species, from the tame animals by their species, and from every creature that crawls on the soil by its species, a pair will come to you so that they may be kept alive.
And you, take with you some of every kind of food that is eaten, and store it up; it will be food for you and for them.”
Noah did this. He did all that God commanded him; so he did.

notes.text: Hebrew bene ha-elohim. There are three main readings. (1) Heavenly beings, as the same phrase means in Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7. This is the oldest known Jewish reading, told at length in 1 Enoch 6–16 (the Watchers) and Jubilees 5, and echoed in Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4; Codex Alexandrinus of the Septuagint reads “angels of God.” (2) Men of Seth’s godly line marrying women of Cain’s line, a view taught by Julius Africanus and Augustine. (3) Kings or powerful men, as in some rabbinic interpretation and Targum Onqelos (“sons of the great ones”).
Hebrew yadon, a verb found only here; its meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint and Vulgate read “remain.” Others render “strive with” or “contend with.”
Hebrew beshaggam, “because also” (they are flesh). It may also be read “in their going astray.”
Either a limit on the human life span or the time left before the flood.

Nephilim is left untranslated. It may come from naphal, “fall,” so “fallen ones” or “those who fall upon others.” The Septuagint reads gigantes, “giants.” The only other use is Numbers 13:33. The Hebrew does not clearly say the Nephilim were the children of these unions; they were already there “in those days.”
Hebrew gibborim, “warriors” or “heroes.”
Literally “men of the name.” Compare the builders who want to make a “name” for themselves in 11:4.
Hebrew yetser, from yatsar, “to form” (2:7): what the heart shapes and plans. Later Jewish teaching speaks of the yetser ha-ra, the “evil inclination.”

Hebrew nacham, which can mean “regret,” “be sorry,” “change one’s mind,” or “be comforted.” It plays on Noah’s name (5:29). Scripture uses human language to express God’s grief while also teaching that God does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19).
From the same root as “pain” and “painful toil” in 3:16–17 and 5:29. God shares the grief that sin brought on people.
Hebrew chen, “favor” or “grace.” Its consonants (ch-n) are those of Noah’s name (n-ch) reversed.
Hebrew tamim, “whole, complete, sound,” the word used for sacrificial animals without defect. It does not mean sinless (see 9:21).
Literally “in his generations.”
Hebrew shachat, “spoiled, ruined.” The same verb is translated “destroy” in 6:13, 17: God brings to ruin what people had already ruined.
Hebrew chamas, violence or brutal wrongdoing.
Thought for thought. Literally “The end of all flesh has come before me.”
Hebrew tevah, a box or chest. The only other use is the basket in which the baby Moses was saved (Exodus 2:3–5).
The wood is unknown, perhaps cypress or another resinous wood, so the Hebrew word is kept. The Septuagint reads “squared timber.”
Hebrew kofer, from kafar, “to cover,” the same root later used for atonement.

Hebrew “300 cubits the length of the ark, 50 cubits its width, and 30 cubits its height.” A cubit is the length of a forearm; counting it as about 18 inches (45 centimeters), the ark was about 450 by 75 by 45 feet (135 by 22.5 by 13.5 meters). Cubit standards varied; a longer cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters) would make the ark somewhat larger.

Hebrew tsohar, found only here. It may mean “roof” or an opening for light (compare tsohorayim, “noon”). “About eighteen inches” is literally “to a cubit,” counting a cubit as about 18 inches (45 centimeters); standards varied.
Hebrew mabbul, used almost only of this flood (compare Psalm 29:10).
Hebrew berit, the first use of “covenant” in the Bible. The promise is fulfilled in 9:8–17.

verses.text: Yahweh told Noah, “Go into the ark, you and your whole household, because in this generation I have found you righteous in my sight.
From every clean animal take seven pairs,{a} each a male with his mate. From the animals that are not clean take one pair, a male with his mate.
Take also seven pairs of the birds of the sky,{b} males and females, so that their kind may live on over the whole earth.
Seven days from now I will make it rain upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe from the surface of the ground every living thing{c} I have made.”
And Noah did all that Yahweh commanded him.
Noah was 600 years old when the flood of waters came on the earth.
Noah went into the ark, and his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives with him, to escape the waters of the flood.
Of the clean animals and of the animals that are not clean, of the birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground,
they came to Noah in the ark in pairs, a male and a female, just as God had instructed Noah.
After the seven days the waters of the flood came on the earth.

In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month (in April–May), on the seventeenth day of the month,{d} on that day all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the floodgates{e} of the heavens were opened.
And the rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights.
On that very day Noah and his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, went into the ark,

they and every wild animal according to its kind, every kind of livestock according to its kind, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind, every winged creature.{f}
They came to Noah and entered the ark in pairs, from every creature that had the breath of life.
The animals that entered were a male and a female from every kind of flesh, as God had instructed him. Then Yahweh closed the door behind him.{g}
The flood lasted forty days on the earth.{h} The water rose and lifted the ark, so that it floated high over the ground.
The waters prevailed{i} and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters.
The waters prevailed more and more on the earth, and all the high mountains under the whole heavens were covered.
The waters rose about 22 feet above them,{j} and the mountains were covered.
All flesh that moved on the earth perished: birds, livestock, wild animals, every swarming creature that swarms on the earth, and every human being.
Every creature on dry land with the spirit of life’s breath in its nostrils{k} died.

Every living thing on the face of the land was blotted out, human and beast, creeping things and birds of the sky. They were blotted out from the earth. Noah alone was left, with those who were with him in the ark.
The waters held sway over the earth for 150 days.{l}

notes.text: Literally “seven seven,” which may mean seven pairs or seven animals (three pairs and one more, perhaps for the sacrifice in 8:20). The Septuagint reads “sevens.” The distinction between clean and unclean animals looks ahead to Leviticus 11.
The Septuagint adds “of the clean birds” and continues, “and of all the birds that are not clean, pairs, male and female.”
Hebrew yequm, a rare word: “everything that stands” or “everything that exists.”

Hebrew “in the second month.” This translation counts the months from the spring new year (Nisan, also called Abib, in March–April), as Exodus 12:2 does for Israel’s festival year, so the second month falls in April–May. The flood account does not say which calendar it follows, and some scholars, like some ancient Jewish interpreters, count from the autumn new year instead, which would put this date in October–November. Hebrew months are lunar, so every modern equivalent is approximate. The Septuagint reads “on the twenty-seventh day.” It also gives the twenty-seventh day in 8:4 and 8:14, so that in the Greek the flood lasts exactly one year.
Hebrew arubbot, “windows” or “lattices,” picturing the sky as a vault with openings (compare 1:6–8).
Literally “every bird, every wing.”

The verse moves from “God” (Elohim) to “Yahweh” (YHWH). Scholars have connected such changes with different sources, and readers have long noted the personal care shown: Yahweh himself closes the door.
The Septuagint reads “forty days and forty nights.”
Hebrew gavar, “grew strong” or “overpowered,” repeated four times (7:18, 19, 20, 24).

Hebrew “fifteen cubits upward,” about 22 feet (7 meters), counting a cubit as about 18 inches (45 centimeters); standards varied. Either above the peaks, or half the ark’s height, so that the ark could float clear of them.
Literally “in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life,” joining the wording of 2:7 and 6:17.
Five months of 30 days, from the seventeenth day of the second month (7:11) to the seventeenth day of the seventh month (8:4).

verses.text: But God remembered{a} Noah, together with every wild animal and every tame animal that was with him in the ark. God caused a wind{b} to sweep over the land, and the flood receded.
The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the heavens was held back.
The waters steadily receded{c} from the earth, and at the end of 150 days the waters had gone down.
In the seventh month (in September–October), on the month’s seventeenth day,{d} the ark settled{e} on the mountains of Ararat.{f}
The waters continued to go down until the tenth month. In the tenth month (in December–January), on the first day of the month,{g} the tops of the mountains became visible.
At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made,
and he sent out the raven. It went out and kept going back and forth{h} until the waters had dried up from the earth.
Then he sent out the dove from him, to see whether the waters had gone down from the face of the ground.

But the dove could find no place to rest{i} its foot, since water still covered the face of the whole earth, and it came back to him in the ark. He put out his hand, caught it, and took it back into the ark with him.
He let seven more days go by and sent the dove out from the ark once again.
The dove came back to him in the evening, and in its beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had gone down from the earth.
He waited seven more days and released the dove, and this time she did not come back to him.

In the six hundred and first year,{j} in the first month (in March–April),{k} on the first day of the month, the waters had dried from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and the face of the ground was dry.
In the second month (in April–May), on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was fully dry.{l}
Then God spoke to Noah, saying,
“Leave the ark, you and your wife, your sons and their wives with you.

Bring out with you every living thing that is with you, of all flesh: birds, livestock, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, so that they may swarm on the earth and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.”
So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives with him.
All the animals, all the creeping things, and all the birds, every creature that moves on the earth, came out of the ark, family by family.
Then Noah built an altar to Yahweh, and he took some of every clean animal and of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar.

Yahweh smelled the soothing aroma,{m} and Yahweh said in his heart, “Never again will I curse the ground on account of humankind, though the human heart forms evil from youth on.{n} Never again will I strike down every living thing as I have done.
As long as the earth remains,{o} sowing and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not cease.”

notes.text: Hebrew zakar. In the Bible, God “remembering” means acting on someone’s behalf, not recalling what was forgotten (compare Exodus 2:24). The verse is the turning point of the flood account.
Hebrew ruach, as in 1:2. The flood account echoes creation: wind over the waters, dry land appearing, and living things told to be fruitful (8:17).
Literally “going and returning.”

Hebrew “in the seventh month”: September–October on the spring-start reckoning used in this translation (see the note on 7:11); on an autumn-start reckoning, March–April. The Septuagint reads “twenty-seventh day” (see 7:11).
Hebrew wattanach, from nuach, “rest,” the word behind Noah’s name (5:29).
Ararat is a region (Assyrian Urartu) in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. The text says “mountains,” not a single peak.
Hebrew “in the tenth month”: December–January on the spring-start reckoning used in this translation (see the note on 7:11); on an autumn-start reckoning, June–July.
Literally “going out and returning.” The Septuagint and Vulgate read that the raven “did not return.”
Hebrew manoach, again from nuach, “rest.”
The Septuagint reads “in the six hundred and first year of the life of Noah,” matching 7:11.
Hebrew “in the first month”: March–April on the spring-start reckoning (see the note on 7:11); on an autumn-start reckoning, September–October.

Hebrew “in the second month”: April–May on the spring-start reckoning (see the note on 7:11). In the Masoretic Text the flood lasts from 2/17 of Noah’s 600th year to 2/27 of his 601st: a lunar year of 354 days plus 11 days, which equals a solar year of 365 days. In the Septuagint (2/27 to 2/27) it lasts exactly one year.
Hebrew reach ha-nichoach, “the restful (or soothing) aroma,” another play on Noah’s name (nuach, “rest”).
Or “for the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth.” The same diagnosis as 6:5 now leads to mercy rather than judgment.
Literally “all the days of the earth.” The verse is a short poem of pairs.

verses.text: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth.
Every animal on earth will fear you and be terrified of you, as will every bird of the sky, all that crawls on the ground, and every fish of the sea. They are placed in your power.
Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green plants, I now give you everything.
But you must not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.{a}
For your lifeblood, too, I will demand an accounting.{b} I will demand it of every beast and of humankind; of each one I will demand the life of the fellow human he takes.{c}
Whoever sheds the blood of a human, by a human{d} his blood will be shed, for in the image of God he made humankind.
As for you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm on the earth and multiply on it.”{e}
Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him,
“As for me, I am establishing my covenant with you and with your offspring after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every animal of the earth with you, all that came out of the ark, every animal of the earth.
I establish my covenant with you: never again will a flood cut off all flesh, and never again will a flood devastate the earth.”
God said, “This is the sign of the covenant that I am setting between myself and you, and every living creature with you, for all the generations that follow:
I have set my bow{f} in the cloud, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
When I gather clouds above the earth and the bow appears among them,
I will remember the covenant between myself and you and all living creatures of every kind of flesh. Never again will the waters become a flood that destroys all flesh.
When the bow is in the cloud, I will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant{g} between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.”
God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.”
The sons of Noah who left the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan.
These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was populated.{h}
Noah, a farmer, began by planting a vineyard.{i}
Drinking of its wine, he grew drunk and lay exposed within his tent.
Ham, Canaan’s father, looked on his father’s nakedness{j} and went out and told his two brothers.

Then Shem and Japheth took a cloak, laid it on both their shoulders, walked in backward, and covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness.
When Noah awoke from his wine and learned what his youngest son{k} had done to him,
he said, “Cursed be Canaan!{l} A servant of servants{m} he will be to his brothers.”
He also said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Shem!{n} And let Canaan be his servant.
May God enlarge Japheth,{o} and may he dwell in the tents of Shem,{p} and let Canaan be his servant.”
Noah lived after the flood 350 years.
Noah’s life came to 950 years in all, and then he died.

notes.text: Literally “flesh with its life (nefesh), its blood.” Blood stands for life, which belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11, 14; compare Acts 15:20).
Hebrew darash, “seek” or “demand.”
Literally “from the hand of each man, his brother, I will require the life of the human.”

The Hebrew is a six-word mirror: shofekh dam ha-adam ba-adam damo yishshafekh, “sheds / blood / of the human // by the human / his blood / will be shed.” “By a human” may also mean “in exchange for the human”; the Septuagint reads “in return for his blood.” The reason given looks back to 1:27.
The Septuagint reads “fill the earth and rule over it,” and some scholars suggest the second Hebrew “multiply” (urevu) was originally “rule” (uredu), as in 1:28.
Hebrew qeshet, the ordinary word for a war bow. The image may be of God hanging up his weapon.
Hebrew berit olam, “everlasting covenant” (compare Isaiah 24:5).
Literally “was spread out” (nafats), looking ahead to the scattering in 10:32 and 11:8–9.
Thought for thought. Literally “Noah, the man of the ground, began and planted a vineyard.” “Man of the ground” (adamah) recalls 2:5, 15 and 5:29.

What Ham did is debated. Some read it as more than looking, since “uncovering the nakedness” of a father is a sexual idiom in Leviticus 18:7–8; others take it as a public act of shame toward his father.
Hebrew qatan, “small,” here “younger” or “youngest.” Ham is usually listed second (5:32; 10:1).

The curse falls on Canaan, not on Ham, and looks ahead to Israel’s later conflict with the Canaanites. This verse was misused for centuries to defend slavery and racism. The text names only Canaan, not Ham’s other descendants (Cush, Egypt, Put; 10:6), and says nothing about skin color or race.
A Hebrew superlative: “the lowest of servants.”
Instead of blessing Shem directly, Noah blesses Shem’s God. Shem means “name,” and the God of Shem is Yahweh, who will give Abram a great name (12:2).
Hebrew yaft, “may he enlarge,” sounds like Yefet, Japheth. The Septuagint reads “make room for.”
“He” may be Japheth, or God dwelling among the descendants of Shem (so the Targums).

verses.text: This is the account of the sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.
The sons of Japheth:{a} Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.{b}
From these the coastland peoples{c} spread out in their lands, each with its own language, by their clans, in their nations.
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim,{d} Put, and Canaan.
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
Cush fathered Nimrod.{e} He was the first on the earth to become a mighty warrior.
He was a mighty hunter before Yahweh.{f} That is why it is said, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before Yahweh.”
The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh,{g} in the land of Shinar.{h}
From that land he went out to Assyria{i} and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-ir,{j} Calah,
and Resen, which lies between Nineveh and Calah, the great city.
Mizraim fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim,
the Pathrusim, the Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came),{k} and the Caphtorim.
Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,{l}
the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite,
the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite,
the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites were scattered.
The territory of the Canaanites reached from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim as far as Lasha.
These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, in their nations.
To Shem also, the father of all the sons of Eber{m} and the older brother of Japheth,{n} children were born.
The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.{o}
The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.{p}
Arpachshad fathered Shelah,{q} and Shelah fathered Eber.
To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg,{r} for in his days the earth was divided; and his brother’s name was Joktan.
Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, and Diklah,
Obal, Abimael, and Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were Joktan’s sons.
Their territory reached from Mesha toward Sephar, the hill country of the east.
These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, in their nations.
Such were the clans descended from Noah’s sons, line by line, nation by nation. From them the peoples branched out across the earth after the flood.{s}

notes.text: The names in this chapter are peoples and places as well as persons. Gomer is usually linked with the Cimmerians, Madai with the Medes, Javan with the Ionian Greeks, and Tubal and Meshech with peoples of Anatolia. The Septuagint adds Elisa to the sons of Japheth.
The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint (“Rhodians”), and 1 Chronicles 1:7 read Rodanim, the people of Rhodes. In Hebrew script the letters d and r look very much alike.
Literally “the coastlands of the nations,” the shores and islands of the Mediterranean. Many scholars think the words “These are the sons of Japheth” have dropped out here (compare 10:20, 31).
Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Cush is the land south of Egypt; Put is probably Libya.
Nimrod sounds like the Hebrew for “we will rebel” (marad). Jewish tradition made him the leader of the builders of Babel. “Mighty warrior” is gibbor, as in 6:4.
“Before Yahweh” may mean “in Yahweh’s sight,” as a mark of greatness, or “in defiance of Yahweh.”
With different vowels the Hebrew for “and Calneh” can be read “all of them”: “Babel, Erech, and Accad, all of them in the land of Shinar.”
Shinar is Babylonia, the land of Sumer and Akkad in southern Mesopotamia.
Or “From that land Asshur went out.” The Hebrew can be read either way; the Septuagint takes Asshur (Assur) as the subject.
Literally “the broad places of the city,” possibly a district of Nineveh rather than a separate city.
Many scholars think this note belongs after “the Caphtorim,” since Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say the Philistines came from Caphtor (probably Crete).
Heth is the ancestor of the Hittites (see Genesis 23).
The name Eber is linked with the word “Hebrew” (ivri).
Or “the brother of Japheth the elder.” The Hebrew does not make clear which brother was older; the Septuagint reads the second way.
The Septuagint adds Cainan to the sons of Shem.
1 Chronicles 1:17 and the Septuagint read Meshech (Greek Mosoch).
The Septuagint reads “Arpachshad fathered Cainan, and Cainan fathered Shelah,” as in 11:12–13 and Luke 3:36.
Peleg means “division,” from palag, “divide.” The division may be the scattering of peoples in 11:1–9, or the land divided by canals.

The Masoretic Text names seventy peoples, a number of completeness (compare Deuteronomy 10:22). With its additions the Septuagint has more; Luke 10:1 has a similar variant, seventy or seventy-two sent out.

verses.text: All the earth had a single language, one set of words.{a}
As people journeyed from the east,{b} they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.
They said to one another, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them hard.”{c} They had brick for stone and bitumen for mortar.
They said, “Come, we will build a city for ourselves, and a tower reaching up into the heavens, and win a name{d} for ourselves, or we will be scattered across the face of the earth.”
Yahweh came down to see the city and the tower that the children of humankind had built.{e}
Yahweh said, “See, they are a single people with a single language, and this is just the start of their doing. From now on nothing they set out to do will be out of reach for them.
Come, we will go down and mix up their speech{f} there, so that no one will understand what another says.”
So Yahweh scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stopped building the city.
That is why its name was Babel,{g} for there Yahweh confused the speech of the entire earth, and from that place Yahweh dispersed them across the whole earth.
These are the generations of Shem.{h} Two years after the flood, at 100 years of age, Shem fathered Arpachshad.
After Arpachshad’s birth Shem lived 500 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.{i}
At 35 years of age Arpachshad fathered Shelah.{j}
After Shelah’s birth Arpachshad lived 403 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 30 years of age Shelah fathered Eber.
After Eber’s birth Shelah lived 403 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 34 years of age Eber fathered Peleg.
After Peleg’s birth Eber lived 430 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 30 years of age Peleg fathered Reu.
After Reu’s birth Peleg lived 209 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 32 years of age Reu fathered Serug.
After Serug’s birth Reu lived 207 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 30 years of age Serug fathered Nahor.
After Nahor’s birth Serug lived 200 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 29 years of age Nahor fathered Terah.
After Terah’s birth Nahor lived 119 more years, and other sons and daughters were born to him.
At 70 years of age Terah fathered Abram,{k} Nahor, and Haran.
This is the account of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.
Haran died during the lifetime of{l} Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.{m}
Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai,{n} and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was the father of Milcah and Iscah.
Now Sarai was barren; she had no child.{o}

Terah set out with Abram his son, with Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and with Sarai, Abram’s wife, his daughter-in-law. Together{p} they left Ur of the Chaldeans, heading for Canaan. But on reaching Haran{q} they stayed there.
Terah’s life came to 205 years,{r} and he died in Haran.

notes.text: Literally “one lip and the same (or few) words.”
Or “journeyed eastward.” Movement east runs through these chapters, away from Eden (3:24; 4:16).

The Hebrew is full of sound play: nilbenah levenim, “let us brick bricks,” and nisrefah lisrefah, “let us burn them for burning”; chemar (bitumen) and chomer (mortar). Southern Mesopotamia had little stone, so people built with baked brick.
Hebrew shem, “name.” The builders try to make a name for themselves; in 12:2 God promises to make a great name for Abram, a descendant of Shem (whose name means “name”).
The tower meant to reach the heavens is so small that Yahweh must “come down” to see it.

Literally “their lip.” “Let us confuse” is navlah, from balal. Its consonants (n-b-l) reverse those of “let us make bricks” (l-b-n) in 11:3: the builders’ plan is turned back on them. On “let us,” see 1:26.

Babel (the Hebrew name for Babylon) sounds like balal, “confuse” or “mix.” In Akkadian the city’s name, Bab-ili, meant “gate of god”; Genesis answers with a pun: not the gate of God but the place of confusion. The Septuagint renders the name “Confusion.”
Another toledot heading. Ten generations from Shem to Abram mirror the ten from Adam to Noah in chapter 5.

The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint add “and he died” after each person in this list, and the Samaritan also gives each total life span. Ages at fatherhood and years that follow differ. Masoretic: Arpachshad 35/403, Shelah 30/403, Eber 34/430, Peleg 30/209, Reu 32/207, Serug 30/200, Nahor 29/119. Samaritan: 135/303, 130/303, 134/270, 130/109, 132/107, 130/100, 79/69. Septuagint: 135/400 (Alexandrinus 430), then Cainan 130/330, Shelah 130/330, Eber 134/270 (Alexandrinus 370), Peleg 130/209, Reu 132/207, Serug 130/200, Nahor 179/125 (Alexandrinus 79/129). No Dead Sea Scroll preserves these numbers.

The Septuagint has an extra generation here: Arpachshad fathers Cainan, and Cainan (130 years, then 330 more) fathers Shelah. Luke 3:36 includes this Cainan, and Jubilees 8 also knows him as Kainam. He is absent from the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and 1 Chronicles 1:18, 24.

Abram means “exalted father”; in 17:5 he is renamed Abraham. He is named first but may not be the eldest: if Terah died at 205 (11:32) and Abram left Haran at 75 after his father’s death (12:4; Acts 7:4), Abram was born when Terah was 130.
Literally “on the face of,” that is, while his father was still alive.
Ur was a great city of southern Mesopotamia. “Of the Chaldeans” uses a later name for the region, updating it for readers. The Septuagint reads “in the land of the Chaldeans.”
Sarai probably means “princess”; in 17:15 she is renamed Sarah. Jewish tradition identifies Iscah with Sarai, but the text does not say so.
The Hebrew says it twice (“barren; there was to her no child”), using a rare word for child (valad). The whole story of the promise to Abram begins from this emptiness.
Literally “they went out with them.” The Septuagint and Vulgate read “he brought them out.”
The city Haran (Hebrew Charan) in northern Mesopotamia is spelled differently in Hebrew from the name of Terah’s son Haran.
The Samaritan Pentateuch reads 145 years. By that number Terah died in the year Abram left Haran (11:26; 12:4), which matches Stephen’s words in Acts 7:4.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Abram, “Go out{a} from your land, from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation; I will bless you and make your name renowned, and you will be a blessing.{b}
I will bless those who bless you, and whoever treats you with contempt I will curse. And in you all the families{c} of the earth will be blessed.”{d}
So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.
Abram took his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, with all the wealth they had amassed and the persons{e} they had gained in Haran, and they left for Canaan. So they arrived in Canaan.{f}
Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh.{g} At that time the Canaanites were in the land.
Then Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “To your offspring{h} I will give this land.” So he built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him.
From there he went on to the hills east of Bethel and set up his tent between Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. He built an altar there to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
Then Abram journeyed on, going by stages toward the Negev.{i}
A famine struck the land, and Abram went down into Egypt to stay as a foreigner,{j} for the famine weighed heavily on the land.
As he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman to see.
When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me, but they will let you live.
Tell them you are my sister,{k} I beg you, so that I am treated well for your sake and kept alive thanks to you.”
When Abram came into Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
Pharaoh’s officials{l} saw her and praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
He treated Abram well because of her, and Abram acquired sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male and female servants, female donkeys, and camels.{m}
But Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues on account of Abram’s wife Sarai.{n}
So Pharaoh summoned Abram and said, “What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you claim, ‘She is my sister,’ and let me take her as a wife? Here she is, your wife. Take her and be gone!”
Then Pharaoh gave his men orders concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.{o}

notes.text: Literally “Go, for yourself” (Hebrew lekh-lekha), a phrase that stresses personal departure. It returns in 22:2, framing Abraham’s story with two calls to go.
Literally “be a blessing.” Some scholars repoint the Hebrew to read “and it (your name) will be a blessing.”
Or “clans.” The Septuagint reads “tribes.”

Or “will bless themselves by you,” that is, use your name in their blessings. The Hebrew verb form allows both senses. The New Testament reads it as a promise that the nations will share Abraham’s blessing (Acts 3:25; Galatians 3:8).
Literally “the souls” (nephesh), probably servants and members of the household. Later Jewish tradition read it as the people Abram and Sarai had won to faith in the one God.
Brenton’s Septuagint lacks “And they came to the land of Canaan,” though he notes that Codex Alexandrinus has it, as the Hebrew does.
Or “the terebinth of Moreh,” a large tree. Moreh may mean “teacher,” suggesting a place where oracles were sought. The Septuagint reads “the high oak.”
Literally “seed,” here and throughout. The Hebrew word is singular in form but usually collective. Paul builds on the singular form in Galatians 3:16.
The Negev is the dry southern region of Canaan. The word also means “south.” The Septuagint reads “the wilderness.”
Hebrew gur, “to live as a resident foreigner,” without the rights of a native. The same verb shapes much of the patriarchs’ story.
Sarai was in fact Abram’s half sister (20:12). The half-truth was still a deception, and the story does not approve it.
Or “princes.” “Pharaoh” is an Egyptian title meaning “great house,” not a personal name.

The mention of camels here and elsewhere in Genesis is debated, since large-scale camel domestication is dated later than the usual dates for Abraham. Some see it as the narrator updating the details for later readers.
Literally “because of the word (or matter) of Sarai.”
Brenton notes that Codex Alexandrinus adds “and Lot with him,” which prepares for 13:1.

verses.text: So Abram went up from Egypt into the Negev, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him.
Abram was very rich{a} in livestock, in silver, and in gold.
He went on by stages from the Negev as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,
It was the site of the altar he had first built there. And there Abram invoked the name of Yahweh.
Lot, who traveled with Abram, also owned sheep, cattle, and tents.
But the land could not support them both living together, because their possessions were so great that they could not stay together.
Strife arose between Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s herdsmen. The Canaanites and the Perizzites were then dwelling in the land.
Then Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, or between my herders and your herders, for we are family.{b}
Is not the whole land in front of you? Please separate from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”
Lot raised his eyes and saw how the whole Jordan plain{c} was watered throughout, like Yahweh’s garden, like Egypt, all the way toward Zoar.{d} That was before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.
So Lot selected the entire Jordan plain for himself and journeyed eastward.{e} In this way the two men parted.
Abram dwelt in Canaan, but Lot dwelt among the towns of the plain, pitching his tent near Sodom.
Now the people of Sodom were evil, great sinners against Yahweh.{f}
After Lot had separated from him, Yahweh said to Abram, “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward, eastward and westward,{g}
Every bit of land within your sight I will give to you and your descendants for all time.
I will make your descendants like the dust on the ground in number. If anyone could count the dust, then your descendants could be counted too.
Get up, walk through the land, its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you.”
Abram moved his tent and went to live by the oaks of Mamre{h} at Hebron, and he built an altar there to Yahweh.

notes.text: Literally “very heavy.” The same root gives the Hebrew word for “glory.”
Literally “for we are men, brothers.” “Brother” is often used for any close relative; Lot was Abram’s nephew.
Hebrew kikkar, literally “circle” or “round,” the well-watered region around the southern Jordan.
The Septuagint reads “Zogora.” Some scholars suggest the original may have read “Zoan,” a city in Egypt, which would fit the comparison with Egypt. This is uncertain.
Or “from the east.” The Septuagint reads “from the east.” The Hebrew miqqedem can mean either.
Literally “evil and sinners to Yahweh, very.” The Septuagint reads “before God.”
Literally “seaward,” toward the Mediterranean.
Or “terebinths of Mamre.” The Hebrew is plural; the Septuagint reads the singular “oak.”

verses.text: In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim,{a}
these kings made war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar.
These all joined together in the Valley of Siddim (the Salt Sea).{b}
Twelve years they had been subject to Chedorlaomer; in the thirteenth they revolted.
In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim{c} in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim,
and the Horites in their hills of Seir, reaching to El-paran at the edge of the wilderness.
Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat,{d} that is, Kadesh, and defeated all the territory of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.

Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, that is, Zoar, went out and drew up their battle lines against them in the Valley of Siddim,
against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.
The Valley of Siddim was riddled with bitumen pits.{e} When the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some of their men fell in there, and the rest escaped to the hills.
The enemy took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and went away.
They also took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, and his goods, and went away, for he was living in Sodom.
A fugitive came and reported it to Abram the Hebrew.{f} Abram was camped by the large trees owned by Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner, and these men were Abram’s allies.{g}
When Abram heard that his relative had been taken captive, he called out{h} his trained men, born in his household, 318 of them, and pursued as far as Dan.{i}
During the night he split up his men and attacked them, he and his servants. He defeated them and chased them all the way to Hobah, which lies north{j} of Damascus.
He brought back all the goods, and he also brought back his relative Lot and his goods, along with the women and the people.
After Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King’s Valley.
And Melchizedek{k} king of Salem{l} brought out bread and wine. He was priest of El Elyon.{m}
He blessed Abram and said, “Blessed be Abram by El Elyon, Maker{n} of heaven and earth.
And blessed be El Elyon, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Then Abram handed him a tenth part of everything.{o}
The king of Sodom then said to Abram, “Give the people to me, and keep the possessions for yourself.”
But Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand{p} to Yahweh,{q} El Elyon, Maker of heaven and earth,
I swear that I will accept nothing of yours, not even a thread or a shoelace, so that you can never claim, ‘I enriched Abram.’
I want nothing except what the young men have already consumed, and the share for the men who marched with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their share.”

notes.text: Or “king of nations,” as the Septuagint reads. None of these four kings has been securely identified in other ancient records, though the names fit known name types from Mesopotamia, Elam, and Anatolia.
The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea. The note “that is…” updates the place name for later readers, as several notes in this chapter do.
The Rephaim, Zuzim, and Emim were peoples remembered as unusually tall (compare Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20). The Septuagint reads “the giants” for Rephaim.
En-mishpat means “spring of judgment.” The Septuagint translates it “the well of judgment.”
Literally “pits, pits of bitumen,” a Hebrew way of saying “full of pits.” The Dead Sea region is known for natural asphalt.

The first use of “Hebrew” in the Bible. The Septuagint translates it “the one who crossed over” (Brenton: “the passer”), linking it with the root avar, “to cross,” though the word is more likely connected with Eber (10:21; 11:14).
Literally “lords of a covenant with Abram.”

Literally “emptied out” or “drew out,” an unusual use of the verb. The Septuagint reads “numbered,” and a different Hebrew verb lies behind some other ancient witnesses. The meaning “mustered” is likely.
Dan was named later (Judges 18:29); the narrator uses the name his readers knew.
Literally “on the left of,” that is, to the north for someone facing east.
Melchizedek means “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness.” He is taken up in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5–7, and in the Qumran text known as 11QMelchizedek.
Salem probably means Jerusalem (compare Psalm 76:2). The name sounds like shalom, “peace” (Hebrews 7:2).
Hebrew El Elyon, “God Most High.” Elyon means “highest.” Here Abram identifies this God with Yahweh (14:22).
Or “Creator” or “Owner.” The Hebrew qoneh can mean either “maker” or “possessor.”
Literally “he gave him a tenth from all.” The Hebrew does not name the subject; Hebrews 7:4 understands that Abram gave the tenth to Melchizedek.
A gesture of taking an oath. The Septuagint reads “I will stretch out my hand.”

The Masoretic Text has the name Yahweh here, and Brenton’s Septuagint also has “the Lord” (kyrios): “the Lord the most high God.” Some other ancient witnesses are reported to lack the divine name and read only “God Most High” (El Elyon), as in 14:18–20.

verses.text: After these things the word of Yahweh came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield;{a} your reward will be very great.”
But Abram said, “Lord Yahweh,{b} what will you give me, since I go on childless, and the heir of my house{c} is Eliezer of Damascus?”
And Abram said, “Look, you have given me no offspring, so a member of my household will be my heir.”
Then the word of Yahweh came to him: “This man will not be your heir; one who comes from your own body will be your heir.”
He brought him outside and said, “Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your offspring be.”
Abram believed{d} Yahweh, and he counted it to him as righteousness.{e}
He said to him, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to possess.”
But he said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will possess it?”
He told him, “Fetch me a heifer, a she-goat, and a ram, each three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon.”
Abram fetched all these, split them down the middle, and set each half facing its partner; the birds, though, he left whole.
When birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.{f}
As the sun was going down, a deep sleep{g} fell on Abram, and a dread, a great darkness, fell upon him.
Then Yahweh said to Abram, “Know for certain that your offspring will be foreigners in a land that is not theirs. They will be enslaved and oppressed there for four hundred years.{h}
But I will bring judgment on the nation they serve, and afterward they will come out with great possessions.
But you yourself will join your ancestors in peace, and you will be laid in the grave after a long and full life.
