In the fourth generation{i} they will come back here, for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet complete.”
After the sun went down and darkness fell, a smoking cooking pot and a blazing torch moved between the halves of the animals.{j}
On that day Yahweh established a covenant{k} with Abram: “I am giving this land to your descendants, from the stream of Egypt{l} to the great river, the Euphrates:
the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”{m}

notes.text: Hebrew magen, “shield.” A slight change of vowels gives “I give you a gift (or payment),” which some scholars prefer because of “reward.” The Septuagint reads “I shield you.”

Hebrew Adonai YHWH, “my Lord Yahweh.” The Masoretic Text points the name here with the vowels of Elohim, so that it is read “God,” and older English Bibles print “Lord GOD.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Master and Lord.”

The Hebrew is obscure: literally “the son of mesheq of my house is Damascus Eliezer.” Mesheq may be a wordplay on Dammesheq, “Damascus,” or a word meaning “acquisition.” The Septuagint takes Masek as the name of Eliezer’s mother.
Or “trusted.” The Hebrew he’emin comes from the root of amen, “firm” or “reliable.” The verse is quoted in Romans 4:3, Galatians 3:6, and James 2:23; the Septuagint reads “Abram believed God.”

The Hebrew does not name the subject of “counted.” The usual reading is that Yahweh counted Abram’s faith as righteousness. A minority reading is that Abram counted Yahweh’s promise as an act of righteousness.
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Abram sat down by them.” Brenton suggests the translators read a Hebrew verb meaning “sat” in place of the one meaning “drove back.”
Hebrew tardemah, the same deep sleep that fell on the human in 2:21. The Septuagint reads “trance” (ekstasis).

Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years. The Septuagint at Exodus 12:40, and reportedly the Samaritan Pentateuch, count that span to include the time in Canaan as well as in Egypt, and Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the Law (Galatians 3:17).
Hebrew dor, “generation,” may here mean a long lifetime or era of about a century, matching the 400 years of 15:13.

In ancient covenant rites the parties walked between cut animals, calling a like fate on themselves if they broke the agreement (compare Jeremiah 34:18–20). Here only the fire, a sign of God’s presence, passes through.
Literally “cut a covenant,” the usual Hebrew idiom, which matches the cut animals.
Probably the Wadi el-Arish, the seasonal stream on the border between Canaan and Egypt, rather than the Nile.
The Septuagint (Brenton: “the Evites”) and some other ancient witnesses add “the Hivites” to the list. This translation follows the Hebrew, which has ten peoples.

verses.text: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children. She had an Egyptian slave woman{a} whose name was Hagar.
So Sarai said to Abram, “Look, Yahweh has kept me from bearing children. Please go in to my slave woman; perhaps I can build a family through her.”{b} And Abram listened to what Sarai said.
After Abram had spent ten years living in Canaan, Abram’s wife Sarai brought her servant, Hagar the Egyptian, and gave her to Abram as a wife.{c}
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress became slight{d} in her eyes.

Then Sarai said to Abram, “The wrong done to me is on you!{e} I put my slave woman in your arms, and when she saw that she had conceived, I became slight in her eyes. May Yahweh judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Look, your slave woman is in your hands. Do to her whatever seems good to you.” Then Sarai treated her harshly,{f} and she ran away from her.
The angel of Yahweh{g} came upon her at a spring in the wilderness, the spring beside the Shur road.
He asked, “Hagar, Sarai’s slave girl, where have you come from, and where are you headed?” “I am fleeing from Sarai my mistress,” she answered.
Then the angel of Yahweh told her, “Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.”
The angel of Yahweh also said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, so that they cannot be counted for multitude.”
And the angel of Yahweh said to her, “Look, you are pregnant and will give birth to a son. You shall call his name Ishmael,{h} for Yahweh has heard your affliction.
He will be a wild donkey{i} of a man, his hand raised against all and the hands of all raised against him, and he will live at odds with{j} all his kin.”
She gave a name to Yahweh, who had addressed her: “You are El Roi,”{k} for she said, “Have I truly looked, even here, upon the one who sees me?”{l}
So the well came to be called Beer-lahai-roi;{m} it is between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.

notes.text: Hebrew shiphchah, a female slave or servant who belonged to her mistress. Ancient marriage contracts from Mesopotamia describe a childless wife giving such a woman to her husband to bear children for her.
Literally “I will be built from her.” There is a wordplay between banah, “to build,” and ben, “son.”
Or “as a concubine.” Hebrew ishshah, “wife” or “woman.” Hagar became a secondary wife; she remained Sarai’s servant (16:6).
Literally “light,” the opposite of “heavy” or “honored.” She looked down on her mistress.
Literally “My violence (chamas) is upon you,” meaning “you are responsible for the wrong I suffer.”
Hebrew anah, “to afflict” or “humble,” the same verb used of Israel’s oppression in Egypt (15:13; Exodus 1:11–12).
The first appearance of “the angel (or messenger) of Yahweh.” In several passages this figure speaks as God himself (16:10, 13; 22:11–12, 15–16).
Ishmael means “God hears.”
Hebrew pere, the wild donkey or onager of the desert, an image of a free, untamed life rather than an insult. The Septuagint reads “a wild man.”
Or “he will live to the east of” or “alongside.” The Hebrew al-pene, literally “upon the face of,” has all three senses. The Septuagint reads “in the presence of.”
Hebrew El Roi, “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.”

The Hebrew is difficult; literally “Have I even here seen after the one who sees me?” Possible senses include “Have I seen God and lived after seeing him?” (by a small emendation) and “Have I seen the back of the one who sees me?” (compare Exodus 33:23).
Beer-lahai-roi probably means “well of the living one who sees me.” The Septuagint reads “the well of him whom I have openly seen.”

verses.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram and said to him, “I am El Shaddai.{a} Walk before me and be blameless,{b}
and I will set my covenant between me and you and multiply you very greatly.”
Then Abram fell on his face, and God spoke with him, saying,
“As for me, here is my covenant with you: you will be the father of a multitude of nations.
No longer shall your name be called Abram; your name shall be Abraham,{c} for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you abundantly fruitful; nations will come out of you, and kings will be among your descendants.
I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land where you are living as a foreigner, all the land of Canaan, as a possession forever. And I will be their God.”
God said to Abraham, “As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.
This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskins, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and you.
Generation after generation, each male among you is to be circumcised on his eighth day, both the slave born in your household and the one purchased with silver from a foreigner not of your line.
Whether he is born in your household or purchased with your silver, he must be circumcised. In this way my covenant will be marked on your bodies as a covenant that lasts forever.
An uncircumcised male, one who has not had the flesh of his foreskin{d} circumcised, will be cut off{e} from his kin, because he has violated my covenant.”
God said to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, for Sarah{f} shall be her name.
I will bless her, and I will also give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she will become nations;{g} kings of peoples will come from her.”
Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed,{h} and said in his heart, “Can a child be born to a man a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
Abraham said to God, “Oh, that Ishmael might live in your favor!”
God said, “No, but{i} Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac.{j} I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you.{k} Look, I will bless him and make him fruitful and multiply him very greatly. He will father twelve chieftains, and I will make him a great nation.
But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this set time next year.”
When he had finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham.

That same day Abraham took his son Ishmael and every male of his household, whether born in his house or purchased with his silver, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskins, just as God had told him.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
On that very day Abraham was circumcised, and Ishmael his son.
And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.

notes.text: Hebrew El Shaddai, traditionally “God Almighty.” The meaning of Shaddai is uncertain. Proposals include “of the mountain,” “of the fields,” and “the one who is sufficient.” “Almighty” follows the ancient Greek and Latin tradition in other books. In this verse Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I am your God.”
Hebrew tamim, “whole,” “complete,” or “with integrity.” It is used of Noah in 6:9.
Abram means “exalted father.” Abraham sounds like av hamon, “father of a multitude.” The name may be a longer form of Abram, given new meaning by the promise.
The Septuagint adds “on the eighth day,” and some other ancient witnesses are reported to have the same addition.
“Cut off” (karat) may mean death, exclusion from the community, or the ending of one’s family line. The same verb is used for “cutting” a covenant (15:18).
Sarai and Sarah are two forms of one name meaning “princess.” The change marks her new role as mother of nations and kings.
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I will bless him, and he will become nations,” referring to the son.
Hebrew tsachaq, “laugh,” the root of the name Isaac. Laughter returns in 18:12–15 and 21:6, 9.
Or “Truly” or “Yes, indeed.” The Hebrew aval can confirm or correct. The Septuagint reads “Yes.”
Isaac (Hebrew Yitschaq) means “he laughs.”
Hebrew shema’tikha, a play on the name Ishmael, “God hears.”

verses.text: Yahweh appeared to Abraham{a} by the large trees of Mamre as he was sitting at the opening of his tent in the warmest part of the day.
Raising his eyes, he saw three men standing close by. On seeing them he hurried from his tent door to greet them and bowed low to the earth.
He said, “Sir,{b} if I have gained your approval, please do not go on past your servant.
Let some water be fetched so you can wash your feet, and then rest yourselves beneath the tree.
I will bring a morsel of bread for you to refresh your hearts.{c} Then you can continue, now that you have come by your servant’s way.” “Go ahead,” they answered, “just as you say.”
Abraham hastened into the tent to Sarah. “Hurry,” he said, “about twenty quarts{d} of fine flour! Knead it and bake some loaves.”
Then Abraham ran to the herd, took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who hurried to prepare it.
Then he took curds{e} and milk and the calf he had prepared and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree while they ate.
They said to him, “Where is Sarah your wife?” He said, “There, in the tent.”
One of them said, “I will come back to you when this season comes round again,{f} and then Sarah your wife will hold a son.” Sarah was listening at the door of the tent behind him.
Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well along in years. The way of women{g} had ceased for Sarah.
So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, “After I am worn out, shall I have pleasure,{h} with my lord so old?”
Yahweh asked Abraham, “What made Sarah laugh and say, ‘Will I truly give birth, old as I am?’
Is any matter too wondrous{i} for Yahweh? At the appointed time, when this season comes round again, I will come back to you, and Sarah will have a son.”
But Sarah denied it, saying, “I did not laugh,” for she was afraid. He said, “No, you did laugh.”
Then the men got up from there and looked down toward Sodom, and Abraham went with them to send them on their way.
Yahweh said, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,
since Abraham will surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him?

I have chosen{j} him so that he will direct his sons and his household after him to follow the path of Yahweh, practicing justice and righteousness, and then Yahweh can fulfill for Abraham everything he promised him.”
Then Yahweh said, “The cry{k} over Sodom and Gomorrah is enormous, and their wrongdoing is extremely grave.
Let me go down and see if their deeds fully match the outcry that has reached me. If not, I will know.”
The men turned away and headed toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood in Yahweh’s presence.{l}
Abraham drew near and said, “Will you indeed destroy the righteous along with the wicked?
What if the city holds fifty who are righteous? Would you destroy it then, and not forgive{m} the place for the sake of those fifty?
Surely you would never do such a thing, killing the righteous together with the wicked, treating the one the same as the other! Surely not you! Will the Judge of the whole earth not act justly?”
Yahweh answered, “If in Sodom I find fifty righteous within the city, I will forgive the entire place for them.”
Abraham answered and said, “Look, I have dared to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes.{n}
What if the fifty righteous are five short? For want of five, will you destroy the whole city?” He answered, “If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it.”
Abraham spoke to him again: “Perhaps only forty will be found in it?” He replied, “Because of those forty I will not do it.”
Then he said, “Please do not let the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there.” He said, “I will not do it if I find thirty there.”
He said, “Please note that I have presumed to speak to the Lord: what if twenty are found there?” He answered, “I will not destroy it, for the sake of the twenty.”
He said, “May the Lord not be angry if I speak only this once more: what if ten are found there?” He answered, “I will not destroy it, for the sake of the ten.”
When Yahweh had finished speaking to Abraham, he went his way, and Abraham returned to his place.

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “God appeared to him.” The chapter moves between Yahweh and the three men without explaining how they relate. Christian readers have long seen a hint of the Trinity here; Jewish tradition usually sees Yahweh accompanied by angels (19:1).
The Hebrew consonants can be read as adoni, “my lord,” a polite address to a guest, or Adonai, “Lord,” as the Masoretic vowels have it. Abraham may not yet know who the visitor is.
Literally “sustain your hearts.” The modest offer of “a bite of bread” becomes a lavish meal, an example of ancient hospitality (compare Hebrews 13:2).

Hebrew “three seahs.” The seah was a dry measure of uncertain size, often reckoned at about 7 quarts (7.3 liters), so three seahs is about 20 quarts or 5 gallons (22 liters) of flour; estimates vary widely, and some are much smaller. Either way it is a lavish amount for three guests.
Or “butter.” Hebrew chem’ah usually means curdled milk or yogurt.
Literally “at the time of life,” probably meaning “when the time comes round again,” about a year from now. The Septuagint reads “according to this time, seasonably.”
A polite expression for menstruation.
Hebrew ednah, related to Eden, “delight.” Brenton notes that the Septuagint reads “The thing has not yet happened to me until now,” taking the word in a different sense.
Or “too hard.” Hebrew pala, used of things beyond human power. Compare Jeremiah 32:17, 27 and Luke 1:37.
Literally “I have known him,” in the sense of a chosen, personal relationship.
Hebrew ze’aqah, the cry of victims for help against injustice. Ezekiel 16:49 names Sodom’s sins as pride, excess, and failure to help the poor and needy.

Ancient Jewish tradition lists this verse among the “corrections of the scribes” (tiqqune sopherim). It says the original read “Yahweh remained standing before Abraham,” changed out of reverence. No surviving manuscript has that reading.
Literally “lift up,” that is, forgive or bear with the place.
Hebrew aphar wa’epher, a sound pair. Compare 3:19.

verses.text: At evening the two angels reached Sodom. Lot was seated at Sodom’s gate,{a} and when he saw them he rose to greet them and bowed low, face to the earth.

“Please, my lords,” he said, “turn in to the house of your servant, spend the night, and wash your feet. Then you may rise early and go your ways.” “No,” they replied, “we will spend the night in the square.”
He urged them so insistently that they came aside with him into his house. He prepared a meal for them and baked flatbread, and they ate.
Before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, young and old, all the people from every quarter.
They shouted to Lot, “Where are the men who came to your house tonight? Send them out to us so we can know them!”{b}
Lot stepped outside to them in the doorway, closing the door after him.
He said, “Please, my brothers, do not do this evil.
See, I have two daughters who have never known a man. I will bring them out to you; do with them as you please. But leave these men alone, since they have come under the shade of my roof.”{c}

“Out of the way!” they answered. And they said, “This fellow came here as an outsider, and now he sets himself up as judge!{d} We will deal worse with you than with them.” They shoved hard against Lot himself and moved in to smash the door.
But the two men inside put out their hands, pulled Lot back into the house to them, and closed the door.
They struck the men who were at the entrance of the house, small and great, with a blinding light,{e} so that they wore themselves out trying to find the entrance.
Then the men said to Lot, “Who else do you have here? A son-in-law, your sons, your daughters, anyone you have in the city, bring them out of this place,
for we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has grown great before Yahweh, and Yahweh has sent us to destroy it.”

Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the men pledged to marry{f} his daughters. “Up! Leave this place,” he said, “for Yahweh is going to destroy the city.” But to his sons-in-law he seemed to be jesting.
At daybreak the angels pressed Lot to hurry. “Up! Take your wife and the two daughters you have here, or you will be swept off in the city’s punishment.”{g}
Still he delayed. Since Yahweh had pity on him, the men took hold of his hand and the hands of his wife and two daughters, led him out, and left him beyond the city.
When they had brought them outside, one{h} said, “Flee for your life! Do not look back, and do not stand still anywhere in the whole plain. Escape to the hills, or you will be swept away.”
But Lot said to them, “Oh no, my lord!{i}
Your servant has won your favor, and you have been very kind to me in keeping me alive. But I cannot flee as far as the hills; the disaster would catch me and I would die.
Look, this town is near enough to flee to, and it is a small one. Please let me escape there. Is it not small? Then my life will be spared.”
He said to him, “Very well, I grant you this request too.{j} I will not overthrow the town you have spoken of.
Hurry! Escape to that town, for I can do nothing until you have come to it.” For this reason the town was named Zoar.{k}
The sun had come up over the earth by the time Lot reached Zoar.
Then Yahweh rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the heavens.{l}
He overthrew those cities and the whole plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.
But Lot’s wife looked back{m} from behind him, and she was turned to a pillar of salt.
Abraham got up early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before Yahweh.
He looked out over Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and there he saw smoke rising from the land, like the smoke of a kiln.
So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities where Lot had lived.
Lot left Zoar and went up to dwell in the hills, he and his two daughters, since he was afraid to stay in Zoar. He and his two daughters made their home in a cave.
The firstborn said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land{n} to come in to us in the way of all the earth.
Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, so that we may preserve offspring from our father.”
So they made their father drink wine that night. The firstborn went in and lay with her father; he did not know when she lay down or when she got up.{o}

Next day the elder said to the younger, “Last night I lay with my father. We will get him drunk with wine again tonight; then you go in and lie with him, so that through our father we may keep his line alive.”
That night they also gave their father wine to drink, and the younger rose and lay with him; and he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.
So Lot’s two daughters conceived by their own father.
The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab.{p} He is the father of the Moabites to this day.
The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi.{q} He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

notes.text: The city gate was the place of business, courts, and civic life. Sitting there may suggest Lot held some standing in the city.
“Know” here means sexual relations, as in 4:1 and 19:8. The demand was for gang rape of strangers who were under a host’s protection, a gross violation of hospitality. Compare Judges 19:22–25.
Literally “the shadow of my beams.” Lot’s offer of his daughters is shocking; the narrative records it without approval, and the later events of 19:30–38 turn on the same daughters.
Literally “and he judges, judging,” a Hebrew way of stressing the verb.
Hebrew sanverim, a rare word used only here and in 2 Kings 6:18. It may mean a sudden dazzling or a confusion of sight.
Or “who had married.” The Hebrew can mean either; 19:8 says the daughters had not known a man, which suggests engagement.
Hebrew awon, “iniquity,” which also means its consequence, “punishment.” The Septuagint reads “the iniquities of the city.”
The Hebrew has “he said.” The Septuagint reads “they said,” as do some other ancient versions.
Or “my Lord.” As in 18:3, the Hebrew vowels read “Lord” (Adonai), but the consonants allow “my lords.”
Literally “I have lifted up your face in this matter also,” an idiom for granting a request.
Zoar sounds like mits’ar, “a small thing” (19:20). Its earlier name was Bela (14:2).
The repetition “Yahweh … from Yahweh” is unusual. Some early Christian writers read it as two divine persons; others see a Hebrew way of saying “from himself.”
Jesus recalls this in Luke 17:32. The salt formations near the Dead Sea gave rise to local traditions about the pillar (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7; Josephus, Antiquities 1.203).
Or “on the earth.” The daughters may have thought the whole world had been destroyed.
In the Masoretic Text the word “when she got up” carries a special scribal dot over one letter, an old mark of doubt or comment, found in only a handful of places in the Torah.
Moab sounds like me’av, “from father.” The Septuagint adds “saying, ‘He is from my father.’”
Ben-ammi means “son of my kin (or people).” The Septuagint reads Amman and adds “saying, ‘Son of my family.’”

verses.text: Abraham moved on from there into the Negev country and lived between Kadesh and Shur. While he was staying as a foreigner in Gerar,
Abraham said of Sarah his wife, “She is my sister.” So Abimelech{a} king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.
God came to Abimelech in a dream in the night and told him, “You are about to die because of the woman you have taken, for she is a man’s wife.”{b}
Now Abimelech had not come near her. He said, “Lord, will you kill a nation even though it is innocent?{c}
Was it not he who told me, ‘She is my sister’? And she too said, ‘He is my brother.’ I acted with an innocent heart{d} and guiltless hands.”
God said to him in the dream, “Yes, I know that you did this with a heart of integrity, and I myself kept you from sinning against me. That is why I did not let you touch her.
Now give the man back his wife. He is a prophet;{e} he will pray on your behalf, and you will live. But if you do not give her back, be sure that you will die, you and everyone belonging to you.”
Early next morning Abimelech summoned all his officials and told them everything, and the men were terrified.

Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, “What is this you have done to us? What offense have I committed against you, that you brought upon me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me deeds that should never be done.”
And Abimelech said to Abraham, “What did you have in mind,{f} that you did this thing?”
Abraham said, “I thought, ‘Surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.’
Besides, she really is my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.
When God caused me to wander{g} from my father’s house, I said to her, ‘This is the kindness you must show me: at every place we come to, say of me, “He is my brother.”’”
Abimelech took sheep and cattle, with male and female servants, and gave them to Abraham; he also gave Sarah, his wife, back to him.
And Abimelech said, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever is good in your eyes.”

To Sarah he said, “Look, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver,{h} about 25 pounds. This is a covering of the eyes{i} for you in the sight of all who are with you, and with everyone you are set right.”{j}
Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female slaves, so that they bore children.
For Yahweh had closed up every womb in the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

notes.text: Abimelech means “my father is king.” It may be a royal title as well as a name (compare 26:1).
Literally “she is married to a husband (ba’al).”
Literally “a righteous nation.” Abimelech echoes Abraham’s plea for Sodom (18:23–25). The Septuagint reads “a nation that sins in ignorance and is righteous.”
Literally “in the integrity of my heart.”
The first use of “prophet” (navi) in the Bible. Here the prophet’s role is to pray for others.
Literally “What did you see?”
The Hebrew verb is plural, which might suggest “the gods made me wander.” But Elohim, “God,” is sometimes used with plural verbs, and Abraham may be speaking in terms a foreign king would understand.

Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms), counting a shekel as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); weight standards varied. The text keeps the literal “pieces of silver” and gives the weight alongside.
The idiom is uncertain. It probably means the payment publicly clears Sarah’s honor, so that others will “cover their eyes” to the matter. The Septuagint reads “the price of your face (or honor).”
Or “you are vindicated” or “you are set right.” The Hebrew nokachat is difficult. The Septuagint reads “speak the truth in all things.”

verses.text: Yahweh visited{a} Sarah just as he had said; Yahweh did for Sarah exactly what he had promised.
Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time that God had told him.
Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.
And Abraham circumcised Isaac his son when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac his son was born to him.
Sarah said, “God has brought me laughter; all who hear of it will laugh with me.”{b}
And she said, “Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.”
The child grew and was weaned, and on the day of Isaac’s weaning Abraham gave a great feast.
But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing.{c}
She said to Abraham, “Send away this slave woman and her son, for this slave woman’s son shall not share the inheritance with my son Isaac.”
The matter was very displeasing{d} to Abraham because of his son.
But God told Abraham, “Do not be troubled over the boy and your slave girl. Do whatever Sarah tells you, for your line will be traced through Isaac.{e}
But I will make a nation of the slave woman’s son too, since he is your offspring.”

Early next morning Abraham took bread and a skin of water and handed them to Hagar, setting them on her shoulder together with the child,{f} and sent her off. She left and roamed the wilderness of Beersheba.
When the skin ran dry, she left the child under a shrub.
She went and sat down at a distance, about a bowshot off, because she said, “Let me not look on the death of the child.” So she sat facing him, raised her voice, and wept.{g}
God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, “What troubles you, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Up! Raise the boy and take a firm hold of him, for of him I will make a great nation.”
God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the water skin, and gave the boy a drink.
God stayed with the boy as he grew. He made his home in the wilderness and became a skilled archer.{h}
He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army{i} said to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do.

So now swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my children or my descendants. As I have shown you loyal kindness, so you will show it to me and to the land where you have lived as a foreigner.”
Abraham said, “I swear it.”
Abraham rebuked Abimelech over a well that Abimelech’s men had taken by force.
Abimelech answered, “I do not know who has done this. You never told me, and I heard of it only today.”
So Abraham took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant.
Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
Abimelech asked Abraham, “Why have you put these seven ewe lambs off by themselves?”
He said, “Accept these seven ewe lambs from my hand, so that they will be my witness that I dug this well.”
For this reason the place was named Beersheba,{j} because the two of them took an oath there.
After making a covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol his army commander left and went back to Philistine country.{k}
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree{l} in Beersheba, and there he called on the name of Yahweh, El Olam.{m}
And Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines for many days.

notes.text: Hebrew paqad, “to visit,” “to attend to,” or “to take note of,” often of God acting to keep a promise.
Or “will laugh at me.” The Hebrew can express shared joy or mocking surprise. The Septuagint reads “will rejoice with me.”
Hebrew metsacheq, from the root of Isaac’s name. It can mean playing, laughing, or mocking (compare Galatians 4:29). The Septuagint adds “with Isaac her son,” and Brenton renders the verb “sporting.”
Literally “evil in the eyes of Abraham, very.”
Literally “in Isaac seed will be called to you.” Quoted in Romans 9:7 and Hebrews 11:18.
The Hebrew order is unclear: either the food and water, or the boy too, are placed on her shoulder. Ishmael was then a teenager (16:16; 21:5). The Septuagint reads “he put the child on her shoulder.”
The Septuagint reads “and the child cried aloud and wept,” which leads into 21:17, where God hears “the voice of the boy.”
The Hebrew rovah qashat is unusual, perhaps “a young bowman” or “one who shoots with the bow.”
The Septuagint adds “Ochozath his friend” (Ahuzzath) here and in 21:32, a name the Hebrew gives only in 26:26.
Beersheba means both “well of seven” and “well of the oath,” since the Hebrew words for “seven” and “swear” share a root. The Septuagint translates it “the Well of the Oath.”
The Philistines are known from records as arriving on this coast around 1200 BC. The name here may be used for earlier people of the same region, or it may update the name for later readers.
Hebrew eshel, “tamarisk,” a hardy tree of the Negev. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “planted a field.”
Hebrew El Olam, “God of eternity” or “the Everlasting God.”

verses.text: Some time afterward God put Abraham to the test.{a} “Abraham!” he called. “Here I am,” Abraham answered.
God said, “Take your son, your one and only son,{b} Isaac, whom you love, and travel to the land of Moriah.{c} Offer him up as a burnt offering,{d} on one of the mountains that I will tell you.”

So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, then got up and went to the place that God had told him.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place far off.
Then Abraham said to his young men, “Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there. We will worship, and we will come back to you.”{e}
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire{f} and the knife, and the two of them walked on together.
Isaac said to Abraham his father, “My father!” And he said, “Here I am, my son.” He said, “Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
Abraham said, “God will see to{g} the lamb for a burnt offering himself, my son.” And the two of them walked on together.
When they came to the place that God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound{h} Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.
Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
But the angel of Yahweh called to him from heaven and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” And he said, “Here I am.”
He said, “Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, since you have not held back your son, your only son, from me.”
Abraham looked up, and there behind him{i} was a ram, caught by its horns in a thicket.{j} He went, took the ram, and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.
So Abraham called the name of that place “Yahweh Yireh,”{k} as it is said to this day, “On the mountain of Yahweh it will be seen.”{l}
The angel of Yahweh called to Abraham a second time from heaven
and said, “I have sworn by myself, declares Yahweh: because you have done this thing and have not withheld your son, your only son,
I will richly bless you and make your descendants as countless as the stars in the sky and the sand along the shore. Your descendants will take hold of the gate{m} of their foes,
and in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed,{n} because you have obeyed my voice.”
Abraham went back to his young men; they rose and traveled together to Beersheba, and Abraham settled in Beersheba.
After these things Abraham was told, “Milcah too has borne children to your brother Nahor:
Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel.”
Bethuel became the father of Rebekah.{o} These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham’s brother.
His concubine, whose name was Reumah, also bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

notes.text: Hebrew nissah, “tested” or “proved.” The narrator tells the reader at the start that this is a test. Jewish tradition calls this chapter the Aqedah, “the Binding” (22:9). Compare Hebrews 11:17–19 and James 2:21–23.
Hebrew yachid, “only” or “unique.” Ishmael had been sent away, so Isaac was the only son left with Abraham and the only son of the promise. The Septuagint reads “the beloved one.”

2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah as the site of Solomon’s temple in Jerusalem. The Septuagint reads “the high land.” The name is linked by sound with ra’ah, “to see,” which runs through the chapter (22:4, 8, 13, 14).
Hebrew olah, literally “that which goes up,” an offering wholly burned on the altar.
The Hebrew verbs are plural: “we will come back.” Hebrews 11:19 sees here Abraham’s faith that God could raise the dead.
Probably a pot of coals for lighting the altar fire.
Literally “God will see for himself the lamb.” In Hebrew “see to” means “provide.” The phrase anticipates the name in 22:14.
Hebrew aqad, used only here in the Bible, the source of the Jewish name for the passage.
Hebrew achar, “behind.” Some Hebrew manuscripts and several ancient versions read echad, “a (single) ram,” which differs by one similar letter.
The Septuagint takes the Hebrew word sevakh, “thicket,” as a name: “a plant of Sabec.”
Hebrew Yahweh yir’eh, “Yahweh will see,” that is, “Yahweh will provide” (compare 22:8). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “The Lord hath seen.”
Or “On the mountain Yahweh will be seen (or will appear),” or “On the mountain of Yahweh it will be provided.” The Hebrew can be vowelled several ways.
The city gate stands for the city itself and its power. The Septuagint reads “the cities of their enemies.”
Or “will bless themselves” (compare 12:3). The verb form here differs from 12:3 and more naturally means “bless themselves.” Acts 3:25 quotes it as a promise to all peoples.
This note about Rebekah prepares for chapter 24.

verses.text: Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of Sarah’s life.{a}
Sarah died in Kiriath-arba{b} (Hebron) in Canaan, and Abraham came to lament over Sarah and to weep for her.
Then Abraham rose from beside his dead and spoke to the sons of Heth:{c}
“I am a foreigner and a resident among you.{d} Give me property among you for a burial place, so that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”
The sons of Heth answered Abraham,
“Hear us, my lord. You are a mighty prince{e} among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold his tomb from you for burying your dead.”
Abraham rose and bowed down to the people of the land, the sons of Heth.
He said to them, “If you are willing for me to bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and plead for me with Ephron son of Zohar,
to let me have the cave of Machpelah{f} that he owns, at the far end of his field. Let him sell it to me at full value here among you, to be mine as a burial site.”
Now Ephron was sitting among the sons of Heth, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the sons of Heth, of all who went in at the gate of his city:
“No, my lord, hear me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead.”{g}
Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land.
and said to Ephron in the people’s hearing, “Please, listen to me. I will pay for the field. Accept the money from me, so I can bury my dead there.”
Ephron answered Abraham,
“My lord, hear me. A piece of land worth about ten pounds{h} of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead.”
Abraham agreed with Ephron and weighed out for him the silver he had named in the hearing of the sons of Heth, about ten pounds of silver by the merchants’ standard weight.{i}
So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, facing Mamre, the field with the cave in it and all the trees in the field throughout its whole boundary, passed
as Abraham’s possession in the sight of the sons of Heth, in front of all who entered the gate of his city.
After this Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah, opposite Mamre, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
The field and the cave in it passed from the sons of Heth to Abraham as property for a burial place.{j}

notes.text: Literally “The life of Sarah was one hundred years, and twenty years, and seven years; these were the years of Sarah’s life.” Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is given.
Kiriath-arba means “city of four,” perhaps four clans or four settlements (compare Joshua 14:15). The Septuagint adds “which is in the valley.”
The sons of Heth (10:15) are a local Canaanite people, elsewhere called Hittites; they were probably not the same as the Hittite empire of Anatolia.
Hebrew ger wetoshav, “a foreigner and a settler,” someone living in the land without owning any of it. This burial cave becomes the first piece of the promised land Abraham owns.
Literally “a prince of God,” a Hebrew way of saying “a very great prince.” The Septuagint reads “a king from God.”
Machpelah may mean “double.” The Septuagint translates it “the double cave.” The traditional site is in Hebron.
The courteous offer of a gift was part of the bargaining. Abraham insists on a purchase so that his ownership could not later be disputed.

Hebrew “four hundred shekels of silver.” A shekel was a weight, not yet a coin; counting it as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), 400 shekels is about 10 pounds (4.6 kilograms). Weight standards varied from place to place and period to period. It was a very high price. The Septuagint reads “didrachms.”
Hebrew “four hundred shekels of silver” (about 10 pounds, 4.6 kilograms; see the note on 23:15), literally “passing to the merchant,” silver of standard, accepted weight.
The cave became the family tomb of Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob (25:9; 49:29–32; 50:13).

verses.text: Abraham was old, well along in years, and Yahweh had blessed Abraham in all things.
Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who managed all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh,{a}
and I will make you swear by Yahweh, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live,
but you will go to my country and to my relatives and take a wife for my son Isaac.”
The servant asked him, “What if the woman will not agree to come with me to this land? Should I then lead your son back to the country you left?”
Abraham said to him, “Be careful that you do not take my son back there.

Yahweh, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth, who pledged to me by oath, ‘To your offspring I will give this land’—he will send his angel before you, and you will take a wife for my son from there.
But if the woman will not agree to come with you, you will be released{b} from this oath to me. Just never lead my son back there.”
So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
The servant took ten of his master’s camels and left, with all sorts of fine gifts from his master in hand. He made his way to Aram-naharaim,{c} to Nahor’s city.
He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at evening, the time when the women go out to draw water.
And he said, “Yahweh, God of my master Abraham, please make things go well for me today, and show loyal love{d} to my master Abraham.
Look, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.

Let the young woman to whom I say, ‘Please lower your jar so that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels too,’ be the one you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown loyal love to my master.”
He had not yet finished speaking when Rebekah came out, with her jar on her shoulder. She was born to Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.
The young woman was very beautiful to look at, a virgin;{e} no man had known her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up.
The servant hurried to meet her and said, “Please give me a little sip of water from your jar.”
“Drink, my lord,” she said. She quickly let her jar down onto her hand and gave him water to drink.
When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, “I will draw for your camels too, until they have finished drinking.”
She quickly tipped her jar out into the trough and hurried back to the well to draw more, drawing enough for every one of his camels.{f}
The man gazed at her in silence, waiting to learn whether Yahweh had made his journey successful or not.
When the camels were done drinking, the man brought out a gold nose ring weighing about a fifth of an ounce,{g} and for her arms two gold bracelets weighing about four ounces.
and said, “Whose daughter are you? Please tell me, is there room in your father’s house for us to spend the night?”
She said to him, “I am the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor.”
And she added, “There is ample straw and feed at our house, and a place to stay the night.”
The man bowed his head and worshiped Yahweh,

and said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withdrawn his loyal love and his faithfulness{h} from my master. As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way to the house of my master’s relatives.”
Then the young woman ran and told her mother’s household{i} about these things.
Rebekah had a brother whose name was Laban. Laban ran out to the man at the spring.

He had seen the nose ring and the bracelets on his sister’s arms, and had heard Rebekah his sister tell what the man had said to her. So he went out to the man and found him still standing by the camels at the spring.
He said, “Come in, you who are blessed by Yahweh. Why are you standing outside? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.”
So the man came into the house. Laban{j} unloaded the camels and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.
Then food was set before him to eat, but he said, “I will not eat until I have told my errand.” He said, “Speak.”
So he said, “I am Abraham’s servant.
Yahweh has blessed my master richly, and he has grown wealthy. Yahweh has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys.
Sarah, my master’s wife, bore my master a son after she had grown old,{k} and he has given him everything he owns.
My master made me take an oath: ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I am living,
but you shall go to the house of my father and to my family, and you shall take a wife for my son.’
I asked my master, ‘What if the woman will not come with me?’

But he said to me, ‘Yahweh, in whose presence I have walked, will send his angel with you and give you success on your journey. You will take a wife for my son from my family and from the house of my father.
You will be released from my oath{l} if you go to my kin; even if they refuse you, you will be released from my oath.’
“When I came to the spring today, I said, ‘Yahweh, God of my master Abraham, if you are indeed making my journey successful, the journey I am on,
see, I am waiting here by the spring. When a young woman{m} comes out to draw, and I ask her, “Please give me a little water to drink from your jar,”
and who says to me, “Drink, and I will draw for your camels too,” let her be the woman whom Yahweh has appointed for my master’s son.’
“Before I had finished speaking in my heart, there was Rebekah coming out with her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, ‘Please let me drink.’
She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels too.’ So I drank, and she watered the camels also.
Then I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ She said, ‘The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
I bowed my head and worshiped Yahweh. I blessed Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, who had guided me along the way of truth to obtain the daughter of my master’s kinsman{n} for his son.
Now, if you are willing to deal with my master in loyal love and faithfulness, tell me; and if not, tell me, so that I may turn to the right hand or to the left.”
Then Laban and Bethuel{o} answered, “This thing comes from Yahweh. We cannot speak to you bad or good.{p}
Look, Rebekah is before you. Take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, as Yahweh has spoken.”
When Abraham’s servant heard what they said, he bowed to the ground before Yahweh.
Then the servant brought out objects of silver, objects of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah; he also gave precious things to her brother and to her mother.
Then he and his companions ate and drank and stayed the night. In the morning when they rose, he said, “Let me go back to my master.”
Her brother and her mother said, “Let the young woman stay with us a few days, ten perhaps.{q} After that she may go.”
He said to them, “Do not hold me up, now that Yahweh has prospered my journey. Send me off, so that I may go to my master.”
They answered, “We will call the girl and ask what she wants.”{r}
So they called Rebekah and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will go.”
So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse,{s} with Abraham’s servant and his men.
They blessed Rebekah, saying to her, “Our sister, may you become thousands of myriads, and may your offspring take possession of the gate of those who hate them.”
Rebekah and her young women rose, rode on the camels, and followed after the man. Thus the servant took Rebekah and departed.
Now Isaac had come from{t} the way to Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the region of the Negev.
Isaac went out to walk{u} in the field toward evening. He looked up and saw camels coming.
Rebekah looked up, and when she saw Isaac, she slipped down from the camel
and asked the servant, “Who is that man walking in the field toward us?” The servant answered, “That is my master.” She took her veil and covered herself with it.
The servant told Isaac all the things he had done.
Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother,{v} and he took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.

notes.text: An oath gesture, found again in 47:29. “Thigh” may be a polite word for the reproductive organs, tying the oath to the family line and the covenant sign of circumcision.
Literally “clean” or “innocent,” released from guilt if the oath is not fulfilled.
Aram-naharaim means “Aram of the two rivers,” the region of the upper Euphrates. The Septuagint reads “Mesopotamia.”
Hebrew chesed, steadfast, loyal love within a relationship of commitment. The word is a key to this chapter (24:14, 27, 49).
Hebrew betulah, a young woman of marriageable age; the clause that follows makes clear that she was a virgin. In 24:43 a different word, almah, “young woman,” is used.
A camel can drink a great deal after a journey. Drawing for ten camels was a heavy task, a sign of Rebekah’s generosity and strength.

Hebrew “a beka (half a shekel) its weight,” about a fifth of an ounce (5.7 grams), and bracelets of “ten shekels of gold their weight,” about 4 ounces (115 grams), counting a shekel as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); weight standards varied. The Septuagint reads “golden earrings of a drachm weight.” 24:47 makes clear the ring was for her nose.
Hebrew chesed we’emet, “loyal love and faithfulness (or truth),” a pair often used of God (Exodus 34:6).
Literally “her mother’s house,” perhaps the women’s quarters, or a sign that her father was no longer living or not the head of the house. Bethuel is barely mentioned (but see 24:50).
The Hebrew has only “he unloaded.” Laban is the most likely subject, though some read it as the servant.
Literally “after her old age.” The Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to read “his old age.”
Hebrew alah, “curse,” the curse that would fall on someone who broke an oath. The Septuagint reads “my curse.”
Hebrew almah, “young woman,” the word used in Isaiah 7:14. Here it describes Rebekah, whom 24:16 calls a virgin.
Literally “brother.” Rebekah was the granddaughter of Abraham’s brother Nahor.

The mention of Bethuel here is surprising, since elsewhere Laban and his mother act for the family (24:28, 53, 55). Some scholars think the name was added, or that it means another member of the household. Josephus says Bethuel was dead.
An idiom meaning “We can say nothing at all against it.”
Literally “days or ten,” an unusual phrase that may mean “a year or ten months,” or “a few days, about ten.” The Septuagint reads “about ten days.”
Literally “ask her mouth.” The family seeks her consent.
Deborah, according to 35:8. The Septuagint reads “her goods.”

The Hebrew is awkward: literally “Isaac came from coming (to) Beer-lahai-roi.” The Septuagint reads “Isaac went through the wilderness to the well of the vision.” Beer-lahai-roi is the well where God met Hagar (16:14).

Hebrew lasuach, a rare verb of uncertain meaning. Proposals include “to walk,” “to meditate,” “to pray,” and “to lament.” The Septuagint reads “to meditate,” and Jewish tradition took this as the origin of the afternoon prayer.
The Hebrew reads “into the tent Sarah his mother,” which looks like a scribal gloss or shortened phrase. The sense is clear: Rebekah takes the place of honor that had been Sarah’s.

verses.text: Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.{a}
She bore to him Zimran and Jokshan, Medan and Midian, Ishbak and Shuah.
Jokshan was the father of Sheba and of Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
The sons of Midian{b} were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the descendants of Keturah.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.
But to the sons of his concubines{c} Abraham gave gifts during his lifetime, and he sent them off to the east country, away from his son Isaac.
These are the days of the years of Abraham’s life: 175 years.
Abraham breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and satisfied,{d} and he was gathered to his people.{e}
Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, facing Mamre,
the field that Abraham bought from the sons of Heth. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife.
After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled near Beer-lahai-roi.
These are the generations{f} of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s slave woman, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of Ishmael’s sons, named in the order of their births: Nebaioth, Ishmael’s firstborn; then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, and Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages and their encampments,{g} twelve chieftains according to their tribes.{h}
Ishmael lived 137 years in all. Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people.
His descendants lived in the territory from Havilah to Shur, which lies east of Egypt on the way to Assyria. He settled at odds with{i} all his kin.
These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham’s son: Abraham fathered Isaac.
Isaac was forty years of age when he took Rebekah as wife—daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram,{j} and sister of Laban the Aramean.
Isaac prayed to Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh answered his prayer, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
The children struggled together{k} within her, and she said, “If it is like this, why am I alive?”{l} So she went to ask Yahweh.
Yahweh said to her, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will separate from your body. One people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”{m}
When her days to give birth were completed, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red,{n} his whole body like a hairy cloak, so they called his name Esau.{o}
After this his brother emerged, his hand grasping the heel of Esau, and he was named Jacob.{p} Isaac was sixty years old at the time she bore them.
The boys grew, and Esau became a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field, but Jacob was a quiet man,{q} dwelling in tents.
Isaac favored Esau, for game was to his liking,{r} but Rebekah favored Jacob.
Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the open country, and he was exhausted.
Esau said to Jacob, “Please let me swallow some of the red stuff, this red stuff, for I am exhausted.” Therefore he was named Edom.{s}
Jacob said, “First sell me your birthright.”{t}
Esau said, “Look, I am about to die. What use is a birthright to me?”
Jacob said, “First give me your oath.” So Esau gave his oath and sold Jacob his birthright.
Jacob gave Esau bread and a stew of lentils; he ate and drank, rose, and left. Thus Esau despised his birthright.{u}

notes.text: Or “had taken.” The Hebrew does not say when this marriage took place; it may have been during Sarah’s lifetime. 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls Keturah a concubine. Keturah may mean “incense,” fitting her descendants’ links with the Arabian incense trade.
Midian became the ancestor of the Midianites, among whom Moses later lived and married (Exodus 2:15–22).
Probably Hagar and Keturah.
Hebrew zaqen wesave’a, “old and satisfied (or full).” The Septuagint reads “full of days,” and some other ancient witnesses also add “of days,” as in 35:29.
An expression for joining one’s ancestors in death, distinct from burial (25:9). It may reflect a belief in continued existence with one’s forebears.
Hebrew toledot, “generations” or “family history,” the heading that divides Genesis into sections (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10, 27; 25:12, 19).
Hebrew tirah, a walled camp or circle of tents used by nomads.
The twelve chieftains fulfill the promise of 17:20. Several names, such as Kedar, Tema, Dumah, and Nebaioth, are known from Assyrian and Arabian records as North Arabian tribes or oases.
Or “to the east of” or “alongside,” as in 16:12. The Hebrew literally reads “he fell upon the face of.” The Septuagint reads “he dwelt in the presence of all his brothers.”
Paddan-aram probably means “field (or plain) of Aram,” the area around Haran. The Septuagint reads “Syrian Mesopotamia.”
Hebrew ratsats, literally “crushed one another,” a violent word. The Septuagint reads “leaped.”
Literally “If so, why this I?” The Hebrew is abrupt. It may mean “Why is this happening to me?” or “Why do I go on living?” The Syriac is reported to read “why do I live?”

The Hebrew rav ya’avod tsa’ir is short and can be read either way: “the older will serve the younger” or, with poetic word order, “the older the younger will serve.” Paul quotes the usual sense in Romans 9:12. The oracle concerns nations, Israel and Edom, as well as two brothers.
Hebrew admoni, “reddish,” a play on Edom (25:30).
The name Esau is not explained in the text. “Hairy” (se’ar) plays on Seir, the hill country where Edom later lived (32:3).
Jacob (Ya’aqov) sounds like aqev, “heel.” The name may mean “may God protect,” but here it is linked with grasping the heel, and later with supplanting (27:36).

Hebrew tam, the word used of Job (Job 1:1), usually meaning “blameless” or “whole.” Here it may mean “mild,” “settled,” or “civilized,” in contrast with the hunter. The Septuagint reads “a simple man.”
Literally “because game was in his mouth.”
Edom means “red.” The Hebrew repeats “the red, this red,” showing Esau’s hungry haste.
The birthright was the firstborn son’s right to a double share of the inheritance and to leadership of the family (Deuteronomy 21:17).
Hebrews 12:16 uses this scene as a warning against treating holy things lightly.

verses.text: Now a famine came upon the land, another besides the first famine in Abraham’s days. And Isaac went to Gerar, to Abimelech, king of the Philistines.{a}
There Yahweh showed himself to Isaac and said, “Do not go down into Egypt. Stay in the land I name to you.

Live as a sojourner in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you. To you and your descendants I will give all these territories, and I will carry out the oath I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and grant to them all these territories, and through your descendants every nation on earth will find blessing,{b}
since Abraham listened to my voice and kept what I entrusted to him: my commands, my decrees, and my teachings.”{c}
So Isaac lived on in Gerar.

The local men asked about his wife, and he told them, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to call her his wife, for he thought, “The men here may kill me to get Rebekah,” because she was lovely to look at.
After he had lived there many days, Abimelech king of the Philistines happened to look down through a window, and there was Isaac fondling{d} his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech summoned Isaac and said, “She is your wife, then! Why did you tell us, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac answered, “I thought I would lose my life on her account.”
Abimelech said, “What have you done to us? Any one of the people could soon have slept with your wife, and you would have laid guilt upon us.”
Then Abimelech gave an order to all the people: “Anyone who lays a hand on this man or on his wife shall be put to death.”
Isaac planted crops in that land, and that same year he harvested a hundredfold,{e} because Yahweh blessed him.
He grew great, and went on growing greater, until he was a man of great wealth.
He owned sheep and cattle and many servants, and the Philistines grew jealous of him.
All the wells that his father’s servants had dug back in Abraham’s lifetime, the Philistines had blocked and filled up with dirt.
Abimelech told Isaac, “Leave us. You have grown far too strong for us.”
So Isaac left and pitched his tents in the Gerar valley{f} and lived there.
Isaac dug again the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had blocked after Abraham’s death, and he called them by the names his father had called them.
Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and struck a spring of running water,{g}
but the shepherds of Gerar argued with Isaac’s shepherds and said, “This water belongs to us.” So he named the well Esek,{h} because they had disputed with him.
They dug a second well, and there was a dispute about it too, so he named it Sitnah.{i}
He moved away from there and dug yet another well, and nobody argued about it. He named it Rehoboth,{j} and said, “At last Yahweh has given us space, and we shall flourish in this land.”
From there he went up to Beersheba.
That night Yahweh appeared to him and said, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Have no fear, for I am at your side. Because of my servant Abraham I will bless you and make your descendants many.”
Isaac built an altar in that place and called upon the name of Yahweh. He set up his tent there, and his servants began digging a well.
Then Abimelech came to him from Gerar, together with Ahuzzath his counselor{k} and Phicol, the general of his army.
Isaac asked them, “Why have you come to me? You hated me and drove me away from you.”
They answered, “We can see plainly that Yahweh is with you. So we thought there should be a sworn agreement between us and you. Let us make a covenant with you
that you will do us no wrong, since we did not lay a hand on you, and we treated you only well, and let you go in peace. Now Yahweh has blessed you.”
Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
Early the next morning they swore oaths to each other. Then Isaac let them go, and they left him in peace.
On that same day Isaac’s servants came with news of the well they had been digging. “We have struck water,”{l} they told him.
He named it Shibah;{m} and so the town is called Beersheba even now.
When Esau was forty, he married Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon the Hittite.{n}
These women brought grief{o} to Isaac and Rebekah.

notes.text: On the Philistines in the time of the patriarchs, see the note on 21:32. This Abimelech may be a successor of the king in chapter 20, since the name may be a royal title (see the note on 20:2).
Or “will bless themselves,” as in 22:18.
Four words for God’s instruction, the last being torah, “law” or “teaching.” The verse describes Abraham as faithful long before the Law of Moses was given.
Hebrew metsacheq, from the same root as Isaac’s name (“he laughs”), here meaning the affectionate play of husband and wife. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “sporting with Rebecca his wife.”

Literally “found a hundred measures.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “found in that year barley an hundred-fold,” which reflects the Hebrew word for “measures” (she‘arim) read with different vowels as “barley” (se‘orim).
Hebrew nachal, a stream valley that may be dry except in the rainy season (a wadi).
Literally “living water,” that is, water flowing from a spring.
Esek means “contention” or “dispute.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates the name “Injury.”
Sitnah means “hostility” or “accusation,” from the same root as satan, “adversary.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “Enmity.”
Rehoboth means “wide places” or “room.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “Room.”
Literally “his friend,” probably a title for a royal counselor. Brenton notes a sense like “he that gives away in marriage,” that is, the king’s groomsman.
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “We have not found water.” The Hebrew lo, “to him,” sounds the same as lo, “not,” and was evidently read that way.
Shibah means “oath” or “seven” (compare 21:31). Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “Oath” and the city “the Well of Oath.”
Brenton notes that Codex Alexandrinus reads “Hivite” here. The lists of Esau’s wives in 28:9 and 36:2–3 give partly different names.
Literally “they were bitterness of spirit to Isaac and to Rebekah.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “they were provoking to Isaac and Rebecca.”

verses.text: Isaac was old, and his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see. He summoned Esau, the elder of his two sons. “My son,” he said. And Esau answered, “I am here.”
Isaac said, “I am an old man now, and I cannot tell when I will die.
So take your hunting gear,{a} your quiver and bow, go out into the countryside, and bring down some game for me.
Then cook me a savory dish of the kind I like and bring it for me to eat, so that I may give you my own blessing{b} before my death.”
Rebekah was listening as Isaac talked with his son Esau. So when Esau had gone off into the countryside to hunt game and bring it home,
Rebekah spoke to her son Jacob: “Now I heard your father speak to Esau your brother, and he said,
‘Bring me some game and cook me a savory dish to eat, and I will bless you in the presence of Yahweh before I die.’
So now, my son, do exactly what I tell you.
Go out to the flock and fetch me two fine young goats, and I will make them into a savory dish for your father, just as he likes it.
Then take it in to your father for him to eat, so that he will bless you before his death.”
Jacob answered his mother Rebekah, “But my brother Esau is a hairy man, and my skin is smooth.
What if my father touches me? I will look like a trickster{c} to him, and I will bring a curse upon myself instead of a blessing.”
His mother said to him, “Your curse be upon me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, fetch them for me.”
So he went and fetched them and brought them to his mother, and she cooked a savory dish the way his father liked it.
Then Rebekah took the finest garments of Esau, her elder son, which she kept at home, and dressed Jacob, her younger son, in them.
She covered his hands and the smooth skin of his neck with the goatskins,
and she handed her son Jacob the savory dish and the bread she had baked.
Jacob went in to his father and said, “Father.” And he answered, “I am here. Which of my sons are you?”
Jacob told his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done what you asked of me. Rise, please; sit and eat from what I hunted, and then bless me.”
Isaac asked his son, “How did you find it so fast, my son?” He answered, “Yahweh your God sent it my way.”
Then Isaac said to Jacob, “Come close, my son, and let me touch you, to learn whether you truly are my son Esau.”
Jacob stepped up to Isaac his father. Isaac felt him and said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.”
He did not know him, for his hands were hairy like his brother Esau’s hands; and so he blessed him.{d}
“Are you truly my son Esau?” he asked. And Jacob said, “I am.”
Isaac said, “Serve it to me, and let me eat my son’s game, so that I may give you my blessing.” Jacob served it to him and he ate, and he brought him wine and he drank.
Then his father Isaac told him, “Come here, my son, and kiss me.”
Jacob drew near and kissed him. Isaac smelled the fragrance of his clothing, and he blessed him, saying, “Ah, the scent of my son is like the scent of a field Yahweh has blessed.{e}
May God grant you dew from the sky and the fat of the land, with grain and new wine{f} in plenty.
May peoples be your servants and nations bow low to you. Rule over your brothers; may your mother’s sons bow low to you. A curse on all who curse you, and a blessing on all who bless you!”
No sooner had Isaac ended the blessing, and Jacob barely stepped out from before his father, than Esau his brother came in from hunting.
He also cooked a savory dish and brought it in to his father. He said to him, “Sit up, Father, and eat some of your son’s game, so that you may give me your blessing.”
His father Isaac asked him, “Who are you?” He answered, “I am Esau, your son, your firstborn.”
Isaac was seized with violent trembling{g} and said, “Then who was it that hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you arrived, and I blessed him. And blessed he shall remain!”
When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out, a great and exceedingly bitter cry, and said to his father, “Bless me, me also, my father!”
But Isaac said, “Your brother came here by trickery and has carried off your blessing.”

Esau said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob?{h} He has cheated me these two times: he took my birthright, and now look, he has taken my blessing.”{i} Then he asked, “Have you not reserved a blessing for me?”
Isaac answered Esau, “I have made him your master. I have given him all his relatives as servants, and I have supported him with grain and new wine. So what is there for me to do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Do you have just one blessing, Father? Bless me as well, Father, bless me too!” And Esau wept aloud.{j}
Then his father Isaac answered him: “Far from the fat of the land shall your home be, and far from the dew of the sky above.{k}
You shall live by the sword and serve your brother; but when you break free,{l} you shall shake his yoke off your neck.”
From then on Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him, and he said to himself, “The time of mourning for my father is not far off; after that I will kill my brother Jacob.”
Someone told Rebekah what her elder son Esau had said. So she sent for Jacob, her younger son, and told him, “Your brother Esau is consoling himself with the thought of killing you.
So, my son, do what I tell you. Leave at once and run to my brother Laban in Haran.
Live with him for a time, until your brother’s rage cools,
until his anger against you passes and he forgets what you did to him. Then I will send word and bring you back. Why should I be robbed of you both on a single day?”{m}

Then Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth.{n} If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth, like these, from the daughters of the land, my life will not be worth living.”

notes.text: Hebrew keli, “equipment” or “weapons.” The word for “quiver” (teli) is found only here in the Bible; its meaning rests on ancient tradition.
“My soul” (nephesh) means “I myself,” with the sense of a full and deliberate blessing. In the ancient world a dying father’s blessing was held to be binding.
Or “a deceiver,” or “one who makes a fool of him.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “as one ill-intentioned.”
This line may summarize the outcome before the blessing itself is given in 27:27–29.
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the smell of an abundant field.”
Hebrew tirosh, freshly pressed wine. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “abundance of corn and wine,” using “corn” in the older British sense of grain.
Literally “trembled a great trembling, to excess.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “was amazed with very great amazement.”
Jacob (Ya’aqov) sounds like the verb aqav, “to grab by the heel,” “to overreach,” or “to supplant.” Compare 25:26 and Jeremiah 9:4.
A wordplay in Hebrew: bekhorah, “birthright,” and berakhah, “blessing.”
Brenton’s Septuagint adds “And Isaac being troubled” before Esau weeps; Brenton notes that these words are not in the Hebrew.

Or “Look, of the richness of the earth will be your dwelling, and of the dew of heaven above.” The Hebrew preposition min can mean “away from” or “a share of.” The words echo 27:28, but the sense is probably the reverse: Edom’s land would be dry. Brenton’s Septuagint takes the second sense: “of the fatness of the earth.”

The Hebrew verb (rud) is uncertain; it may mean “roam free,” “grow restless,” or “break loose.” Compare 2 Kings 8:20–22, where Edom revolts from Judah. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “there shall be a time when thou shalt break and loosen his yoke.”
That is, Jacob killed by Esau, and Esau then condemned for murder (9:6) or driven away as a fugitive.
The sons of Heth were a local Canaanite people (10:15; 23:3). Esau’s Hittite wives are named in 26:34–35.

verses.text: Then Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and commanded him, “You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women.
Get up, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel your mother’s father, and take a wife from there, from the daughters of Laban your mother’s brother.
May El Shaddai{a} bless you and give you many children and increase your number, until you grow into a gathering of peoples.{b}
May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, so that you may possess the land where you are living as a foreigner, which God gave to Abraham.”
So Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, mother of Jacob and Esau.

Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and dispatched him to Paddan-aram to take himself a wife from there, and that in blessing him he had charged him, “You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan,”
and that Jacob had heeded his father and mother and had set out for Paddan-aram.
Esau understood that his father Isaac took no pleasure in the daughters of Canaan.
Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, in addition to the wives he had, Mahalath{c} the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebaioth.
Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran.
He reached a certain place{d} and spent the night there, for the sun had gone down. Taking one of the stones of that place, he put it under his head and lay down there to sleep.
He dreamed, and there was a stairway{e} resting on the earth, with its top touching heaven; and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.{f}
And there was Yahweh, standing above it,{g} and he said, “I am Yahweh, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. To you and to your offspring I will give the land on which you are lying.

Your offspring will be as the dust of the earth, and you will spread abroad to the west, to the east, to the north, and to the south; and in you and in your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.{h}
Look, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”
Jacob awoke out of his sleep and said, “Yahweh is truly here, in this very place, and I was not aware of it!”
He was afraid and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
Jacob rose early in the morning, took the stone that he had put under his head, set it up as a standing stone,{i} and poured oil on top of it.
He called the name of that place Bethel,{j} but the name of the city was Luz at first.{k}
Then Jacob made a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and keep me on this road that I am traveling, and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
so that I come back in peace to my father’s house, then Yahweh will be my God,{l}
and this stone that I have set up as a standing stone shall be a house of God; and of everything you give me, I will surely give you a tenth.”

notes.text: Traditionally “God Almighty”; see the note on El Shaddai at 17:1. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “my God.”
Hebrew qehal ammim. Qahal, “assembly,” is later used of Israel gathered for worship. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “gatherings of nations.”
Called Basemath in 36:3. Brenton’s Septuagint spells the name “Maeleth.”
Literally “the place,” perhaps implying a known holy site. The word returns again and again in this story.
Hebrew sullam, found only here. It may mean a ladder, or a ramp or stairway like those on ancient temple towers (compare 11:4). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “ladder.”
Or “on him,” that is, on Jacob; the Hebrew can mean either. Jesus alludes to this verse in John 1:51.
Or “standing beside him.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the Lord stood upon it.”
Or “will bless themselves.” See the note on 12:3. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “all the tribes of the earth.”
Hebrew matsevah, a standing stone set up as a memorial or to mark a holy place. Later law forbade such pillars when they were tied to the worship of other gods (Deuteronomy 16:22).
Bethel means “house of God.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates the name: “the House of God.”
Brenton’s Septuagint joins the Hebrew words for “but Luz” (ulam luz) into one name: “the name of the city before was Ulam-luz.”
Or “and if Yahweh will be my God, then this stone…” The Hebrew can be divided so that the vow’s condition runs through this clause.

verses.text: Then Jacob went on his journey{a} and came to the land of the people of the east.
As he looked, he saw a well out in the open country, and three flocks of sheep were resting near it, because the flocks drank from that well. A great stone covered its opening.
The shepherds would wait until every flock had come together there. Then they rolled the stone off the opening, watered the sheep, and set the stone back over the well.
Jacob said to them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”
