He said to them, “Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?”{b} They said, “We know him.”
He said to them, “Is it well with him?”{c} They said, “It is well. And look, here comes Rachel his daughter with the sheep.”
He said, “The sun is still high, and it is too early to bring the animals in. Give the sheep water, then take them back out to graze.”
They said, “We are not able until all the flocks have been gathered together and the stone has been rolled off the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep.”
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

When Jacob saw Rachel, daughter of Laban his mother’s brother, with the flock of Laban his mother’s brother, he stepped forward and rolled the stone from the well’s opening, and he watered the sheep of Laban, brother of his mother.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and lifted up his voice and wept.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s relative,{d} and that he was Rebekah’s son, and she ran and told her father.
When Laban heard that Jacob, his sister’s son, had come, he hurried out to him, threw his arms around him, kissed him, and took him home. Jacob told Laban everything that had happened,
and Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh!” And he stayed with him a month.{e}
Laban said to Jacob, “Is it because you are my kinsman that you must serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?”
Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were tender,{f} but Rachel was beautiful in form and beautiful to look at.{g}
Jacob loved Rachel, and he said, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter.”
Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you than give her to another man. Stay with me.”
So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her.
Then Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my time is completed, so that I may go in to her.”
So Laban gathered all the people of the place and made a feast.
In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob went in to her.{h}
Laban gave Zilpah, his slave woman, to his daughter Leah to be her slave woman.
When morning came, behold, it was Leah! So Jacob said to Laban, “What is this that you did to me? Was it not for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?”{i}
Laban said, “It is not done in our place to give the younger before the firstborn.
Finish this one’s bridal week,{j} and then we will give you the younger one as well, for another seven years of work for me.”
Jacob agreed. He finished out Leah’s week, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.
Laban gave Bilhah, his slave woman, to his daughter Rachel to be her slave woman.
Jacob lay with Rachel too, and he loved her more than Leah. He stayed and worked for Laban another seven years.
When Yahweh saw that Leah was unloved,{k} he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben,{l} for she said, “Because Yahweh has looked on my affliction; surely now my husband will love me.”
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Because Yahweh has heard that I am unloved, he has given me this son also.” And she called his name Simeon.{m}
Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi.{n}
And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, “This time I will praise Yahweh.” Therefore she called his name Judah.{o} Then she stopped bearing.

notes.text: Literally “Jacob lifted up his feet.” Brenton gives the Greek in his note as “having lifted up his feet, went.”
“Son” here means descendant; Laban was Nahor’s grandson (24:29).
Literally “Is there peace (shalom) to him?”
Literally “brother.” Jacob was Laban’s nephew.
Literally “a month of days.” Brenton’s note gives the Greek the same way; his text reads “a full month.”

Hebrew rakkot, “tender,” “soft,” or “weak.” It may be praise (gentle eyes) or a contrast with Rachel’s beauty. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “weak.” The names Leah and Rachel may mean “wild cow” and “ewe.”
Literally “beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.”
The bride was probably veiled (compare 24:65), and the evening dark.
Hebrew rimmitani, from the same root as the “deceit” (mirmah) by which Jacob took Esau’s blessing (27:35). The deceiver is deceived.
The wedding feast lasted seven days (compare Judges 14:12).
Literally “hated,” a Hebrew way of saying “loved less” (compare 29:30; Deuteronomy 21:15; Malachi 1:2–3). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “hated.”
Reuben sounds like re’u ben, “See, a son!” and like Leah’s words ra’ah be‘onyi, “he has looked on my affliction.”
Simeon sounds like shama, “he has heard.”
Levi sounds like yillaweh, “he will be joined.”
Judah sounds like odeh, “I will praise.”

verses.text: When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or else I am dead!”{a}
Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in the place of God, who has kept from you the fruit of the womb?”
She said, “Here is Bilhah, my servant. Sleep with her, and let her bear children upon my knees,{b} so that through her I too may be built up with children.{c}”
So she gave him Bilhah her slave woman as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Then Rachel said, “God has judged me, and he has also heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan.{d}
Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, “I have struggled with mighty wrestlings{e} against my sister, and I have prevailed.” So she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, she took Zilpah her slave woman and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Then Zilpah, Leah’s slave woman, bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, “Fortune has come!”{f} and she named him Gad.
Zilpah, Leah’s slave woman, bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, “What joy is mine! The women will count me blessed.” And she named him Asher.{g}
In the days of wheat harvest Reuben went out and found mandrakes{h} in the field and brought them to Leah his mother. Then Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

Leah answered her, “Was it not enough that you took my husband? Now will you take my son’s mandrakes as well?” Rachel replied, “Very well, he will sleep with you tonight, and your son’s mandrakes will be the price.”
When Jacob came in from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You must come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he lay with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, “God has given me my wages, because I gave my slave woman to my husband.” So she called his name Issachar.{i}
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, “God has given me a fine dowry. This time my husband will hold me in honor,{j} since I have given him six sons.” And she named him Zebulun.
Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.{k}
Then God remembered Rachel. God listened to her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son and said, “God has taken away my disgrace.”
And she called his name Joseph,{l} saying, “May Yahweh add to me another son!”
After Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me away, so that I may go to my own place and my own country.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, and let me go, for you know the service I have given you.”
But Laban answered, “If you look on me with kindness, stay. I have seen by the signs{m} that Yahweh has blessed me for your sake.”
He said, “Name your wages, and I will give it.”
He answered, “You yourself know how I served you and how your livestock fared under my care.
The little you had before I came has grown into a multitude, and Yahweh has blessed you wherever I set foot.{n} But now, when shall I do something for my own house as well?”
He said, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said, “You shall not give me anything. If you will do this one thing for me, I will again pasture your flock and keep it.
Today I will go through all your flocks and take out of them each sheep that is speckled or spotted, each dark lamb, and each goat that is spotted or speckled. Those will be my pay.{o}
In time to come my honesty will speak for me. Whenever you come to check my pay, any goat among mine that is not speckled or spotted, and any lamb that is not dark, you may count as stolen.”
“Agreed,” said Laban. “It will be just as you say.”

That same day Laban set apart the male goats that were streaked and spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted, every one with white in it, and every dark one among the lambs, and he placed them in the care of his sons.
He set three days’ travel between himself and Jacob; and Jacob went on shepherding what remained of Laban’s flocks.
Jacob cut green branches of poplar, almond, and plane tree,{p} and stripped the bark in white stripes, laying bare the white wood beneath.
Then he placed the stripped branches in the drinking troughs, facing the flocks, at the places where the flocks came for water. The animals bred when they came to drink,
the flocks mated in front of the rods, and the flocks bore young that were striped, speckled, and spotted.{q}
Jacob separated the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the striped and all the dark in the flock of Laban. He put his own flocks apart and did not put them with Laban’s flock.
Whenever the stronger of the flock were mating, Jacob would lay the rods in the troughs before the eyes of the flock, so that they would mate among the rods,
but for the feebler of the flock he would not put them there. So the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s.{r}
Thus the man grew exceedingly rich, and had large flocks, female and male servants, camels, and donkeys.

notes.text: Literally “if not, I am dying.” Rachel later dies giving birth to her second son (35:16–19).
A rite of adoption or of claiming the child as one’s own (compare 48:12; 50:23).
Literally “I will be built,” a play on ben, “son.” See the note on 16:2.
Dan sounds like dan, “he has judged” or “vindicated.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “God has given judgment for me.”

Literally “wrestlings of God,” a Hebrew way of saying “mighty wrestlings” (compare the note on 23:6). Naphtali sounds like niphtalti, “I have wrestled.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “God has helped me, and I contended with my sister and prevailed.”

The written Hebrew reads begad, “with good fortune”; the Masoretic reading tradition divides it as ba gad, “good fortune has come.” Gad was also the name of a god of fortune (Isaiah 65:11). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “It is happily.”
Asher sounds like ashrei, “happy” or “blessed.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I am blessed, for the women will pronounce me blessed.”

Hebrew duda’im, a plant whose root and fruit were believed to help conception; the name sounds like dodim, “love.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “apples of mandrakes” and dates this to “the day of barley-harvest.”
Issachar sounds like sakhar, “wages” or “hire” (30:16). Brenton’s Septuagint explains the name: “Issachar, which is, Reward.”
Or “will dwell with me.” Zebulun sounds like both zebed, “gift,” and zabal, a rare verb meaning “honor” or “dwell.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “my husband will choose me.”
Dinah’s name, from the same root as Dan, is not explained. Her story is told in chapter 34.
Joseph sounds like both asaph, “he has taken away” (30:23), and yoseph, “may he add.”
Or “I have grown rich.” Hebrew nichashti usually means “I have practiced divination” (compare 44:5). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I would augur well.”
Literally “at my foot.” Brenton notes that both the Greek and the Hebrew literally read “at my foot.”

In that region sheep were usually white and goats dark, so the speckled, spotted, and dark animals would have been few. Brenton’s Septuagint has Jacob take “every grey sheep among the rams” together with the speckled and spotted goats.

The trees cannot be identified with certainty. Hebrew livneh, “poplar,” sounds like lavan, “white,” and like Laban’s name; the wordplay runs through the passage. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “storax tree and walnut and plane-tree.”
Ancient herders believed that what a mother saw at mating could mark her young. Jacob later credits the result to God, not to his own method (31:9–12).

The meaning of “stronger” and “feebler” is uncertain; they may refer to sturdy and weak animals or to animals breeding at different seasons. Brenton notes that the Septuagint, by making the birthing time the reason, has “obscured the passage.”

verses.text: Word reached Jacob that Laban’s sons were complaining, “Jacob has seized everything our father owned. Out of our father’s goods he has built up all these riches.”{a}
And Jacob saw that Laban’s face was not toward him as it had been before.{b}
Then Yahweh said to Jacob, “Return to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will be with you.”
Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah and had them come out to the open country where his flocks were.
and said to them, “I see that your father’s face is not toward me as it was before. But the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have served your father with all my strength.
Yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times.{c} But God did not let him harm me.
If he said, ‘The speckled will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore speckled young. And if he said, ‘The striped will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore striped young.
So God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me.
At the time the flocks were breeding, I had a dream. I looked up and saw that the he-goats leaping on the flock were striped, speckled, and mottled.
Then the angel of God said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob.’ And I said, ‘Here I am.’
He said, ‘Look up and see: all the male goats that mount the flock are streaked, speckled, and spotted, for I have seen everything Laban is doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel,{d} where you anointed a standing stone, where you made a vow to me. Now rise, go out from this land, and return to the land of your birth.’”
Rachel and Leah replied, “Do we have any share left, or anything to inherit, from our father’s household?
Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and he has completely used up the money paid for us.{e}
All the riches God has stripped from our father are ours and our children’s. So go ahead and do everything God has said to you.”
So Jacob got up and set his sons and his wives on camels.
He drove away all his livestock and all the goods he had gained, the livestock he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s household gods.{f}
Jacob also stole the heart of Laban the Aramean{g} by keeping from him the news that he was running away.
He fled with all that he had. He rose, crossed the River,{h} and turned his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
Two days later, on the third day, someone told Laban that Jacob had run away.
Taking his kinsmen with him, he chased after Jacob for a seven days’ journey and overtook him in the hills of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, “Be careful that you say nothing to Jacob, either good or bad.”{i}
Laban overtook Jacob, who had his tent pitched on the mountain; and Laban and his kinsmen camped in the hill country of Gilead.
And Laban said to Jacob, “What have you done? You have deceived me and carried off my daughters like captives of the sword!
Why did you run away in secret and cheat me? You did not tell me, or I would have sent you off with joy and with songs, with tambourine and with lyre.
You did not even let me kiss my grandsons and my daughters goodbye. Now you have acted foolishly.
It is in my power to do you harm. But the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, ‘Be careful that you say nothing to Jacob, either good or bad.’
Now you have left because you were homesick for your father’s house. Even so, why have you taken my gods?”
Jacob replied to Laban, “I was afraid. I told myself that you might seize your daughters from me.

As for your gods, whoever is found to have them will not stay alive. With our kinsmen watching, search for anything of yours that I have, and take it back.” Jacob had no idea that Rachel had taken them.
Laban searched Jacob’s tent, then Leah’s tent, then the tent of the two servant women, and found nothing. After he came out of Leah’s tent, he went into Rachel’s.
Now Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel’s saddle and sat on them. Laban felt all through the tent but did not find them.
Rachel said to her father, “My lord, do not be angry that I do not stand up in your presence. It is the time of month for me.”{j} He searched everywhere, but the household gods did not turn up.
Jacob was angry and found fault with Laban, and in reply Jacob said to Laban, “What is my crime? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?
You have searched through all my belongings; what have you found of all your household possessions? Put it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, and let them judge between the two of us.
I have spent twenty years with you now. Your ewes and your female goats never miscarried, and I never ate the rams of your flock.

When an animal was mauled by beasts, I never brought it back to you; I made good the loss myself. You demanded payment from me for anything stolen, whether it was taken in the daytime or in the night.
That was my life: the heat wore me down by day and the frost by night, and sleep would not come to my eyes.
These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.

Had the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac,{k} not stood with me, you would have sent me off now with nothing in my hands. But God took note of how I was wronged and how hard I worked, and last night he gave his judgment.”

Laban answered Jacob, “These women are my daughters, these children are my grandchildren, these flocks are my flocks. Everything in front of you belongs to me. Yet what can I do now for my daughters here, or for the children they have had?
So come, you and I will cut a covenant, and it will stand as a witness between us.”{l}
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a standing stone.
And Jacob said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.{m}
Laban said, “This heap is a witness between me and you today.” That is why it was named Galeed,
and also Mizpah,{n} because he said, “May Yahweh watch between me and you when we are out of each other’s sight.
If you treat my daughters badly, or marry other wives besides them, remember that even when no one else is present with us, God is watching as witness between us.”
Then Laban said to Jacob, “See this heap and see the standing stone, which I have set up between me and you.{o}
This mound bears witness, and the pillar bears witness, that I will not cross over past this mound into your land, and you will not cross over past this mound and this pillar into mine, to do harm.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.”{p} So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Jacob offered a sacrifice there on the mountain and invited his kinsmen to share the meal. They ate together and stayed the night on the mountain.
Early in the morning Laban rose and kissed his grandsons and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned to his home.{q}

notes.text: Literally “all this glory” (kavod), here meaning wealth and the honor that goes with it.
Literally “was not with him as yesterday and the day before,” a Hebrew way of saying “as before.” Brenton notes the same idiom in the Greek.
“Ten times” means “again and again.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “changed my wages for the ten lambs.”
Hebrew ha’el bet-el, “the God of Bethel.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I am God that appeared to thee in the place of God.”
Literally “he has eaten, yes eaten, our money,” that is, the bride price that should in part have come to the daughters. Laban had been paid in fourteen years of Jacob’s labor.
Hebrew teraphim, small figures kept in the home, possibly images of ancestors or household protectors, and perhaps linked with inheritance or divination. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “images.”

Literally “stole the heart of Laban,” meaning he deceived him. The same verb is used of Rachel stealing the household gods (31:19). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Jacob hid the matter from Laban the Syrian.”
That is, the Euphrates.
Literally “from good to bad,” meaning that Laban must not try to persuade or threaten Jacob into returning.
That is, she was having her monthly period. Later law treated anything she sat on at that time as unclean (Leviticus 15:19–23), which adds irony to Laban’s gods being hidden under her.
Hebrew pachad yitschaq, “the Fear of Isaac,” that is, the God whom Isaac feared, or possibly “the Kinsman of Isaac.” The title appears again in 31:53. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the fear of Isaac.”
The Hebrew says “let it be a witness” without naming what “it” is; the covenant is probably meant.

Both names mean “heap of witness,” Laban’s in Aramaic and Jacob’s in Hebrew. The Aramaic words are the first in the Bible. Galeed sounds like Gilead. Brenton’s Septuagint translates the names: “the Heap of Testimony” and “the Witness Heap.”
Mizpah means “watchtower” or “lookout,” from tsaphah, “to watch.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the vision.”
Brenton’s Septuagint arranges 31:48–52 differently and numbers one part as an extra verse.
The verb “judge” is plural in Hebrew, which may suggest that Laban thought of two gods. The words “the God of their father” are absent from Brenton’s Septuagint.

In the Hebrew text this verse is 32:1, and the verses of chapter 32 are numbered one higher than in English. Brenton’s Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering. This translation uses the English numbering.

verses.text: Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is God’s camp!” So he called the name of that place Mahanaim.{a}
Jacob sent envoys ahead of himself to Esau his brother, to the land of Seir, the territory of Edom.
He instructed them: “You shall say this to my lord Esau: ‘Your servant Jacob says: I have been staying with Laban as a resident alien, and I have remained until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, and flocks, and male servants and female servants. I am sending this message to my lord, hoping to find favor in your sight.’”
The messengers returned to Jacob with this report: “We came to your brother Esau; he is already on his way to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.”
Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps,
He reasoned, “Should Esau attack one group and destroy it, the other group can get away.”
Jacob said, “God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, Yahweh, who said to me, ‘Go back to your land and to your kindred, and I will treat you well,’
I am too small for all the steadfast love{b} and all the faithfulness you have shown me, your servant. When I crossed this Jordan I had nothing but my staff, and now I have grown into two companies.
Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I fear him, that he may come and strike me, the mothers with the children.{c}
But you said, ‘I will surely do you good and make your offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for multitude.’”
Jacob spent the night there. Then, out of what he owned, he chose a present for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty milking camels and their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He handed them over to his servants, each drove separately, and told his servants, “Cross over before me, and put a space between drove and drove.”
He gave orders to the man leading the first drove: “When my brother Esau comes upon you and asks, ‘Whose man are you? Where are you headed? Who owns these animals in front of you?’
then answer, ‘They are your servant Jacob’s. He is sending them as a present for my lord Esau, and he himself is following after us.’”
He commanded the second and the third and all who followed the herds in the same way: “You shall say the same thing to Esau when you find him,
and you shall also say, ‘Your servant Jacob is behind us.’” For he thought, “I will appease him{d} with the present going before me, and after that I will see his face; perhaps he will accept me.”{e}
So the gift went on ahead of him, and he himself stayed that night in the camp.
During that night he rose, took his two wives and his two slave women, along with his eleven children, and crossed the Jabbok at the ford.{f}
He sent them over the stream, together with all his possessions.
And Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled{g} with him until the break of dawn.
The man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, so he struck the hollow of Jacob’s hip, and the hip was wrenched as the two wrestled.
Then he said, “Let me go, for the dawn has broken.” But Jacob said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Jacob.”
He said, “Your name shall not be called Jacob any longer, but Israel,{h} because you have contended with God and with men, and you have prevailed.”
Jacob asked, “Please tell me your name.” He replied, “Why do you ask about my name?” Then he blessed him there.
Jacob named the place Peniel,{i} “because,” he said, “I saw God face to face, and still I am alive.”
The sun was coming up over him as he went on past Penuel,{j} and he limped on account of his hip.
For this reason the Israelites, even now, do not eat the thigh sinew{k} over the hip joint, because Jacob was struck at the hip joint, on that sinew.

notes.text: Mahanaim means “two camps.” The word returns in 32:7 and 32:10, where Jacob divides his people into two camps. Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “Encampments.” In the Hebrew text this verse is 32:3; see the note on 31:55.
Hebrew chesed, God’s loyal, covenant love. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Let there be to me a sufficiency of all the justice and all the truth,” taking the opening words differently.
Literally “the mother upon the children,” a proverb for total slaughter (compare Hosea 10:14).

Literally “I will cover his face,” an expression for making amends. The word “face” runs through 32:20–31 and 33:10, leading up to Peniel, “face of God.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I will propitiate his countenance.”
Literally “perhaps he will lift up my face.”
The Jabbok (Yabboq) sounds like the verb for “wrestled” (ye’aveq) in 32:24, and like Jacob’s name.
Hebrew ye’aveq, found only here and in 32:25. Hosea 12:3–4 says that Jacob “strove with God” and “strove with the angel.”
Israel probably means “God strives” or “may God rule,” but here it is explained as “he strives with God.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “for thou hast prevailed with God, and shalt be mighty with men.”
Peniel means “face of God.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “the Face of God.”
Penuel is another spelling of Peniel, used for the town in Judges 8:8 and 1 Kings 12:25.
Probably the sciatic nerve. This custom is not found in the Law of Moses but was kept in later Jewish practice.

verses.text: Jacob looked up and saw Esau approaching with four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servant women.
He placed the servant women and their children at the front, Leah and her children behind them, and Rachel and Joseph at the very back.
He crossed over in front of them and bowed himself to the earth seven times, until he had come close to his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him,{a} and they wept.
When Esau lifted his eyes and saw the women and the children, he asked, “Who are these that are with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
Then the slave women came near, they and their children, and bowed down.
Leah likewise and her children came near and bowed down. Last of all Joseph and Rachel came near, and they bowed down.
Esau asked, “What was the meaning of all those droves I came upon?” Jacob said, “I hoped to win my lord’s favor.”
But Esau said, “I have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have for yourself.”
Jacob said, “No, please. If I have found favor in your eyes, then accept my gift from my hand. For truly I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you have received me favorably.{b}
Please take my blessing{c} that has been brought to you, for God has been gracious to me, and I have everything.” He pressed him, and he accepted it.
Then Esau said, “Let us set out on our journey, and I will go ahead of you.”

Jacob replied, “My lord can see that the children are young and weak, and I have to think of the sheep and cattle that are nursing. If the animals are pushed hard even one day, the whole flock will die.

Let my lord please pass on ahead of his servant. I will move along at an easy pace, according to the pace of the livestock before me and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir.”{d}
Esau said, “Let me at least leave with you some of the people who are with me.” But he said, “Why should you? Let me only find favor in my lord’s sight.”
So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
But Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built himself a house and made shelters for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.{e}
After his return from Paddan-aram, Jacob arrived in peace{f} at the city of Shechem in Canaan, and he set up camp facing the city.
For a hundred qesitah{g} he purchased the plot of ground where he had put up his tent from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem.
There he set up an altar and called it El Elohe Israel.{h}

notes.text: In the Hebrew text the word “and kissed him” is marked with special dots by the scribes, an old sign that the word was discussed or doubted. Some later interpreters took the dots to question Esau’s sincerity.
Compare 32:30. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I have seen thy face, as if any one should see the face of God.”
That is, the gift. The word berakhah, “blessing,” recalls the blessing Jacob took from Esau (27:35–36).
There is no record that Jacob went to Seir; he turned west instead (33:17).
Succoth means “shelters” or “booths.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “Booths.”
Hebrew shalem, “whole” or “in peace,” fulfilling Jacob’s vow in 28:21. Brenton’s Septuagint takes it as a place name: “Jacob came to Salem, a city of Secima.”

Hebrew qesitah, a unit of money or weight whose value is unknown, so no modern equivalent is given. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “a hundred lambs.” Joshua 24:32 says Joseph’s bones were buried in this plot, and John 4:5 refers to it.
Hebrew El Elohe Israel, “God, the God of Israel” or “God is the God of Israel.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “and called on the God of Israel.”

verses.text: Once Dinah, Leah’s daughter by Jacob, went out to see the young women who lived in that region.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite,{a} the chief of that land, saw her; and he took her, lay with her, and humiliated her.{b}
His heart was bound to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. He loved the girl and spoke to her heart.{c}
So Shechem spoke to his father Hamor, saying, “Get me this girl as my wife.”
News came to Jacob that he had defiled Dinah his daughter. His sons were out in the open field with his herds, and Jacob kept silent until they came in.
And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Jacob’s sons came in from the field when they heard it. The men were distressed and furiously angry, because he had committed an outrage{d} in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter—a thing that must not be done.
But Hamor spoke with them, saying, “The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife.
Intermarry with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.
Settle among us. The country lies before you. Stay here, move about freely, and get land of your own.”
Shechem also said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give.
Set the bride price{e} and the gifts as high as you like, and I will pay whatever you ask. Just let me have the girl for my wife.”
Because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah, Jacob’s sons gave Shechem and Hamor his father a crafty answer.{f}
They told them, “We are not able to do such a thing. To give our sister to a man without circumcision would bring shame upon us.
We will consent on one condition: you must become like us, with every male of yours circumcised.
After that we will give you our daughters and marry your daughters. We will settle among you, and we will be a single people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter and go.”
Their words pleased Hamor and Hamor’s son Shechem.
The young man lost no time in doing it, for Jacob’s daughter was his delight. He was the most respected man in his whole family.
Hamor and Shechem his son went to their city gate and addressed the men of the city.
“These men are peaceable with us; let them settle in the land and trade in it, for the land is spacious enough for them. We will take their daughters as wives and give them our daughters.
Only on this condition will the men consent to dwell with us and become a single people: every male among us must be circumcised, just as they are circumcised.
Their herds, their goods, and every animal they own, will these not become ours? Let us only consent to their terms, and they will settle among us.”
And all who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.{g}
Three days later, while the men were still sore, Simeon and Levi, two of Jacob’s sons and full brothers of Dinah, took up their swords, entered the unsuspecting city,{h} and put every male to death.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the edge of the sword, took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went away.
The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister.
They carried off sheep, cattle, and donkeys, and everything else, both inside the city and out in the fields.
All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, they captured and carried off, and all that was in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have ruined me. You have made my name a stench{i} among the people who live in this land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. We are only a handful. If they band together and fall on me, I will be wiped out, my household and I.”
They replied, “Was he to use our sister as a harlot?”{j}

notes.text: Brenton notes that Codex Alexandrinus reads “the Chorrhaean” (Horite). Brenton’s main text reads “the Evite,” that is, Hivite.
Hebrew ’innah, “humbled,” “violated.” The verbs describe a forced act.
A Hebrew idiom for speaking kindly or tenderly, as one who woos. Brenton notes that the Greek is a literal version of this Hebrew idiom.
Hebrew nevalah, a word for a grave moral outrage, a deed of senseless wickedness (compare Deuteronomy 22:21; 2 Samuel 13:12). “In Israel” here may mean the family of Israel, that is, Jacob.
Hebrew mohar, the payment from the groom to the bride’s family (compare Exodus 22:16–17; Deuteronomy 22:29).
Hebrew mirmah, the same word used of Jacob’s deceit in 27:35. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “craftily.”
Probably meaning all the men who took part in the city’s public life (compare 23:10).
Or “came against the city unexpectedly.” Hebrew betach, “in security,” may refer either to the city or to the attackers. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “came upon the city securely.”
Literally “making me stink,” that is, making me hateful. Jacob’s judgment on Simeon and Levi returns in 49:5–7.
The chapter ends with the brothers’ question unanswered.

verses.text: God said to Jacob, “Get up, go up to Bethel and live there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, “Put away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your clothes.
Let us rise and go up to Bethel, and I will make an altar there to the God who answered me on the day of my distress and has been with me on the road I have traveled.”
They handed over to Jacob every foreign god they had, along with the rings from their ears.{a} Jacob buried them beneath the great tree{b} near Shechem.
As they set out, a dread from God{c} lay on the towns all around, and no one chased after Jacob’s sons.
And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him,
He built an altar there and called the place El Bethel,{d} because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother.
And Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under an oak. So its name was called Allon-bacuth.{e}
God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.
God said to him, “Your name is Jacob, but you will be called Jacob no more. Your name will be Israel.” And so he named him Israel.{f}
God said to him, “I am El Shaddai.{g} Be fruitful and increase. A nation, and a gathering of nations, will spring from you, and kings will descend from you.{h}
This land, which I gave to Abraham and to Isaac, I now give to you, and after you I will give it to your descendants.”
Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob raised up a standing stone in the place where he had spoken with him, a standing stone of stone. He poured a drink offering upon it and poured oil upon it.
So Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They set out from Bethel.{i} While there was still a stretch of road{j} before Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and her labor was severe.
At the worst of her pains the midwife told her, “Take heart. This one is a son for you too.”
As her soul went out (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni,{k} but his father called him Benjamin.{l}
Rachel died there and was buried beside the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.{m}
and Jacob set up a standing stone over her tomb. It is the standing stone of Rachel’s tomb, to this day.
Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.{n}
While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine. And Israel heard of it.{o} Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.
The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s slave woman: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.{p}
Jacob came home to his father Isaac at Mamre near Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, the place where Abraham and Isaac had stayed as sojourners.
Now the days of Isaac were a hundred and eighty years.
And Isaac breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.{q}

notes.text: Earrings could be amulets or bear the marks of other gods (compare Exodus 32:2–4; Judges 8:24–27). Brenton’s Septuagint adds that Jacob hid them “and destroyed them to this day.”
Or “terebinth.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the turpentine tree.” Compare 12:6.
Or “a great terror.” Literally “a terror of God,” which can mean a terror sent by God or a very great terror (compare the note on 30:8).
Hebrew El Bethel, “God of Bethel.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads simply “Bæthel,” as do some other ancient witnesses.
Allon-bacuth means “oak of weeping.” Brenton’s Septuagint translates it “The Oak of Mourning.”
Compare 32:28, where the name is first given.
Traditionally “God Almighty”; see the note on El Shaddai at 17:1. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I am thy God.”
Literally “from your loins.”
Brenton’s Septuagint places here the words of 35:21, “and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Gader,” and Brenton marks them in brackets.
Hebrew kivrat-ha’arets, a distance whose length is unknown (also in 48:7). Brenton’s Septuagint treats it as a place name, “Chabratha.”
Ben-oni means “son of my sorrow” or, less likely, “son of my strength” (compare 49:3). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “The son of my pain.”
Benjamin means “son of the right hand,” that is, a son of honor or of good fortune. It can also mean “son of the south,” since the right hand pointed south for one facing east.

Compare 48:7. First Samuel 10:2 places Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem; the identification with Bethlehem may reflect a later tradition. Matthew 2:18 quotes Jeremiah 31:15, where Rachel weeps for her children.
Or “Migdal-eder,” meaning “tower of the flock.” Compare Micah 4:8.
Brenton’s Septuagint adds “and the thing appeared grievous before him.” In the Hebrew text there is a space within the verse here, as if a paragraph ends. Compare 49:4.
Benjamin, born near Ephrath (35:16–18), is included in this summary.
Isaac’s death is reported here to close his story, though the account of Joseph that follows begins while Isaac is still alive (compare 25:26; 37:2; 41:46; 47:9).

verses.text: These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom).
Esau took his wives from the Canaanite women: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter{a} of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth.{b}
By Esau, Adah gave birth to Eliphaz, and Basemath gave birth to Reuel.
Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.

Then Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the people of his household, his livestock, all his animals, and all the property he had acquired in the land of Canaan, and went to a land away from his brother Jacob.
Their herds and goods had grown too large for them to stay side by side, and the country where they were sojourning could not feed so many animals.
So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, and Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna, a secondary wife of Eliphaz son of Esau, gave birth to Amalek{c} for Eliphaz. These were descendants of Adah, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau’s wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
These were the chiefs{d} of the descendants of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau—Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, Chief Kenaz,
Korah,{e} Gatam, and Amalek. These are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah.
Reuel son of Esau had these sons: Chief Nahath, Chief Zerah, Chief Shammah, and Chief Mizzah. They were the chiefs from Reuel in Edom, grandsons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
Oholibamah, Esau’s wife, had these sons: Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, and Chief Korah. They were the chiefs from Oholibamah, Anah’s daughter, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite,{f} the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam;{g} and Lotan’s sister was Timna.
These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found the hot springs{h} in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father.
These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Dishon:{i} Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
The Horite chiefs were Chief Lotan, Chief Shobal, Chief Zibeon, Chief Anah,
Chief Dishon, Chief Ezer, and Chief Dishan. They were the Horite chiefs, clan by clan, in Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites.{j}
Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place. The name of his city was Avith.
Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the River{k} reigned in his place.
Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar{l} reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs descended from Esau, by their families and their places, by name: Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth,
Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon,
Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar,
Chief Magdiel, Chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, by their settlements in the land they possessed. This is Esau, the father of Edom.{m}

notes.text: Brenton’s Septuagint reads “son of Sebegon,” agreeing with 36:24, where Anah is a son of Zibeon. Some other ancient witnesses are reported to read the same.
Esau’s wives are named differently in 26:34 and 28:9 (Judith, Basemath the daughter of Elon, and Mahalath). The traditions may preserve alternate names.
Amalek became the ancestor of the Amalekites, Israel’s enemies (Exodus 17:8–16).
Hebrew alluph, “chief” or “clan leader.” The word may also mean “clan” (compare the note on 36:43).
Korah is not among the sons of Eliphaz in 36:11 or 1 Chronicles 1:36; he appears as a son of Oholibamah in 36:5, 14, and 18. The Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to lack the name here.
The Horites were the earlier people of Seir (14:6; Deuteronomy 2:12, 22).
Called Homam in 1 Chronicles 1:39.
Hebrew yemim, found only here; the meaning is uncertain. “Hot springs” follows an ancient Latin tradition. Brenton’s Septuagint keeps the word untranslated: “who found Jamin in the wilderness.”
Hebrew Dishan, but Dishon in 36:25 and 1 Chronicles 1:41. The two names are close in Hebrew.
Or “before an Israelite king reigned over them.” The note appears to come from a time when Israel already had kings, or it looks ahead to them.
Probably the Euphrates, though a smaller river nearer Edom may be meant.
Called Hadad in 1 Chronicles 1:50, and his city Pai. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Arad the son of Barad,” and his city “Phogor.”
The list of chiefs in 36:40–43 may name clans or regions as well as persons.

verses.text: Jacob made his home in Canaan, the country where his father had stayed as a sojourner.

These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, at seventeen years of age, was tending the flock together with his brothers, and he was a youth{a} with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives. Joseph brought a bad report about them to their father.{b}
Now Israel loved Joseph more than any of his other sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a long robe with sleeves.{c}
But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.
Joseph had a dream, and he told it to his brothers, which made them hate him all the more.
He said to them, “Please listen to this dream that I have dreamed:
There we were, binding sheaves in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, and your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers answered, “So you think you will be king over us? You will be our master?” And his dreams and what he said about them made them hate him still more.
He dreamed still another dream and recounted it to his brothers: “Look, I have had another dream, and this time the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”

When he recounted it to his father and to his brothers, his father scolded him and said, “What kind of dream is this that you have had? Are we really to come, I and your mother{d} and your brothers, and bow down to the ground before you?”
His brothers envied him, but his father kept turning the thing over in his mind.
Some time later his brothers had gone to graze their father’s sheep and goats around Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Your brothers are grazing the flock at Shechem, are they not? Come, I am sending you to them.” Joseph answered, “I am ready.”
Israel told him, “Go and find out how your brothers are getting on, and how the flock is, and come back and tell me.” So he sent him off from the valley of Hebron, and Joseph arrived at Shechem.
A man came upon him as he was roaming about in the open country and asked him, “What are you looking for?”
“I am looking for my brothers,” he replied. “Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?”
The man answered, “They have moved on from here. I overheard them saying, ‘We will go to Dothan.’” Joseph went on after his brothers and came upon them at Dothan.
They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they plotted against him to kill him.
“Look,” they said to each other, “the dreamer is coming.{e}
Now is our chance. We will kill him and toss his body into one of these cisterns, and say a wild beast ate him. Then we will find out what his dreams come to!”
Reuben heard this and tried to save him from them. “We must not kill him,” he said.

“Do not spill his blood,” Reuben told them. “Put him down into this cistern out here in the desert, but keep your hands off him.” He meant to rescue Joseph from them and bring him back home to his father.
When Joseph reached his brothers, they tore off his coat, the long-sleeved coat he had on,
And they took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
They sat down to their meal. Glancing up, they spotted a line of Ishmaelite traders coming from Gilead, their camels loaded with gum, balm, and resin,{f} bound for Egypt.
Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And his brothers listened to him.

When Midianite merchants passed by, his brothers drew Joseph up out of the cistern, and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, about eight ounces.{g} So they brought Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes
He went back to his brothers and cried, “The boy is not there! And I, what am I to do now?”
They took Joseph’s coat, killed a young goat, and soaked the coat in its blood.
They had the long-sleeved coat carried to their father with the message, “We came across this. Look closely and see if it is your son’s coat.”{h}
Jacob knew it at once. “It is my son’s coat!” he cried. “Some savage beast has eaten him. Joseph has surely been torn apart!”
Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his waist and mourned for his son many days.
His sons and daughters all came to console him, but he would not be consoled. “I will go down mourning to my son in Sheol,”{i} he said. And his father wept for him.
In Egypt, meanwhile, the Midianites{j} sold Joseph to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh’s court officials{k} and commander of the guard.{l}

notes.text: Or “he was an assistant.” Hebrew na’ar can mean “youth” or “servant.”
Literally “brought their evil report to their father.” Brenton notes that some copies read “they brought an evil report of Joseph.”

Hebrew ketonet passim, also used of a princess’s robe in 2 Samuel 13:18–19. Passim may refer to long sleeves or a robe reaching to the hands and feet; its exact meaning is uncertain. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “a coat of many colours.”
Rachel had died (35:19). The dream may count her among the family as a whole, or this story may stand apart from the order of chapter 35.
Literally “this lord of dreams,” a mocking expression.
The precise identity of these resins is uncertain. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “spices, and resin, and myrrh,” and Brenton notes that one of the Greek words is literally “stacte.”

Hebrew “twenty of silver,” that is, twenty shekels (compare Leviticus 27:5), about 8 ounces (230 grams), counting a shekel as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); weight standards varied. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “twenty pieces of gold.” The verse names both Midianites and Ishmaelites as traders (compare 37:25, 36; 39:1; Judges 8:24), and it is not clear whether “they” who drew Joseph up were the brothers or the Midianites.
Hebrew haker-na, “please recognize.” The same words return in 38:25, when Tamar confronts Judah.
Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Hades.”
Hebrew Medanim, a variant spelling of Midianites; compare 25:2.
Hebrew saris, often “eunuch,” but also used of a high court officer, married or not (compare 39:1, 7). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the eunuch of Pharao.”
Or “chief of the executioners” or “chief butcher.” Brenton notes on 39:1 that the Greek reads “chief cook,” and that the Hebrew word can mean either a cook or a guardsman.

verses.text: At that time Judah left his brothers and went down, and turned aside to a certain Adullamite whose name was Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her and went in to her,
and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er.
She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan.
Once more she bore a son, Shelah. Judah was at Chezib{a} at the time of his birth.
And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of Yahweh, and Yahweh put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her,{b} and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew that any child would not be counted as his own. So each time he lay with his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed on the ground, to keep from giving his brother descendants.
His conduct displeased Yahweh, and Yahweh took his life as well.

Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up,” for he thought, “He too may die, like his brothers.” So Tamar departed and lived in the house of her father.
After many days Judah’s wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When his time of mourning was over, Judah went up with his friend Hirah of Adullam to the men who were shearing his sheep at Timnah.
And when Tamar was told, “Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep,”

she put away her widow’s clothing, covered her face with a veil, wrapped herself, and sat down at the gateway of Enaim,{c} beside the road to Timnah. She knew that Shelah was grown, yet she had not been given to him in marriage.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face.
Not knowing that she was his son’s wife, he went over to her by the road and said, “Come, let me sleep with you.” She asked, “What will you pay me to sleep with me?”
He said, “I will send you a kid from the flock.” And she said, “Only if you give a pledge until you send it.”
He said, “What pledge shall I give you?” She replied, “Your seal and your cord,{d} and your staff that is in your hand.” So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him.
She rose and left. She took off her veil and dressed again in her widow’s clothing.
Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend from Adullam, to get back the things he had left with the woman, but his friend could not find her.
And he asked the men of the place, “Where is the shrine woman{e} who was at Enaim by the roadside?” And they said, “No shrine woman has been here.”
He went back to Judah and said, “I did not find her; and the men of the place said, ‘There has been no shrine woman here.’”
Judah said, “Then she may keep what she has, or we will be made fools of. I did send the goat, after all, and you could not find her.”
About three months later Judah was told, “Tamar your daughter-in-law has played the prostitute. Moreover, she is pregnant by her prostitution.” And Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.”

While she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, “By the man who owns these things I am with child.” And she said, “Look closely{f} and see whose these are, this seal and cord, and this staff.”
Judah knew them and said, “She is more in the right than I am,{g} because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” He never slept with her again.
When her time to give birth came, it was found that she was carrying twins.
While she was in labor, one child stretched out a hand; the midwife took a scarlet thread, tied it around his hand, and said, “This one came out first.”
But he pulled his hand back, and out came his brother. She said, “So you have broken out!” And he was named Perez.{h}
Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.{i}

notes.text: Brenton’s Septuagint reads “she was in Chasbi when she bore them,” with Judah’s wife as the subject. Chezib is probably Achzib in the lowlands of Judah (Joshua 15:44).
The custom later called levirate marriage, in which a brother married a dead man’s widow to give the dead man an heir (Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Ruth 4).
Or “in an open place.” Enaim means “two springs” or “eyes”; Hebrew petach enayim can be read “the opening of the eyes.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “by the gates of Ænan.”

A cylinder or stamp seal worn on a cord around the neck, used to sign documents; the staff likely bore its owner’s marks. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Thy ring, and thy bracelet, and the staff,” and gives “necklace” as an alternative in his note.

Hebrew qedeshah, a woman associated with a shrine. Hirah uses this word, which may have sounded more respectable, though Judah had taken her for an ordinary prostitute (zonah, 38:15). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “harlot” in both places.
The same words used when Jacob was shown Joseph’s robe (37:32). The deceiver of his father is now deceived by a garment and a goat.
Or “She is in the right, not I.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Thamar is cleared rather than I.”
Perez means “breach” or “breaking out.” He became an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–22) and appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).
Zerah means “rising” or “brightness,” perhaps alluding to the scarlet thread.

verses.text: Now Joseph had been brought down into Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian who served Pharaoh as an official and commander of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelite traders who had taken him there.
Yahweh was with Joseph, and everything went well for him while he lived in the household of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that Yahweh was with him and that Yahweh made everything he did succeed in his hands.
Joseph won his master’s trust and became his personal servant. Potiphar put him over his household and handed everything he owned into his care.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; the blessing of Yahweh was on all that he had, in house and field.
Potiphar left everything he had in Joseph’s hands. With Joseph there, he gave no thought to anything except the bread he ate.{a} Joseph had a fine figure and a handsome face.{b}
And after a time his master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, “Lie with me.”
But Joseph refused. “Look,” he told his master’s wife, “my master trusts me so fully that he gives no thought to what goes on in the house. All he owns he has put into my hands.
No one in this house is greater than I am, and he has not kept anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How could I then do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
Though she pressed Joseph day after day, he would not give in to her and lie with her, or even be near her.
On a certain day he went into the house to do his work, and not one of the men of the household was there inside,
she caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me.” But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.
When she saw that he had run outside and left his cloak in her hands,
she called the men of her house and said to them, “Look, he has brought in among us a Hebrew man to make sport of us.{c} He came in to me to lie with me, but I screamed loudly.
When he heard me scream for help, he ran outside, leaving his cloak here with me.”
Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home,
Then she told him her tale: “That Hebrew slave you brought into our house came to me to toy with me.
When I screamed for help, he left his cloak with me and ran outside.”
Joseph’s master heard his wife’s account, “This is what your slave did to me,” and he was furious.{d}
And Joseph’s master took him and put him into the prison,{e} the place where the king’s prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.
Yahweh was with Joseph, extended steadfast love{f} to him, and granted him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
The chief jailer gave Joseph charge over everyone held in the prison, so that Joseph saw to everything that was done there.
The chief jailer did not trouble himself about anything under Joseph’s care, for Yahweh was with Joseph and gave success to all he did.

notes.text: Literally “except the bread that he ate.” This may mean that Potiphar kept charge of his own food, perhaps for reasons of Egyptian purity (compare 43:32), or it may be a euphemism for his wife (compare 39:9).
The same words are used of Rachel, Joseph’s mother, in 29:17. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “handsome in form, and exceedingly beautiful in countenance.”
Hebrew letsacheq, from the same root as Isaac’s name. Here it carries a sexual sense (compare 26:8). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “to mock us.”
The text does not say against whom his anger burned. That Joseph was imprisoned rather than executed may suggest that Potiphar had doubts.
Literally “the round house,” a word used only in this story (39:20–40:5). It may refer to a fortress prison.
Hebrew chesed, loyal love. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “poured down mercy upon him.”

verses.text: After a while, two servants of the king of Egypt, his cupbearer and his baker, gave offense to their master, the king.
Pharaoh was enraged at these two officials, his chief cupbearer and his chief baker.
and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined.
The commander of the guard assigned them to Joseph, who waited on them. They had been held there for some time
when the two of them, the king of Egypt’s cupbearer and baker who were held in the prison, both had dreams on the same night. Each man had his own dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
Joseph came in to them the next morning and saw that they looked downcast.
So he asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, “Why are your faces downcast today?”
They told him, “Each of us has had a dream, and nobody can explain it.” Joseph said, “Is it not God who explains dreams? Tell me about them.”
The chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream. “I dreamed,” he said, “that a grapevine stood in front of me,
with three branches on it. As soon as it put out buds, it burst into flower, and its bunches grew ripe grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh’s cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.”
Then Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head{a} and put you back in your post. You will hand Pharaoh his cup again, as you used to do when you were his cupbearer.
But when things go well for you, think of me. Be kind to me, speak of me to Pharaoh, and get me released from this place.
For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit.”{b}
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, “I also had a dream: there were three baskets of white bread{c} on my head,
In the top basket were baked goods of every kind for Pharaoh, but birds kept eating them out of the basket on my head.”
And Joseph answered and said, “This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift your head off you and hang you from a tree,{d} and the birds will eat the flesh from you.”
On the third day, Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a banquet for all his servants, and in the presence of his servants he lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker.
He put the chief cupbearer back in his post, and the cupbearer once again handed Pharaoh his cup.
But he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
But the chief cupbearer gave no thought to Joseph. He forgot all about him.

notes.text: An idiom for showing favor or for pardoning; also used of taking a census or a count. In 40:19 the phrase is turned grimly, “lift up your head from you,” and in 40:20 it is used in both senses at once.
Hebrew bor, “pit” or “dungeon,” the same word used of the pit into which his brothers threw him (37:24).
Or “baskets of white wicker” or “baskets with holes.” The meaning of Hebrew chori is uncertain. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “three baskets of mealy food.”
Or “impale you on a stake.” The body was displayed after death (compare Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “hang thee on a tree.”

verses.text: When two full years{a} had gone by, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing beside the Nile,{b}
and seven cows, attractive and fat, came up out of the Nile and grazed among the reeds.{c}
After them seven more cows came up from the river, wretched and lean, and they stood next to the first cows at the water’s edge.
The wretched, lean cows devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He went back to sleep and had a second dream. Seven heads of grain, full and fine, grew up on a single stem.
Behind them seven more heads came up, shriveled and burned by the east wind.{d}
The thin ears devoured the seven plump and full ears. Then Pharaoh woke, and behold, it was a dream.

So in the morning his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all the magicians{e} of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh.
The chief cupbearer spoke up and said to Pharaoh, “Today I must call to mind my faults.
Pharaoh was furious with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker under guard in the house of the captain of the guard,
One night each of us had a dream, he and I, and each dream carried its own meaning.
There was a Hebrew youth in that place with us, a slave of the commander of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he explained them, telling each of us what his own dream meant.
It all turned out just as he explained it to us. I was given back my post, and the other man was hanged.”
Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they hurried him out of the dungeon. He shaved, put on fresh clothing, and came into Pharaoh’s presence.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have had a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, “It is not in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”{f}
Pharaoh told Joseph, “In my dream I stood on the riverbank of the Nile.
Seven cows, fat and attractive, came up out of the Nile and grazed among the reeds.
Then seven other cows came up behind them, feeble and very ugly and thin, worse than any I had ever seen in all the land of Egypt.
And the lean and ugly cows ate up the first seven fat cows,
Yet after they had swallowed them, no one could tell they had swallowed anything. They looked as wretched as before. Then I woke up.
In my dream I saw too seven heads of grain, full and fine, coming up on a single stem.
Behind them seven more heads sprang up, shrunken, lean, and burned by the east wind,
and the thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. And I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me.”
Joseph told Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s two dreams have one meaning. God has made known to Pharaoh what he is going to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years; the dreams are one.
The seven thin and ugly cows that rose up behind them are seven years, and the seven ears, empty and scorched by the east wind, will be seven years of famine.
That is what I meant when I said to Pharaoh that God has let Pharaoh see what he is going to do.
There will come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt,
but seven years of famine will follow them, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine will devour the land,
The famine that follows will be so harsh that no one will remember the good years in the land.
Pharaoh was given the dream twice because God has firmly decided the matter, and God will soon carry it out.
So now Pharaoh should look for a man of understanding and wisdom and put him in charge of Egypt.
Pharaoh should also name officials throughout the land and collect a fifth of Egypt’s harvest in the seven years of plenty.{g}
They should gather all the food of the good years ahead and pile up grain in the towns under Pharaoh’s control, and guard it there as food.
This food will be held in store for the country, ready for the seven years of famine that will come upon Egypt, and the land will not be ruined by the famine.”
This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.
Pharaoh asked his officials, “Could we ever find another man like this, who has the spirit of God in him?”{h}
And Pharaoh told Joseph, “God has made all this known to you, so no one else has your understanding and wisdom.
You shall be over my house, and all my people shall be ruled by your word.{i} Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you.”
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, “See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh removed his signet ring from his own hand and placed it on Joseph’s hand; he dressed him in robes of fine linen and hung a chain of gold around his neck.
He had Joseph ride in the chariot of his second-in-command, and men shouted before him, “Abrek!”{j} In this way Pharaoh put him over the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh told Joseph, “I am Pharaoh. But no one in all Egypt will move hand or foot unless you allow it.”
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah.{k} He also gave him as wife Asenath,{l} daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.{m} And Joseph went forth over the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he took up his post before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He left Pharaoh’s presence and traveled throughout Egypt.
During the seven plentiful years the earth produced abundantly,
Joseph collected all the food grown in Egypt during those seven years and stored it in the towns, placing in each town the food from the fields that surrounded it.
The grain Joseph piled up was beyond counting, like the sand of the sea. In the end he gave up keeping records, because there was too much to measure.
Two sons were born to Joseph before the years of famine began. Their mother was Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, the priest of On.
Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh. “For,” he said, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”{n}
The name of the second he called Ephraim, “For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”{o}
The seven years of plenty that had been in the land of Egypt ended,
and the seven years of famine began to arrive, just as Joseph had said. Famine struck every land, but throughout the land of Egypt there was bread.
When the whole land of Egypt grew hungry, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph; do whatever he tells you.”
When famine covered the whole land, Joseph unsealed all the stores{p} and sold grain to the Egyptians, for the famine grew harsh in Egypt.
People from every land came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, since the famine was harsh throughout the world.

notes.text: Literally “two years of days.” Brenton notes the same idiom in the Greek.
Hebrew ye’or, an Egyptian word for the Nile or its channels. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the river.”
Hebrew achu, an Egyptian loanword for marsh grass, found also in Job 8:11. Brenton notes that the Septuagint keeps the word in Greek letters; his text renders it “sedge.”
The hot, dry wind from the desert, called the khamsin.
Hebrew chartummim, an Egyptian loanword for priestly scholars skilled in sacred writings and magic (compare Exodus 7:11). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “interpreters.”
Literally “God will answer the peace (shalom) of Pharaoh,” that is, an answer for his welfare. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Without God an answer of safety shall not be given to Pharao.”
Or “organize the land.” The verb may mean “take a fifth” or more generally “prepare.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “take up a fifth part.”
Or “a spirit of the gods.” Pharaoh, as an Egyptian, may mean it in the second sense. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the Spirit of God.”

Literally “at your mouth all my people shall kiss.” The meaning is uncertain; it may mean “do homage” or “be ruled.” Brenton notes that the Greek has “mouth,” and his text reads “all my people shall be obedient to thy word.”
Probably an Egyptian word, perhaps meaning “Attention!” or “Make way!” though it sounds like a Hebrew word for “kneel.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “a herald made proclamation before him.”
Probably an Egyptian name meaning “God speaks and he lives” or “the one who is called life.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Psonthomphanech.”
Asenath probably means “belonging to Neith,” an Egyptian goddess. The later Greek work Joseph and Aseneth tells of her conversion.
On is Heliopolis, a center of sun worship, near modern Cairo. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “priest of Heliopolis.” Potiphera, “the one whom Ra has given,” is a fuller form of Potiphar.
Manasseh sounds like nashshani, “he has made me forget.”
Ephraim sounds like hiphrani, “he has made me fruitful.”
Literally “all that was in them”; the Hebrew lacks a noun. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “all the granaries.”

verses.text: Jacob heard that grain could be bought in Egypt, and he said to his sons, “Why do you just stand there staring at each other?”
He told them, “I hear there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we can stay alive and not starve.”
So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt.
Jacob would not let Benjamin, Joseph’s full brother, go along with the others, for fear that something might befall him.
The sons of Israel were among those coming to buy, for the famine had come upon the land of Canaan as well.
Now Joseph governed the land, and he was the one selling grain to everyone who came. Joseph’s brothers came and bowed low before him, faces to the ground.
Joseph knew his brothers the moment he saw them, but he acted as a stranger{a} and spoke harshly. “Where are you from?” he asked. “From Canaan,” they replied, “to buy food.”
And Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph called to mind the dreams he had had about them. “You are spies!” he told them. “You came to find where our land lies open.”{b}
They said to him, “No, my lord, your servants have come to buy food.
We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies.”
“Not so,” he told them. “You came to find where our land lies open.”
And they said, “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan, and the youngest is now with our father, and one is no more.”
But Joseph answered, “What I said to you stands. You are spies!
In this way you will be tested: by the life of Pharaoh,{c} you shall not leave here unless your youngest brother comes.

Send one of your number back for your brother, and the rest of you stay here in chains. Your words will be put to the proof, to show whether there is any truth in you. Otherwise, by Pharaoh’s life, you are spies!”
Then he locked them all up under guard for three days.
On the third day Joseph told them, “I fear God. Do as I say, and you will live.
If you are honest men, let one brother stay behind, bound in the prison where you are held, while the others go home with grain for your hungry families.
Then bring your youngest brother back to me. That will prove your words true, and you will not die.” They agreed to this.

They said to one another, “We are surely being punished for what we did to our brother. We saw how he suffered when he pleaded with us for mercy, and we would not listen. That is why this suffering has come upon us.”
Reuben answered them, “Did I not warn you, ‘Do no wrong to the boy’? But you would not hear me. And now his blood is being demanded of us.”{d}
They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them.
Joseph turned aside from them and wept. Then he came back and talked with them, and he had Simeon taken from among them and tied up while they watched.
Joseph gave orders for their bags to be filled with grain, for the silver of each one to be returned to his own sack, and for food to be supplied for the journey. And it was done for them.
Then they loaded their donkeys with their grain and departed.
At the lodging place{e} one of them unfastened his sack to give his donkey fodder, and he saw his money—there it was in the mouth of his sack.
“My silver has been returned!” he called to his brothers. “Look, it is right here in my sack!” Their hearts sank. Shaking, they looked at each other and said, “What has God done to us?”
When they came to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan, they told him all that had happened to them, saying,
“The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly to us and took us to be spies of the land.
But we said to him, ‘We are honest men; we have never been spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.’
The man who is lord of the land said to us, ‘This is how I will know that you are honest: leave one of your brothers with me, take food for your starving households, and be on your way.
