Bring me your youngest brother, and then I will know that you are no spies but honest men. I will give your brother back to you, and you may do business in the land.’”
As they emptied their sacks, there was each man’s bundle of money in his sack. And when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid.
Jacob their father said to them, “You have taken my children from me. Joseph is lost, Simeon is lost, and now you would carry off Benjamin. All these things fall on me!”
Reuben told his father, “If I fail to bring him home to you, you may put my own two sons to death. Leave him in my care, and I will bring him back.”
Jacob answered, “No, my son is not going with you. His brother is dead and only he remains. Should any harm come to him on the way, you would bring my gray head down to Sheol in sorrow.”{f}

notes.text: Hebrew wayyitnakker, “he made himself a stranger,” a play on wayyakkirem, “he recognized them,” in the same verse.
That is, the weak and unguarded places of the land. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “to observe the marks of the land are ye come.”
An oath formula. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “by the health of Pharao.”
Literally “his blood is required.” Compare 9:5–6.
Hebrew malon, a place to spend the night, not necessarily a building.
Hebrew Sheol; see the note on 37:35. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “bring down my old age with sorrow to Hades.”

verses.text: Now the famine was severe in the land.
When the grain they had brought from Egypt was used up, their father told them, “Go back down and buy us a little more food.”
Judah said to him, “The man gave us a solemn warning: ‘You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.’
If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy you food.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down, for the man said to us, ‘You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.’”
Israel said, “Why did you bring this trouble on me by telling the man that you still had a brother?”

They said, “The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our kin. He asked, ‘Is your father alive? Do you have another brother?’ We simply answered what he asked. How could we know he would say, ‘Bring your brother down here’?”
And Judah said to Israel his father, “Send the boy with me, and we will get up and go, so that we may live and not die, both we and you and also our little ones.
I myself will be surety for him;{a} you may demand him at my hand. If I do not bring him to you and set him in your presence, I will have sinned against you all my days.
Had we not wasted all this time, we could have gone there and back twice by now.”

Then Israel their father said to them, “If it must be so, then do this: put some of the choicest produce of the land in your containers and take a present down to the man—some balm, some honey, resin, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds.{b}
Take twice the silver with you, and take back the silver that was put back in the openings of your sacks. It may have been a mistake.
Take also your brother, and get up, go again to the man.
May El Shaddai{c} give you mercy in the man’s sight, so that he releases your other brother to you, and Benjamin too. And I, if I am to be bereaved, then bereaved I will be.”
So the men took the gifts, twice the amount of silver, and Benjamin. They set off for Egypt and presented themselves to Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, “Bring the men into the house, and kill an animal and get it ready, for the men are going to eat with me at noon.”
The steward followed Joseph’s orders and took the men into Joseph’s house.

The men grew frightened when they were taken to Joseph’s house. “We are being brought in here because of the silver that went back into our sacks the last time,” they said. “He wants to attack us, overpower us, make slaves of us, and take our donkeys.”
So at the entrance of the house they went up to Joseph’s steward and spoke to him.
and said, “Please, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food.
But when we stopped for the night and opened our sacks, every man found his own silver in the top of his sack, the full weight of it. Now we have brought it back with us.
We have brought more silver as well, to buy food. We have no idea who put our silver back in our sacks.”
“All is well,{d}” he said. “There is nothing to fear. It was your God, the God of your father, who placed treasure in your sacks for you. Your silver reached me.” Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The steward took the men into Joseph’s house. He gave them water to wash their feet and gave feed to their donkeys.
they prepared the present for Joseph’s coming at noon, for they heard that they should eat bread there.
When Joseph came home, they brought him the present that was in their hands into the house, and bowed down to the ground before him.
And he inquired about their welfare and said, “Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?”
They answered, “Your servant our father is in good health; he is still living.” And they bent low and bowed down.
Looking up, he saw his brother Benjamin, his mother’s son, and asked, “Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about?” And he said, “May God be gracious to you, my son.”
Joseph hurried away, deeply stirred at the sight of his brother, and looked for somewhere to weep. He went to his private room and wept there.
After washing his face he came out again. Holding himself in check, he said, “Bring in the meal.”

They set a place for him by himself, for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because Egyptians could not eat bread with Hebrews; it is an abomination to Egypt.{e}
And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men looked at one another in amazement.
Joseph had servings carried to them from his own table, and Benjamin’s serving was five times larger than anyone else’s.{f} So they feasted and drank freely with him.{g}

notes.text: Hebrew e‘ervennu, “I will be his guarantor.” Judah offers himself as guarantor; he later fulfills this pledge in 44:32–34.
Several of these items appear in 37:25 as the goods of the traders who carried Joseph to Egypt. Brenton’s Septuagint lists “gum and honey, and frankincense, and stacte, and turpentine, and walnuts.”
Traditionally “God Almighty”; see the note on El Shaddai at 17:1. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “my God.”

Hebrew shalom lakhem, a greeting that also reassures: “All is well with you.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “God deal mercifully with you,” and Brenton explains the steward’s last words as meaning that he was satisfied with the money paid.
Greek historians also report that Egyptians avoided eating with foreigners. Compare 46:34.
Literally “five hands,” meaning five times as much. Brenton notes that the Greek says it “was magnified beyond the portions of all five times.”
Literally “drank and became drunk with him,” that is, drank freely.

verses.text: He ordered the steward of his house, “Fill the sacks of the men with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in the mouth of his sack,
Put my cup, the silver one, in the top of the youngest one’s sack, along with the silver he paid for his grain.” The steward did what Joseph said.
As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away with their donkeys.
They were not far from the city when Joseph told his steward, “Go after those men at once. When you catch up with them, ask them, ‘Why have you paid back good with evil?
Is this not the cup my lord drinks from, the one he uses to read omens?{a} What you have done is wicked.’”
When he overtook them, he spoke to them these words.
They said to him, “Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing!
Why, we even brought back to you from Canaan the silver we found in the tops of our sacks. Why would we steal silver or gold from your master’s house?
If any of us, your servants, is found to have it, he must die, and the rest of us will be slaves to my lord.”
“Very well, then,” he said, “as you say. But only the one who is found with it will be my slave. The rest of you will go free.”
Then each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground, and each man opened his sack.
He began the search with the oldest and finished with the youngest, and the cup turned up in Benjamin’s sack.
They ripped their garments in grief. Each man loaded his donkey again, and they went back to the city.
Joseph was still at home when Judah and his brothers arrived, and they threw themselves on the ground before him.
Joseph asked them, “What have you done? Surely you knew that a man such as I can read omens?”

Judah said, “What can we say to my lord? How can we speak, and how can we prove ourselves innocent? God has uncovered the guilt of your servants. See, we are my lord’s servants, we and the one in whose hand the cup was found.”
But Joseph said, “I would never do that! Only the man who had the cup will be my slave. The rest of you may return in peace to your father.”
Then Judah approached him and said, “Pardon me, my lord; permit your servant to say a word in the ears of my lord, and let your wrath not burn hot against your servant, for you are as Pharaoh.
My lord asked his servants, saying, ‘Have you a father, or a brother?’
We said to my lord, ‘We have a father, an old man, and a young child born in his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loves him.’
Then you said to your servants, ‘Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.’
We said to my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.’
But you told your servants, ‘Your youngest brother must come down with you, or you will never see my face again.’
When we went back to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.
And when our father said, ‘Go again, buy us a little food,’
we said, ‘We are not able to go down. If our youngest brother is with us, then we shall go down, for we cannot see the man’s face unless our youngest brother is with us.’
Then your servant my father said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons.
The one went out from me, and I said, “Surely he has been torn to pieces,” and I have not seen him since.
If you take this one from me too, and some harm befalls him, you will bring my gray head down to Sheol in misery.’{b}
So now, when I go to my father, your servant, and the boy is not with us, since his life is bound up with the boy’s life,{c} then,
as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol.
Your servant gave my father a pledge for the boy’s safety. I said, ‘If I fail to bring him home to you, I will bear the guilt before my father all my days.’
So now, I pray, let your servant stay instead of the boy as a slave to my lord, and let the boy go up with his brothers.{d}
How could I go back up to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see the misery it would bring on my father.”

notes.text: Divination by cup was practiced by watching the patterns of oil or other liquids on water. Joseph may only be claiming the power to keep up his disguise (compare 44:15). Brenton’s Septuagint adds at the start of this verse, “Why have ye stolen my silver cup?”
Hebrew Sheol; see the note on 37:35. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “to the grave,” and Brenton notes that the Greek is “Hades.” The same applies in 44:31.
Literally “his soul is bound up with his soul.” Compare the language of love in 1 Samuel 18:1.
Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph as a slave (37:26–27), now offers himself as a slave in place of Rachel’s other son.

verses.text: Joseph could no longer keep control of himself before everyone standing around him. “Have them all leave my presence!” he called out. So none of them were there with him when Joseph revealed himself to his brothers.
His weeping was so loud that the Egyptians heard it, and the news reached Pharaoh’s house.
Joseph told his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still living?” His brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence.
“Please come closer,” Joseph told them, and they came closer. “I am Joseph, your brother,” he said, “the one you sold to be taken to Egypt.
Now do not be grieved, and do not let it burn in your eyes that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
Two years now the famine has gripped the land, and five more years are coming when no one will plow or reap.
God sent me here before you to make sure you would have descendants left on the earth, and to save your lives in a great deliverance.{a}
So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh,{b} and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Go quickly back to my father and tell him, ‘Your son Joseph says this: God has made me master over all Egypt. Come down to me without waiting.
You will settle in the region of Goshen{c} and be close to me, you, your sons, and your grandsons, with your sheep and cattle and everything you own.
I will take care of you there, for five years of famine are still ahead. Otherwise you and your family and all that is yours will be reduced to want.’
And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you.
Tell my father how greatly I am honored in Egypt, and tell him everything you have seen. Then bring my father down here quickly.”
Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck.
He kissed each of his brothers and wept over them; and afterward his brothers spoke with him.
The news reached Pharaoh’s house: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” And it was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and of his servants.
Pharaoh told Joseph, “Give your brothers these orders: ‘Load up your animals and return to Canaan.
Bring your father and your households to me, and I will give you the best part of Egypt’s land; you shall eat the fat of the land.’
And you are ordered to do this: take wagons out of the land of Egypt for your little ones and your wives, and bring your father and come.
Do not worry about leaving your belongings behind, for the finest of all Egypt will be yours.’”
The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons at Pharaoh’s command, and he also gave them food for the road.
He gave every one of them a new set of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver, about seven and a half pounds, and five sets of clothes.{d}
He sent to his father these things: ten donkeys carrying the best goods of Egypt, and ten female donkeys carrying grain, bread, and food for his father along the way.
Thus he dismissed his brothers, and they set out; he said to them, “Do not fall out with one another{e} on the road.”
So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob.
And they told him, “Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt.” And Jacob’s heart went numb,{f} for he did not believe them.
But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived.
And Israel said, “It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.”

notes.text: Or “to keep alive for you many survivors.” The words “remnant” and “survivors” later become key words in the prophets for those whom God preserves.
A title for a chief adviser of the king; compare Egyptian titles such as “father of the god.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “as a father of Pharao.”
Goshen was in the eastern Nile Delta. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the land of Gesem of Arabia.”

Hebrew “three hundred of silver,” that is, three hundred shekels, about 7½ pounds (3.4 kilograms), counting a shekel as about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); weight standards varied. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “three hundred pieces of gold.” Compare 37:28, where Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver.
Or “do not be agitated” or “do not be afraid.” The Hebrew verb ragaz means to tremble, whether with anger or fear. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Be not angry by the way.”
Literally “his heart grew cold.” Brenton notes that the Greek reads “amazed in mind.”

verses.text: So Israel set out with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, “Jacob, Jacob.” And he said, “Here I am.”
He said, “I am God,{a} your father’s God. Have no fear of going down into Egypt, for I will make a great nation of you there.
I will go down to Egypt with you myself, and I will bring you back up again without fail. And Joseph’s own hand will close your eyes.”
Jacob left Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried their father Jacob, with their little ones and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent for his transport.
They took their cattle and the possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and they entered Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him,
his sons and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters and his sons’ daughters; he brought all his offspring with him to Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt—Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn,
and the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.{b}
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan); and the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob,{c} and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah, born to Jacob in Paddan-aram, along with his daughter Dinah; the total of his sons and daughters was thirty-three.{d}
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah, with Serah their sister. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter; and these she bore to Jacob, sixteen persons.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
And to Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, bore to him.{e}
And the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.{f}
These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob, fourteen persons in all.
The son{g} of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob, seven persons in all.
All the persons who came with Jacob into Egypt, his own offspring,{h} apart from the wives of Jacob’s sons, numbered sixty-six persons.
Joseph’s sons, who were born to him in Egypt, numbered two. In all, the persons of the house of Jacob who came to Egypt numbered seventy.{i}
Jacob sent Judah on ahead to Joseph, so that Joseph could guide him to Goshen.{j} And they arrived in the region of Goshen.
Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while.
Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.”
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, ‘My brothers and my father’s household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.’
So when Pharaoh summons you and asks, ‘What work do you do?’

you shall say, ‘Your servants have been herdsmen from our youth until now, we and our fathers alike,’ so that you may settle in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.”{k}

notes.text: Hebrew ha’el, “the God,” or “El.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I am the God of thy fathers.”
The lists of Simeon’s sons in Numbers 26:12–13 and 1 Chronicles 4:24 differ: Jemuel is called Nemuel there, and Ohad is not named.
Called Jashub in Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1, and some ancient witnesses are reported to read Jashub here as well.
The total includes Jacob himself and Dinah, but not Er and Onan, who had died (compare 46:12).
Brenton’s Septuagint adds here the sons of Manasseh and Ephraim: “Machir. And Machir begot Galaad,” and “Sutalaam, and Taam. And the sons of Sutalaam; Edom.” Compare Numbers 26:29–36.
Brenton’s Septuagint arranges this list differently, making Gera, Noeman, Anchis, Ros, and Mamphim sons of Bela, and adding “Gera begot Arad.” Compare Numbers 26:38–40 and 1 Chronicles 8:1–5.
Hebrew “sons,” although only one is named. Called Shuham in Numbers 26:42.
Literally “who came out from his thigh.” Brenton notes that the Greek reads “thighs.”

Brenton’s Septuagint reads “The sons of Joseph… were nine souls” and gives the total as “seventy-five souls,” counting the descendants it adds in 46:20. Stephen follows this number in Acts 7:14, and some other ancient witnesses are reported to read seventy-five in Exodus 1:5 as well. Seventy is the number of the nations in chapter 10.
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “to meet him to the city of Heroes, into the land of Ramesses.” Heroopolis was a city in the eastern Nile Delta.
Compare 43:32. Joseph’s advice keeps his family apart in Goshen, where they can remain a distinct people.

verses.text: Joseph went to Pharaoh and told him, “My father and brothers have arrived from Canaan with their sheep and cattle and all their goods. They are in the region of Goshen now.”
And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” And they said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were.”

They said to Pharaoh, “We have come to sojourn in the land, for your servants’ flocks have no pasture, because the famine is heavy in the land of Canaan. Now, please, let your servants live in the land of Goshen.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Your father and your brothers have come to you here.{a}

The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them live in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock.”
Joseph brought his father Jacob in and presented him to Pharaoh, and Jacob gave Pharaoh his blessing.{b}
And Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How many are the days of the years of your life?”

And Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojourning{c} are a hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning.”
And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.
Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses,{d} as Pharaoh had commanded.
Joseph supplied food to his father, his brothers, and all his father’s family, as much as each household needed for its little ones.{e}
There was no food anywhere in the land, for the famine was extremely severe, and the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan were worn out because of the famine.
Joseph took in all the silver to be found in Egypt and Canaan as payment for the grain people bought, and he brought the silver to Pharaoh’s palace.
When the silver of Egypt and Canaan had run out, all Egypt came to Joseph and said, “Give us bread! Must we die in front of you because we have no silver left?”
“Then bring me your animals,” Joseph said. “Since your silver has run out, I will trade you food for your livestock.”
They brought their animals to Joseph, and he gave them food for their horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and donkeys. Through that year he fed them in return for all their herds.

When that year had passed, they came to him the next year and said to him, “We cannot conceal from my lord that our money is gone and the herds of cattle belong to my lord; nothing remains before my lord except our bodies and our land.

Why should we perish in front of you, we and our land as well? Take us and our land in payment for bread. We and our fields will belong to Pharaoh. Only give us seed, so that we may live and not die, and our land not be left barren.”
So Joseph acquired all the farmland of Egypt for Pharaoh. Every Egyptian sold his field, because the famine pressed so hard on them, and the land came into Pharaoh’s hands.
He moved the people to the cities,{f} from one end of the territory of Egypt to the other.
The priests’ land was the only land he did not acquire. The priests received a set portion from Pharaoh and lived on what he allotted them, so they had no need to sell their land.
Joseph told the people, “Today I have acquired you and your land for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you. Plant the fields.
When the crops come in, a fifth part goes to Pharaoh. Four parts will be yours, as seed for the fields and as food for yourselves, your households, and your children.”
“You have kept us alive,” they said. “If it pleases my lord, we will be Pharaoh’s servants.”
Joseph made this a law for the land of Egypt, still in force today: a fifth belongs to Pharaoh. Only the priests’ land never passed to Pharaoh.{g}
So Israel made his home in Egypt, in Goshen. They held land there, bore many children, and increased greatly.
And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were a hundred and forty-seven years.

As the time of Israel’s death came near, he called for his son Joseph and said, “If you care for me, place your hand under my thigh{h} and swear to treat me with faithful love. Do not bury me in Egypt.
When I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their grave.” Joseph replied, “I will do as you ask.”
“Swear to me,” he said, and Joseph swore to him. Then Israel bowed down at the head of the bed.{i}

notes.text: Brenton’s Septuagint arranges 47:5–6 differently, with Pharaoh’s reply to the brothers’ request and his words to Joseph in another order.
Or “greeted Pharaoh.” The Hebrew verb barakh can mean a formal greeting or farewell (compare 47:10), but the narrative gives it the weight of the promise in 12:3.
Or “my life as a foreigner,” from the same root as ger, “foreigner” or “resident alien.” Compare Hebrews 11:13.
Rameses was a city of the eastern Nile Delta, named after the later kings called Ramesses (compare Exodus 1:11). The name may update an older place name for later readers.
Literally “according to the mouth of the little ones.”

Or “he made slaves of them,” as Brenton’s Septuagint reads: “he brought the people into bondage to him, for servants.” The Hebrew words for the two readings look alike, and the Samaritan Pentateuch is reported to agree with the Septuagint.
Records from Egypt show land held by the crown and by the temples, and a tax on harvests, though the exact rate varied.
A solemn form of oath; see the note on 24:2.

Hebrew mittah, “bed.” With different vowels the same letters read matteh, “staff.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Israel did reverence, leaning on the top of his staff,” and Hebrews 11:21 quotes this form.

verses.text: Some time later Joseph was told, “Your father is sick.” He took his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him.
Someone told Jacob, “Look, your son Joseph has come to see you.” Israel summoned his strength and sat up on the bed.
And Jacob said to Joseph, “El Shaddai{a} appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,
and said to me, ‘I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples, and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.’
Now your two sons, born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are.
Any children born to you after them will be yours; in their inheritance they will be named after their brothers.{b}

As for me, when I was coming from Paddan, Rachel died beside me, to my sorrow, in the land of Canaan on the road, while there was still some distance{c} to go to Ephrath; I buried her there on the road to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).”
Israel caught sight of Joseph’s sons and asked, “Whose are these?”
Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” He said, “Bring them to me, I pray, and let me bless them.”
Israel’s eyes had grown dim with old age, so that he could hardly see. Joseph brought the boys close to him, and he kissed them and held them in his arms.
And Israel said to Joseph, “I never expected to see your face; and now God has let me see your offspring also.”
Then Joseph brought them out from between his knees,{d} and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near him.

But Israel reached out his right hand and placed it on Ephraim’s head, though he was the younger, and placed his left hand on Manasseh’s head. He crossed his hands on purpose,{e} although Manasseh was the firstborn.
And he blessed Joseph and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd{f} all my life long to this day,

the angel who has rescued{g} me from every harm, may he bless these boys. Through them may my name live on, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. May they increase into a great host upon the earth.”
When Joseph noticed his father’s right hand resting on the younger boy, Ephraim, it troubled him. He grasped his father’s hand to move it over to Manasseh’s head.
“No, my father,” Joseph said, “this is the firstborn. Place your right hand on his head.”

His father refused and said, “I am aware of it, my son, I am aware. From him also a people will arise, and he also will be great; yet his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will become a multitude{h} of nations.”
He blessed them on that day and said, “Israel will use your names in blessing, saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” So he set Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am dying, but God will be with you and will bring you back to your fathers’ land.
And to you, above your brothers, I give one shoulder of land,{i} which I seized with sword and bow from the hand of the Amorites.”

notes.text: Traditionally “God Almighty”; see the note on El Shaddai at 17:1.
Later children of Joseph are to be counted under Ephraim and Manasseh, not as tribes of their own.
Literally “a stretch of land” (compare 35:16). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “as I drew nigh to the horse-course of Chabratha of the land of Chanaan.”
That is, from Jacob’s knees, where they had been set as a sign that he received them as his own (compare 30:3; 50:23). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “they did reverence to him.”
Or “acting wisely with his hands.” The Hebrew verb can mean “to cross” or “to act with understanding.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “guiding his hands crosswise.”
Or “who has fed me.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “the God who continues to feed me.”
Hebrew go’el, the family member who rescues a relative, buys back land, or avenges blood. This is the first use of the word in the Bible.
Literally “fullness.”

Hebrew shekhem, “shoulder” or “ridge,” which is also the name of the city Shechem (compare 33:18–19; Joshua 24:32; John 4:5). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “I give to thee Sicima, a select portion above thy brethren.”

verses.text: Then Jacob called his sons and said, “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in the last days.{a}
Assemble and listen, O sons of Jacob, listen to Israel your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn,{b} my might and the beginning of my strength, excelling in dignity and excelling in power.
Unstable{c} as water, you will not keep first place, for you climbed into your father’s bed and defiled it. Onto my couch he climbed!
Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords.{d}
Into their council let my soul not enter; with their assembly, my glory,{e} do not unite. For in their anger they slew men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen.{f}
Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel.{g} I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you.{h} Your hand will grip your enemies by the neck. Your father’s sons will bow low before you.
Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up.{i} He crouched, he lay down like a lion, and like a lioness; who dares rouse him?
The scepter will not leave Judah, nor the staff of command from between his feet,{j} until Shiloh comes,{k} and the peoples will obey him.
He ties his foal to the vine and his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he washes his garments in wine, his robe in the blood of grapes.
His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.{l}
Zebulun will live by the seashore. Ships will find shelter with him, and his border will run toward Sidon.
Issachar is a sturdy donkey,{m} lying down among the saddlebags.
When he saw how good his resting place was, and how pleasant his land, he lowered his shoulder to the load and became a laborer under forced service.
Dan shall judge{n} his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan shall be a snake beside the road, a viper along the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.
I wait for your salvation, Yahweh.
Gad: raiders shall raid him, but he shall raid at their heels.{o}
Asher’s bread will be rich, and he will provide food fit for a king.
Naphtali is a deer set free, who gives birth to beautiful fawns.{p}
Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall.{q}
The archers savagely assailed him; they shot at him and pressed him hard,
yet his bow remained steady; his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, from there, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel,{r}
by the God of your father, who will help you, and by Shaddai,{s} who will bless you: blessings of the heavens above, blessings of the abyss that lies below, blessings of the breasts and of the womb.

Your father’s blessings are greater than the blessings of the age-old mountains, greater than the riches of the lasting hills.{t} May they rest on Joseph’s head, on the crown of the one who was set apart{u} among his brothers.
Benjamin is a wolf that tears its prey. In the morning he eats what he has caught, and in the evening he shares out the plunder.”
These are all the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them when he blessed them. He gave each one the blessing that belonged to him.
Then he commanded them and said to them, “I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
in the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre in Canaan. Abraham bought it along with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site of his own.
There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah,
the field and the cave that is in it, which were bought from the sons of Heth.”
When Jacob had finished giving his sons their charge, he gathered his feet up onto the bed, breathed out his life, and was gathered to his people.

notes.text: Or “in days to come.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “in the last days.”
Brenton notes that “thou my first-born” may also be read as an address, since the Greek does not always distinguish the two forms.
Or “boiling over” or “reckless.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “insolent like water.” Reuben’s act is told in 35:22.
The Hebrew word translated “swords” is rare and uncertain. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “accomplished the injustice of their cutting off.” Compare chapter 34.
Or “my heart” or “my soul,” reading a Hebrew word with different vowels (compare Psalm 16:9).
Literally “hamstrung an ox.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “houghed a bull.”

Brenton notes that the Greek for “cruel” is more literally “hardened” or “aggravated.” Levi was later scattered among the cities of Israel (Joshua 21), and Simeon’s land lay within Judah (Joshua 19:1–9).
A play on the name Judah, “praise” (compare 29:35).
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “from the tender plant, my son, thou art gone up.”
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “nor a prince from his loins,” and Brenton notes that the Greek reads “thighs.”

Or “until tribute comes to him,” or “until he comes to whom it belongs,” dividing or pointing the Hebrew letters differently. Shiloh was also the name of the town where the tabernacle later stood. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “until there come the things stored up for him; and he is the expectation of nations.” Many Jewish and Christian interpreters have read this verse as a promise of the Messiah.
Or “Dark are his eyes from wine, and white his teeth from milk.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “His eyes shall be more cheering than wine.”
Literally “a donkey of bone.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Issachar has desired that which is good; resting between the inheritances.”
A play on the name Dan, “judge” (compare 30:6).
A play on the name Gad, which sounds like the Hebrew words for “raiders” and “raid.”
Or “who gives beautiful words.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Nephthalim is a spreading stem, bestowing beauty on its fruit.”

The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. Or “Joseph is a wild donkey’s colt, a wild colt by a spring; wild donkeys on the ridge.” “Fruitful” plays on the name Ephraim (compare 41:52). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Joseph is a son increased; my dearly loved son is increased; my youngest son, turn to me.”

“The Mighty One of Jacob” is Hebrew abir ya‘aqov, a title of God. The next words may also be read “from there is the Shepherd.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “thence is he that strengthened Israel from the God of thy father.”
Shaddai, traditionally “the Almighty”; see the note on 17:1. Brenton’s Septuagint reads “and my God helped thee.”
Or “mightier than the blessings of my forebears, to the bounds of the everlasting hills,” reading the Hebrew words differently.
Hebrew nazir, “one set apart” or “one consecrated,” the word later used for a Nazirite (Numbers 6). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “of whom he took the lead.”

verses.text: Joseph threw himself on his father’s face, weeping over him and kissing him.
And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel.
The embalming took forty days, the full time it requires, and the Egyptians mourned for Jacob seventy days.{a}
And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,
‘My father had me take an oath. He said, “I am dying. Bury me in the grave I dug for myself{b} in Canaan.” So let me go up now and bury my father, and then I will come back.’”
Pharaoh replied, “Go and bury your father, just as you swore to him.”
Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went up all of Pharaoh’s servants, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
Joseph’s whole household went too, with his brothers and his father’s household. Only their little ones, their sheep, and their cattle stayed behind in Goshen.
And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.
They came to the threshing floor of Atad, across the Jordan, and there they mourned with a very great and heavy lamentation; and he observed seven days of mourning for his father.

The Canaanites living there saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad and said, “The Egyptians are mourning bitterly here.” For this reason the place, which lies across the Jordan, was named Abel-mizraim.{c}
So Jacob’s sons carried out his instructions.
They took him to Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre, the cave Abraham had bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site of his own.
Once his father was buried, Joseph went back to Egypt, together with his brothers and everyone who had gone with him for the burial.
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph hates us and pays us back in full for all the evil that we did to him?”
They sent word to Joseph: “Before his death your father gave us this instruction:

‘This is what you shall say to Joseph: “Please forgive{d} your brothers’ transgression and their sin, for they treated you badly.” So now, please pardon the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept while they spoke to him.
Then his brothers came themselves and threw themselves down in front of him. “We are your slaves,” they said.
Joseph told them, “Do not fear. Am I in God’s place?{e}
As for you, you planned evil against me, but God planned it for good, to bring about what is happening today, the saving of many people alive.{f}
So now, do not be afraid. I myself will sustain you and your little ones.” He comforted them and spoke to their hearts with kindness.
Joseph stayed in Egypt, he and his father’s house, and Joseph lived one hundred ten years.{g}
And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were born upon Joseph’s knees.{h}
Joseph told his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land he promised by oath to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”
Joseph had the sons of Israel swear an oath. “God will surely take note of you,” he said, “and then you must bring my bones up from this place.”{i}
So Joseph died, being a hundred and ten years old. They embalmed him,{j} and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.

notes.text: Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Egypt mourned for him seventy days.” Egyptian sources also describe a long period of embalming and mourning, especially for persons of rank.
Or “that I bought for myself.” The Hebrew verb can mean either “dig” or “buy” (compare 23:16–20). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “which I dug for myself.”
Abel-mizraim sounds like “mourning of Egypt” but means “meadow of Egypt.” Brenton’s Septuagint reads “The mourning of Egypt.”
Literally “lift up” or “bear.” Brenton notes that the Greek is literally “accept.”
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “Fear not, for I am God’s.”
Brenton’s Septuagint reads “that much people might be fed.” Compare 45:5–8.
A hundred and ten years was the Egyptian ideal of a full and blessed life. Joshua also dies at this age (Joshua 24:29).
A sign that Joseph received them into his family (compare 30:3; 48:12). Brenton’s Septuagint reads “were borne on the sides of Joseph,” and Brenton notes that the Greek reads “thighs.”
Compare Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32; Hebrews 11:22.

Brenton notes that the Greek reads “buried him” here, though his text reads “they prepared his corpse.” Genesis ends with the hope of 50:24: God will visit his people and bring them to the promised land.
